# EPIGRAMMA
### AGAINST
## ZOILUS. <note>Zoilus was a Greek grammarian known as the "scourge of Homer" for his harsh criticism; his name became a common term for a spiteful or nitpicking critic.</note>

> *O envious one, who always seeks to violate virtue,*
> *And always has your teeth in another’s skin.*
> *These things are not measured by just any man’s scale,*
> *These things were found blameless by the Sages <note>original: "Sophis"</note> of the past.*
> *They are not to be attacked rashly by anyone’s unbridled whip <note>original: "mastige," from the Greek word for whip or scourge</note>,*
> *Therefore, do no harm here, or else teach us better.*
> *Guelders <note>original: "Gelria"</note> is my fatherland, but Venlo <note>original: "Venloa"</note> is my own soil,*
> *Know that I speak only according to the law given to me.*
> *Yet do not turn your face away from this pitch-black little staff <note>likely referring to the writer's pen or the printed lines</note>,*
> *But rather read; perhaps what you itch for will be found within,*
> *And do not bring your censure upon it with a gloomy grin,*
> *Unless the final page has been read by you.*

# A Word to the Fit Reader
### A Brief Interjection.

1. My judicious brother, because there is today an infinite wantonness for speaking ill, and I myself have more than once been heavily lashed in this regard—simply because I had occasionally produced some works of my late-night studies for the public good—it happened perhaps that some things were included which were meant <term>metaleptically</term><note>original: "metalepticè"; a rhetorical figure where one thing is inferred from another</note> or <term>tropologically</term><note>original: "tropologicè"; a figurative or metaphorical interpretation, often used in biblical exegesis</note>. These were not immediately obvious to everyone’s grasp, and yet I had not added an index for the more recondite words and phrases. Therefore, having now been made more cautious by my own injury, I have proposed to set down <term>glosses</term><note>original: "gloſſemata"; explanatory notes or interpretations</note> and paragraphs for the more abstruse vocabulary and the sharper sentiments.

2. For there are some who are so superficial in their knowledge, and so stubborn, that they easily condemn, nitpick, and utterly despise everything which they themselves do not know or do not perceive. They approve or endorse nothing except solely that which has been known and discovered by themselves. As soon as a construction or a word occurs which they perhaps do not grasp at first glance, they say: "This is made up; it is not accepted Latin, because I have never read nor heard this before." By this, they wish to indicate clearly enough that it is therefore not to be tolerated at all. Truly a clever saying, worthy of the mouth of a Plato or a Socrates! As if, indeed, these little glory-seekers and gluttonous readers—or "all-knowing" men with large noses—ought to have read or heard everything that lies hidden in the wide-roaming field of Latinity, which one may rightly call a most profound ocean, scarcely explorable even with the measuring line of all our years.

3. Nevertheless, the <term>malignant habit</term><note>original: "cacoëthes"; a Greek-derived term for an incurable itch or bad habit</note> of slandering and the poison of envy so spread and grow cancerous, that he who brings his works to light in the present face of this ulcerated age seems to do nothing more than prepare a sort of banquet for detractors and malevolent men. These men tear apart and gnaw at everything that is served—I do not say merely with sour, stinging tongues and bites, but with violent outbursts and <term>Theonine teeth</term><note>original: "Theoninis dentibus"; a classical reference to Theon, a notoriously sharp-tongued critic in Rome, symbolizing vicious slander</note>—not only those things which displease them...

<summary>The author defends his use of complex Latin and figurative language against "superficial" critics, announcing his intent to provide explanatory glosses to prevent further misunderstanding and slander.</summary>
<keywords>preface, Latinity, literary criticism, rhetoric, tropes, glosses, envy, Theonine teeth</keywords>

# A Fitting Interlude

not only [those things], but even those which are greatly pleasing from time to time; they are not unlike cats, which are accustomed to snarl at someone all the more fiercely the more elegant the morsel they feel has been offered to them. For as human dispositions are now, by Hercules, no matter, no business, or no small work is undertaken for such just causes that there are not those present who would mark it with a spit <note>original: "obelent" — to mark a passage as spurious or doubtful with an obelus (†)</note> or prick it with their stings.

->*By Pollux, no one shall go safer than Antimachus, nor Homer,*<-
->*And envious Fate <note>original: "Parca" — one of the Fates in Roman mythology</note> even twitches at the great Gods.*<-

4. It happened not so long ago, about a year ago, that that treatise on universal medicine <term>universal medicine: a hypothetical alchemical remedy, often called the Elixir or Panacea, capable of curing all diseases</term>, which is woven in here at the end of the book, and was translated by me in London, England, from German into Latin, was shown to certain men most highly skilled in the affairs of nature and both arts <note>likely referring to the "arts" of medicine and alchemy</note> to be examined; they were to give their judgment and their vote as to whether it was worthy to be struck by the printing types or not. Among them, the greater part were Doctors, some even divine, and no less conspicuous in lineage than in wisdom.

5. Among these men, I had intended in my mind to attach a dedication of that aforementioned treatise to one who was very sickly, and is now altogether dead (but otherwise a very great Lover of Learning <note>original: "Philomago"</note>, a Patron of the muses, and almost an equal to Hermes <note>referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary father of alchemy</note>). This was because he had known me to some extent, and I him. Hence, I had composed for that purpose another somewhat more secret little note <note>original: "pictatium"</note>, in which, in plain and not lengthy discourse (on account of a certain special reason known only to God and myself), I had communicated to him my own true mind regarding the Invention of the Philosophers <term>Invention of the Philosophers: the discovery of the Philosopher's Stone</term>. Therefore, I imagined deep down that the matter would turn out entirely according to my wish.

6. But alas, how often the firm hopes of mortals tend toward the contrary! For three or four days later, when I asked the printer whether he had any resolution regarding that work, he replied that a "black bean" had fallen between them <note>original: "fabam nigram" — an ancient Greek method of voting for condemnation or rejection</note>; it was judged and shouted out that that translation was not good Latin, but was teeming with barbarisms <term>barbarisms: non-standard or "corrupt" use of language, often a critique by Renaissance humanists against medieval or technical Latin</term> and lacked flavor. In that work, however (although the whole thing was completed within more or less a fleeting [period]), except for the title alone and a very few [words]...

# A Fitting Word to the Reader
->An Interlude.<-

<margin>1.</margin> My judicious brother, because today there is an infinite lewdness for speaking ill, and I myself have more than once been heavily lashed in this regard—simply because I had occasionally produced some works of my midnight vigils for the public good—it happened that some things were included which were taken <term>metaleptically</term><note>original: "metalepticè"; a rhetorical figure where one thing is substituted for another through a chain of associations</note> or <term>tropologically</term><note>original: "tropologicè"; a figurative or metaphorical interpretation, often used in biblical exegesis to find moral meaning</note>. These were not immediately obvious to everyone’s grasp, and yet I had not added an index for the more recondite words and phrases. Therefore, having now been made more cautious by my own injury, I have proposed to provide <gloss>interpretations</gloss> and <gloss>explanatory notes</gloss> for the more abstruse vocabulary and the more acute sentiments.

<margin>2.</margin> For there are some so half-learned and so stubborn that they easily condemn, twitch at, and spit upon everything which they themselves do not know or perceive. They approve or assent to nothing except solely that which has been known and discovered by them personally. As soon as a syntax or a word occurs which they perhaps do not grasp at first glance, they say: "This is made up; it is not accepted Latin, because I have never read nor heard this before." By this, they wish to indicate quite clearly that it is therefore not to be tolerated at all. Truly a clever saying, worthy of the mouth of a Plato or a Socrates! As if, indeed, these little glory-seekers and gluttonous readers—or "all-wise" men with large noses—ought to have read or heard everything that lies hidden in the wide-wandering field of Latinity, which one may rightly call a most profound ocean, scarcely explorable in full by the measuring-line of our short years.

->### A Fit Word to the Reader<-

words, perhaps not so common, yet most appropriate to the matter, not even a single letter has been changed; I, however, dropping my ears <note>original: "auriculas dimittens" - a classical idiom meaning to be humbled or dejected, like a discouraged donkey</note>, and at the same time greatly astonished by such a sinister consensus, immediately went to meet these Attic judges <note>A reference to refined but harsh critics</note>, today one, tomorrow another, and I asked of each most humbly that they would not obstruct my light—if they please—but rather show some favor, and deign to offer their fair judgment; for three or four men, likewise not unlearned, had judged the matter quite skillfully.

7. I told my stories to the deaf <note>original: "Surdis fabulas" - a Latin proverb meaning to waste one's breath</note>; nothing was achieved; everyone seemed to exist as if in a ferment <note>agitated or angry</note>; many even listening to me with haughty disdain and haste, finally did not blush to say to my face (for what will these "summits" of society not speak out?) namely, that the translator, whoever he was, did not at all understand the <term>Chemical Art</term> <note>Alchemy or early chemistry</note>, nor was I of such great authority that I could use archaic styles <note>original: "archaïzare"</note>, or reveal my own genius, and that the version, made from German into Latin <note>original: "è germanismo in latinismum"</note>, had been done childishly; Oh, you blind men, have you ever seen colors? And along with these words, they politely showed me their backs several times.

8. But while I, as if already at the door, most recently entreated a certain one of them that he might consider the matter fraternally and with judgment, he added still, slackly and lightly at the very moment of departure, that when the printer <note>original: "typographus"</note> returned, he would see what he had to say; and above all these things mentioned, some had preached much to me about my "shoulders" <note>metaphor for one's capacity to carry a burden</note>, and if the opportunity had occurred, they would have held fast to that line of Horace:

> Take up a subject, you who write, equal to your
> Strengths, and consider long what they refuse to bear.
> <note>A famous quote from Horace's *Ars Poetica* advising writers not to take on tasks beyond their abilities.</note>

No doubt they would have also sung this against me: because they seemed to want to indicate through this that I would be far unequal to completing such a great work—namely, to translate something from one language into another, especially the Roman tongue.

9. And although I freely acknowledge <insert>agno-</insert> my power here to be of a trifle, and of nothing—

# Interlude
<note>original: "Interverbium"</note>

I recognize this, and I would not wish to compare myself to any man, even the least of them, much less gloriously prefer myself. Nevertheless, if humility were not so beautiful a grace before God and so useful among men, I would almost dare to assert that most of those men—however much they may be of "wiped nose" <note>A Latin idiom for being highly discerning or sophisticated</note> and "anointed hearth" <note>A Latin idiom for being wealthy or well-to-do</note>—with all their wisdom and skill, would scarcely be able to do the same a second time.

10. And you will say this with me even more fully, fair reader, if you will only weigh the matter a little more strictly in the balance. For then you will find a most clear reason, not for criticizing, but rather for vehemently wondering: namely, how I—in so brief a space of time, with equal daring and fear—undertook this work (such as it is), even while out of my element and a foreigner, without property or money on my journey, without fire in the strongest part of winter, and having neither book nor companion. Indeed, in the worst of days, which the burdens of extreme necessity and the most diverse cares of seeking food and clothing completely extort from me, I have remained awake for such "filing" <note>original: "limam"; referring to the meticulous polishing or editing of a literary work</note> as you see here;

->*But my Muse is unrefined; we sing such odes as we can,*<-
->*Which the bird, not learned in song, has often repeated.*<-
<note>original: "Sed mea musa rudis..." The author uses a poetic couplet to apologize for his lack of formal polish.</note>

11. Furthermore, whether at noon or toward evening, having dined among those most skilled and sagacious Aristarchuses <note>A reference to Aristarchus of Samothrace, used here to mean severe or highly critical scholars</note>, I perpetually returned home with a belly as empty as my mind was broken and scrupulous. But along the way, I tossed and turned many kinds of thoughts through my soul: for sometimes, bowing my neck, I would cry out in a rough manner: Oh, what a parasite, what a false judge <note>original: "spseudocrites," a hybrid of Greek and Latin implying a hypocritical critic</note> the world is! Puppies are judged by moles. What an unregulated school it is! Ants are instructed by magpies. What a turbulent sea! Small fish are devoured by the large. How poorly ordered the stable is! Sheep are oppressed by oxen. The poor and those of good mind, depressed in various ways, are rejected and neglected; others flourish, happy as much in their vices as in their riches. He does not obtain his right, but loses his case, who nevertheless defends a most just cause. Alas, for the [affairs] of mortals...

<summary>The author describes the extreme hardships—poverty, cold, and lack of resources—under which he composed this work, while critiquing the social injustice where the wealthy and critical "Aristarchuses" overlook the virtuous poor.</summary>

# A Fitting Word to the Reader

moroseness, but oh, the wicked and deadly demons of the sons of Adam! When the poor man speaks with entreaties, the rich man speaks out wildly; for whatever the rich say, whatever they do, it is praised and accepted by everyone, whether it be good or evil.

> *No evil man is happy, yet what rich man does not act as he pleases?* <note>Original Latin: "Nemo malus fælix, quis dives non facit aptè?"</note>

This one reality brings forth both tears and the most sorrowful thoughts.

> *Alas, shameful poverty, you have nothing harder in you*
> *Than that you make men ridiculous and like braying beasts!* <note>A paraphrase of the Roman satirist Juvenal, suggesting that the greatest sting of poverty is the mockery it invites.</note>

12. Sometimes I even said to myself, surely fortune favors fools; it still happens in the world today, just as in the age of Solomon, that animals are valued more than the learned and the literate.

> *Whole towns worship the dogs, but no one worships the Goddesses of Wisdom.* <note>Original Latin: "Oppida tota canes venerantur, nemo Dianas." A metaphor for valuing base things over divine wisdom.</note>

The little lords please, the wretched lie low, and the erudite and wise are fit for burial. Great merchants of sulfurous goods <note>likely referring to traders of gunpowder or base commodities</note> are held in higher price than Plato himself.

> *A man well-dressed is believed by a thousand*
> *To be skilled because of his clothes, even if he is an idiot.*
> *If you lack a garment, and are not dressed respectably;*
> *If your hat is worn, if your cloak is foul and torn,*
> *If your gown is a bit dirty, and one shoe lies open*
> *With broken leather, or if, the wound having been sewn up,*
> *More than one scar shows the thick and recent thread,*
> *You are of no praise, even though you retain everything you hear.* <note>A poetic lament on how intellectual merit is ignored if the scholar appears impoverished.</note>

13. Meanwhile, however, while I was so pleasantly arguing with myself, there occurred to me repeatedly passages from that truly golden little book (which, by my own judgment, easily takes the palm from all the volumes in the world touching on similar subject matter, as much by its strong essence of things and gravity of opinions as by the hidden pull of the Holy Spirit) and, from the moment I saw and read it, it has always uniquely tasted sweet to my heart—

<summary>The author laments the social injustice where wealth is equated with wisdom and poverty with ridicule, noting that even the most learned are ignored if they lack fine clothing. He concludes by introducing a "golden book" inspired by the Holy Spirit that offers him comfort against these worldly vanities.</summary>

<keywords>poverty, wealth, social status, Solomon, Plato, scholarship, vanity, Holy Spirit, injustice</keywords>

# Interlude

<margin>Signature: B 2</margin>

...concerning the *Imitation of Christ* <note>A famous 15th-century devotional book by Thomas à Kempis</note>, these words are the perpetual companion of my life and my path:

14. *It is good for us that we sometimes have some troubles and adversities, for they often recall a man to his own heart, so that he may know himself to be in exile, and not place his hope in any worldly thing. It is good for us that we occasionally suffer detractors, and that we are thought of poorly and imperfectly, even if we act and intend well; these things often help toward humility and defend us from vainglory. For then we better seek God as our internal witness, when outwardly we are despised by men and not well-trusted.* <note>original Latin: "Bonum nobis est, quòd aliquando habemus aliquas gravitates..."</note>

15. Therefore, since I am so unrefined, dull, and ignorant, and the world judges so foolishly, and my efforts become so loathsome to men—to You, O unchangeable **Tetragrammaton!** <term>Tetragrammaton: The four-letter Hebrew name of God (YHWH), often used in mystical or scholarly contexts to denote the Divine Name's holiness</term> to whom the smallness of my person is not unknown, You who never waver in Your judgment, with whom the foolish and unpolished often prevail more than the prudent and the learned: to You I offer up this unformed firstborn of my spirit and meager talent. Before You, I say, I most heartily acknowledge my infancy, my childhood, and my lack of knowledge through the two following written bonds <note>original: "syngraphis," referring to formal written agreements or documents</note>, and with emphasis.

<summary>The author reflects on the spiritual benefits of being misunderstood by the world, quoting Thomas à Kempis to justify his own perceived lack of talent. He dedicates his "unformed" first work to God, using the sacred name Tetragrammaton.</summary>

# SOLILOQUY
## The Paraphrast’s Morning Prayer,

->*In which he is accustomed to offer himself to the Ruler of Nature as a daily sacrifice, and to consecrate his vow to Him.*<-

---

<margin>1.</margin>Awaken and leap forth from the melancholy of the mind, O my soul! Why are you torn apart by vain sorrow? Why are you exhausted by superfluous cares? Listen to what the Lord God wishes to instill within you. Blessed is the soul that has become poor and a pilgrim for the sake of Jesus. Blessed is the soul that reads of Christ the Lord speaking within itself, and is nourished by the honeycomb of consolation from His mouth. Blessed are the ears that obey the whispers of God’s breath <note>original: "labellis inhalantis Dei," literally the lips of God breathing into the soul</note>, and fall asleep to the idle tales of this world. Blessed are the eyes which are closed to fleshly things, but open to spiritual things. Blessed is the mouth that draws milk from the veins of the divine breast, and grows numb to the nursing-scenes of this life <note>The author uses a nursing metaphor to describe the soul's total dependence on divine sustenance over worldly comforts</note>. Truly blessed is the heart that rouses itself as soon as the heavenly Bridegroom knocks, and pays no heed to the slippery deceptions of this world. Blessed, I say, are those who devote themselves to God and shake themselves free from every worldly dream.

2. Take notice of these things, O my soul; indeed, turn yourself quickly with your whole heart toward God. Bolt the doors of your senses <term>sensualitas: the faculty of physical perception and worldly desire</term>, breathe out your private prayers, and aspire to dwell alone with yourself. Seek the company of no one, but rather groan in devoted prayer to God, so that you may be able to perceive what the Lord God murmurs within you, and that you may maintain a sorrowful mind <term>compunctio: a piercing of the heart by regret for sin or longing for God</term> and a pure conscience. Consider the entire amphitheater of the world as nothing; place the serious matters of God before all outward things. For you cannot be free for Him and simultaneously take delight in temporal affairs. If God is to draw near to you with His holy Angels, it is necessary for you to distance yourself from acquaintances, from dear ones, and from friends, and to keep your mind secluded from all human consolation.

<vocab>Soliloquy, Paraphrast, Ruler of Nature, melancholy, soul, Christ, heavenly bridegroom, sensuality, compunction</vocab>

<summary>A meditative morning prayer urging the soul to reject worldly distractions and "sensuality" in favor of an internal, mystical union with God. The text emphasizes the "blessedness" of closing one's physical senses to better hear the divine voice.</summary>
<keywords>soliloquy, spiritual awakening, asceticism, divine consolation, interior life, detachment, morning devotion</keywords>

--- Page 27 ---
<meta>This page continues the morning meditation (Soliloquium Matutinum) from the previous section, focusing on the soul's dialogue with Christ.</meta>

-># MORNING SOLILOQUY<-

->B 3<-

3. These things your most beloved says: I am your lot, your salvation, and your peace; keep yourself with me, and you shall find peace. Cut away siren-like <note>original: "sirenicam" - referring to the tempting but deadly song of the Sirens in mythology</note> desire, abandon this bitter, gall-filled, and wretched world, and you will find rest. Let go of things that perish, seek things that endure; for what are all transitory things but deceptions? Follow me, because I am the way, the truth, and the life <note>original: "via, veritas, & vita" - a reference to John 14:6</note>; without the way there is no going, without the truth there is no knowing, without the life there is no living. I am the way you ought to follow, the truth you ought to yield to, the life you ought to desire. I am the way of salvation, the universal <note>original: "sphæralis" - literally "spherical," implying completeness or the heavenly spheres</note> truth, the life beyond time. I am the straightest way, the supreme truth, the true life, the blessed life, the uncreated life. If you sigh to inherit this, disdain the present life; if you wish to dwell in heaven, live as a pilgrim on earth; if you desire to triumph with me, carry the cross with me: for only the bearers of the cross find the way of happiness and of true light.

4. O sweetest, O most honeyed first-martyr <term>Protomartyr: usually refers to St. Stephen, but here applied to Jesus as the first to suffer for the truth</term> Jesus! Since your way is so narrow and despised by the world, I beseech you, grant that I may strive to follow you despite all the world's reproach. For the servant is not greater than his Lord, nor the disciple above the master. Let your servant be continually exercised in your life, because therein is my salvation and my holiness. Indeed, you, Lord my God, have written me in your hands; you are my only good, you stand in my heart, you are my desire, and therefore it is necessary to run after you, to weep, and to pray. But who am I, that I should dare to speak so confidently to you? I am a most poor, most lost, and most shameful little man <note>original: "homunculus" - a diminutive, often self-deprecating term for a human being</note>, a most abject wanderer, and the most worthless dust—undoubtedly much more wicked and contemptible than I know or dare to say.

5. I am, O highest and most awesome Father, that shapeless, faithless, and wasteful prodigal son <note>original: "nepotinus ille prodigus" - referring to the Parable of the Prodigal Son in Luke 15</note>, who, carried away by the raging North Wind of youth and impatient of any yoke for the love of liberty, behaved insolently toward you. Following the violent impulse of my passions and deserting your house, I withdrew into far-off and foreign regions, where, by living softly and acting dissolutely, I poured out and buried in the mud all my talents and substance.

<summary>A devotional dialogue where Christ calls the soul to abandon worldly desires for the 'Way, Truth, and Life,' followed by the speaker's humble confession of unworthiness and a comparison to the Prodigal Son.</summary>
<keywords>Christ as the Way, spiritual pilgrimage, carrying the cross, humility, Prodigal Son, repentance, morning prayer</keywords>

--- Page 28 ---
<meta>This page continues the author's internal dialogue with God, focusing on the necessity of divine guidance over human intellect.</meta>

# ->SOLILOQUY<-

6. Teach me, nevertheless, to conduct myself worthily and humbly before you today, since you are my wisdom—you who know me in truth, and have known me before the foundation <note>original: "fundum," likely referring to the foundations of the world</note> was laid, and before I was born into the world. You also continually undertake a greater care for me, your little dependent, than a mother's heart feels for her tiny offspring, or than I have, or am even able to carry, for myself.

7. Behold, therefore, my purpose depends upon your will and stands at your good pleasure; I trust in your grace rather than in my own wisdom. For a man proposes, indeed, but you always dispose, nor is a man's way within his own power. The more humble one is in himself and the more subject to God—and the more one is united within himself and inwardly simplified—the wiser and more peaceful he will be in all things. Such a person grasps more and higher things without labor, because he drinks the light of understanding <term>lumen intelligentiæ: a spiritual illumination believed to come directly from God rather than study</term> from above. God walks with the humble, associates himself with the lowly, and draws near to the little ones.

8. There is a wide enough difference between the wisdom of an enlightened and devout man and, conversely, the knowledge of a lettered and well-versed scholar <term>scholasticus: a student or teacher of Scholasticism, the formal academic philosophy of the medieval schools</term>. That doctrine which flows from above by divine influence is always much nobler than that which is laboriously acquired by our own wit. For it is better to taste a very little with humility and slight understanding than to possess entire wagonloads of the sciences with vain self-satisfaction. He will remain small for a long time and lie prostrate below, who considers anything to be great except the one, immense, eternal Good; and whatever is not God is truly nothing, and by right ought to be counted as nothing.

9. Truly, therefore, he is great who is small in his own eyes and holds every peak of honor as nothing. Truly prudent is he who considers all earthly things as filth so that he may gain Christ. And truly well-taught is he who executes the will of God and neglects his own mind. He who seeks anything other than God alone or the salvation of his soul shall reap nothing but various distastes, anxieties, and bitterness; nor can he remain peaceful for long who does not aspire to be the least and subject to all.

<summary>The author reflects on the superiority of divinely inspired wisdom over academic learning, emphasizing that true peace and understanding come from humility and total dependence on God's will. He argues that earthly honors and intellectual pride are worthless compared to the "light of understanding" granted to the lowly.</summary>

<keywords>humility, divine grace, wisdom vs. knowledge, scholasticism, spiritual simplicity, providence, salvation of the soul</keywords>

-># MORNING PRAYER<-
<note>original: "MATUTINUM"</note>

10. He who leans more upon his own industry or his own reasoning than upon the humble discipline of Jesus Christ will rarely and only slowly become an enlightened man. This is because God wishes us to be entirely subject to Him, and to transcend all human reason through an inflamed love. To always act well, and yet to hold a modest opinion of oneself, is the mark of a humble soul. Those who are lowly in heart and simple in spirit dwell in an abundance of peace, while the haughty and the conceited are never satisfied. True peace of mind is not found by following one's passions or by chasing after one's own desires, but by resisting them. *Delight yourself in the Lord, and He will give you the desires of your heart* <note>A reference to Psalm 37:4</note>. If there is any joy to be found in this world, it is surely tasted by the man of a hollowed and small heart <note>meaning a heart emptied of worldly pride</note>; and if, conversely, there is tribulation or anguish anywhere, it is best known by a burdened conscience.

11. My son, because you know these things and have read them all, you will be blessed if you fulfill them. *He who has my commandments and keeps them, he it is who loves me; and I will love him and manifest myself to him* <note>John 14:21</note>, and I will make him sit with me upon the high throne of my Father. O most generous and honey-sweet Lord Jesus, brightness of eternal glory, comfort of my wandering soul on its pilgrimage! Provided that my desire is righteous and not infected by my own convenience—just as You have spoken and promised—so let it be done, and may I be worthy to obtain it. My mouth is now before You without a voice, and my sighing speaks to You: how long will my most longed-for Messiah delay His coming? Let Him come to me, an orphan, and make me glad; let Him stretch out His hand and rescue a poor wretch from all anguish. Oh, how long and bitter is this delay from the nest of my eternal dwelling place!

12. Come, for without You no day or hour will be joyful; for You are my joy, and without You my table is tasteless. Oh, oh, my Emmanuel <note>Hebrew: "God with us"</note>, honey and milk are under Your tongue! Drop down, O most precious Lord; Your hungry little worm licks the ground, for You bedew the honeycombs of eternal life. By unfolding me in the love of Your most healthful and perfect desire, wound my heart with Your dart, so that I may learn to taste with the inner mouth of the heart how sweet it is to love, and to melt and swim in Your love. Here, if anyone loves, he surely knows what this voice cries out.

<summary>A devotional meditation emphasizing that spiritual enlightenment comes through humility and the resistance of worldly passions, concluding with a mystical longing for union with Christ.</summary>
<keywords>humility, peace of mind, Jesus Christ, Messiah, Emmanuel, spiritual longing, divine love, conscience</keywords>

# MORNING SOLILOQUY

13. Truly blessed is he who understands what it means to love Jesus, and to despise oneself for the sake of Jesus: for the love of Jesus causes a man to trample upon himself. The soul that loves God finds all things beneath God to be loathsome; it is necessary to exchange one beloved for another <note>original: "dilectum pro dilecto permutare" — a common mystical theme of replacing earthly affection with divine love</note>, because Jesus wishes to be loved alone above all things. Do you perceive these vows, my little soul, how your Beloved is manfully jealous? Your little Beloved is of such a nature that he will not admit a stranger, but prefers to possess your heart alone, and to sit like a King upon his own throne.

14. O most tender Suitor, O most deeply wounded little Lover, tell me, I pray, where you graze your flock, beautiful Bridegroom, you who are born among the lilies; where do you rise in the morning, where do you rest at midday? Where are you, most pleasant Jesus, you who so encompass my soul? Let me kiss you just once with the kiss of my mouth, so that you may turn toward me the diamond-like and magnetic rays of your eyes—which make me fly away—so that I may, I say, find you alone from now on and forever, and unveil my whole heart to you alone. May I perish for love of you, just as my soul has burned for you; and now let no one despise me, nor any creature move me or look upon me, but let you alone speak to me, and I to you, just as a beloved is accustomed to speak to his beloved, and a friend to feast with his companion. In truth, you are my Beloved, chosen from among all others, in whom it has pleased my soul to store up its comfort for the remaining days of its life. Amen.

# H O M I L Y
## Of the same with the Messiah at Evening,
### I N  W H I C H
### *He was accustomed to meet that jealous little Monarch of his heart daily,*
->*and to cast himself down at his feet.*<-

1. Grant to me, most loving and most indulgent Jesus, your Spirit, that it may be with me, and work with me, and persevere with me even unto my final breath. Grant me to constantly desire and will that which is more acceptable to you and pleases you more; let your will be mine, and let my will always follow yours and harmonize perfectly with it. Let there be for me one "yes" and one "no" with you, nor let me be able to will or not will anything, except what you will or do not will. <note>The author uses the language of "mystical union," where the human will seeks to dissolve into the Divine will.</note>

2. Let me have no care for the shadow of a great name, nor for the familiarity of many, nor for the private affection of men; let me refuse to be singularly loved or praised. These things nourish pride, generate distractions, and create the greatest darkness in the heart. You help the humble, and you humble the one who presumes much of himself; you defend and free the humble, you love and console the humble; you incline yourself to the humble person, you bestow great grace <term>grace: divine favor or assistance</term> upon the humble, and after his suppression, you lift him up to glory; you reveal your secrets to the humble, and sweetly draw and invite him to yourself.

3. It is good for me, therefore, Lord, that you have humbled me and made me poor, so that I may learn your justifications <note>original: "justificationes," referring here to divine laws or righteous decrees</note> and cast away the vain elations and presumptions of the heart. It is useful to me that confusion has repeatedly covered my face, so that I might seek you for consolation rather than men. Oh, how gladly and frequently you would speak your loving words to me and manifest hidden things, if only I would observe your coming more diligently, and as soon as possible to you knocking at the door of my heart—

<summary>A devotional evening prayer or homily focusing on the total submission of the human will to God and the spiritual necessity of humility. The author argues that worldly fame and human affection are distractions that hinder a direct relationship with the Divine.</summary>
<keywords>humility, divine will, Jesus, prayer, pride, spiritual discipline, evening devotion</keywords>

<meta>The speaker continues their humble address to the Divine, following the previous page's themes of self-reflection and the recognition of past errors.</meta>

-># HOMILY<-

...to open [my heart] first, oh, what great thoughtlessness and negligence on my part!

4. In truth, O most loving Shepherd, I am that lost little sheep <note>A reference to the Parable of the Lost Sheep in Luke 15</note>, which you—after my winding wanderings—have hunted down, gathered up brotherly upon your shoulders, and readopted into the green pastures of your vineyard. Hosanna, therefore; grace, grace to you, my purple-clad Light-bringer <note>original: "Purpurate Lucifator"; likely referring to Christ in his royal/suffering majesty</note>, who long ago, through the prayers and sighs of my mother Monica <note>Saint Monica, the mother of St. Augustine, known for her persistent prayers for her son's conversion</note>, bound me humbly to you in her very presence. I beseech you, by that friendship which exists between you and me, do not deny this light to my understanding: namely, that from now on and forever I may give myself entirely to your paternal disposition and offer myself to your will. May I be as willing to be poor, desolate, despised, and rejected throughout my life as I would be to be wealthy, honored, pleasing, or much-praised in the mouths of men.

5. Ah, sweet Jesus, unrewardable Word-born Son <note>original: "Verbigena"; a poetic term for Christ as the One born of the Word</note>, turn all fleshly consolation into bitterness for me hereafter—anything that draws me away from the love of eternal things and evilly entices me toward itself by the spark of some present, delectable good. Grant me, I pray, instead of transitory earthly knowledge and all the decaying magnificence of this false world, a crumb of ambrosia and of your pure heavenly wisdom, which renounces all these lowest things and yearns for you alone. Your tablets and your letters are the most delightful wisdom, a wisdom so profound it surpasses all the teaching of the Philosophers and the wise men of this world.

6. May I always conduct myself as a pilgrim, as a Hermit and an exile upon the earth, whom the turmoils of the flesh do not concern. For he who desires to reach the interior, to attain your spiritual delights, must turn aside with you far from the crowd; it is certainly better to remain hidden, to put everything else aside, and to take care of one's own soul—keeping oneself alone before one's eyes—rather than to neglect oneself, wear oneself out with phantoms, and, leaving one's own field unharvested, plow the land of another.

7. Let me not be ashamed or weary of always listening gladly to others for the love of you, and of appearing poor and without honor in this life, becoming a fool for your sake. O, would that I were a lover of nothing of myself, but could resign myself wholly to you, and fully leave myself behind, annihilate, and cast myself away for your sake!

<summary>The author offers a deeply personal prayer of surrender, identifying with the 'lost sheep' and St. Augustine's conversion, while renouncing worldly honor and intellectual pride in favor of divine wisdom.</summary>
<keywords>repentance, St. Monica, Shepherd, heavenly wisdom, asceticism, self-denial, spiritual pilgrimage</keywords>

# EVENING PRAYERS
<note>original: "Vespertina"</note>

8. Come now, grant that I may die to all things in the world, to live as a monk <note>original: "monachari"; to live a life of solitary devotion</note>, and for your sake to love being despised and unknown in this age! In exchange for all the new wines of the world, grant the most sweet taste of your spirit; and in place of fleshly love, pour in the sweetness of your name. Grant that I may find rest in you above all desired things, and that my heart may find peace from you, so that I may learn to seek and find you before all else, to savor and love you before all else. May I be refreshed in you above every creature, find joy above all health and beauty, take pleasure above all science and art <term>artem: here referring to human skill or craft</term>, be gladdened above all treasures and wealth, be made bright above all glory and honor, find delight above all things visible and invisible, and finally, come to rest above everything that is not you, my God.

9. Because you, O Lord my God, alone are the best above all things; you alone are the most powerful, you alone the most sufficient, you alone the most sweet and comforting; you alone are the most beautiful and most perfect, you alone the most noble and most glorious, and the most honored above all. You are the pure torch of the soul <note>original: "mera fax animæ"</note>, the true peace of the heart, the only rest, life, salvation, and the only refuge; outside of you, all things are hard and restless. Therefore, with this torch, I say, and in this peace, may I sleep and rest in that very same thing—that is, in you, the one supreme and eternal Good. Through the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit <note>original: "Sanctum Flamen"; a poetic Latin term for the 'Breath' or Spirit</note>, Amen.

## Authority & Majesty

1. **T**he great wonders of the entire world upon these stages—
*Will they not be brought forth only through the inspired mouths of the Sibyls* <note>The Sibyls were ancient prophetesses believed to voice divine oracles.</note>
*Which the Initiate <note>original: "Symmifta"</note> shall recount here in an unaccustomed tragic style?*
*Or which of those truth-telling Sisters <note>The Muses or Sibyls.</note>
*Will that Interpreter <note>original: "Gloffarius"</note>—as if he were a holy Good Spirit <note>original: "Eudæmon"</note> bargaining from the tripod of the Gods—*
*Lead into the theater with a Magic lute, like a Prophet-Bard?*

2. *What is this Hermes-born decree of grace* <note>Refers to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary father of alchemy and hermetic philosophy.</note>
*Which, by mediating with the Spirits of the dead,*
*Brings forth all the beings of the Underworld and the Gods above?*

3. *What does this small tablet—without a guardian,*
*Without hope of a name, and outside of time—*
*Bring into the light, so rare and so dear?*

4. *Indeed, what does this new little book, of a new sort,*
*Recently gifted with a Latin translation,*
*Teach with such a fresh and bold authority?*

<summary>This page serves as a poetic invocation and justification for the text, questioning the divine or supernatural origins of the knowledge being presented. It frames the work as a "Hermetic decree" translated into Latin that reveals secrets of both the heavens and the underworld.</summary>
<keywords>Authority, Majesty, Sibyls, Hermes Trismegistus, Hermeticism, Prophecy, Latin translation, Underworld</keywords>

## Concerning these Great Oracles.

1. He shall bring to light the monuments of the ancient Sages <note>original: "Sophorum," referring to the wise men of antiquity</note>,
*The fates of the learned Goddesses, worthy of their own temples,*
*Covenants indeed Mortal, yet inspired through him,*
*The Winged Messenger who is named from the Elysian court <note>A reference to Mercury/Hermes, the messenger of the gods</note>;*
*When the light had departed from the ether, and the nourishing Moon* <note>original: "Phœbe," a poetic name for the moon goddess</note>
*Was circling the middle of the heavens with her nocturnal chariot.*

2. *By following the thread of the Cretan maiden <note>original: "Gnosidis," referring to Ariadne, who provided the thread to escape the Labyrinth</note> directly back,*
*He comes forth to overcome the windings of Daedalus,*
*Which are covered with a thousand errors and snares.*

3. *The golden vessels of a blessed life,*
*The majestic commands of the Assembled Throne,*
*And the profound sayings of the Elders he discloses.*

4. *He marks out the most ancient things of the Magi,*
*Which nevertheless do not grow old at all in the world,*
*But always seem new through Fathers and Grandfathers,*
*And new to their late-born sons;*
*For these new little things are newer than the new.* <note>The author uses a play on words—"novis noviora sunt novella"—to emphasize that ancient wisdom possesses a perpetual, living freshness that surpasses modern novelties.</note>

<summary>This page introduces a series of "Great Oracles" or prophetic verses, claiming they represent ancient wisdom brought to light through divine inspiration and the guidance of a messenger-figure. The text emphasizes that this ancient knowledge remains eternally new and superior to the confusing "labyrinth" of mortal error.</summary>

# TRIUMPHALIA

->TO THE<-

### Students of the gold-producing art <note>original: "Auriparæ artis"; referring to alchemy</note>, transmitted to an anonymous Paraphraser by a certain intimate companion of his own circle.

1. Exult! For now there comes into the light
A book obtained from a majestic urn,
A book set free for the attentive ear,
A book refined by the mystic art,
A book driven by the midnight lamps <note>original: "nocturnis umbilicis"; literally the rollers of a scroll, implying late-night study</note>:

A book worthy of applause, and entirely famous,
Which, through worn-out pens and a weary hand,
Through a broken desk and a scraped-out place,

Stuffed sumptuously from the kitchen of Midas,
Let it rush immediately into the midst of the circle,
And let it satisfy the long hungers of men
With its own feasts, and quench their thirst,
And let it gladden the sorrowful hearts of the craftsmen
With its chosen mysteries and emblems;
2. Straightway, like a strap with a sounding magic-wheel <note>original: "rhombo"; a bullroarer or spinning instrument used in ancient mysteries</note>
Held tight with a golden, resounding boom,
The acts of the assembled council of the Gods

### The Translator’s Exhortation
->TO THE<-
### Lover of Golden Truth,
->CONCERNING<-
### His own Sibylline Oracles. <note>The "Sibylline Oracles" here refers to prophetic or cryptic wisdom, common in alchemical literature.</note>

Ignore the trifles of those writers, I tell you as your interpreter,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Who teach things more slippery than our own brains can hold.
And with me as your advisor, spare yourself the <term>Chymists</term> <note>Early chemists or alchemists.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;With their glyphs, types, and rugged paths; they chant nothing but naked names.
Avoid, I say, the double-tongued books of the "Philosophers,"
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Which sound like the mouth of the Sphinx, with things scarcely known to the Gods.
For almost as many as have written such things, have always
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Passed through shadows, making the difficult even harder to grasp.
They have always spoken in an ambiguous or figurative tone,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Swift in their outward brightness, like a flowering fig tree <note>A reference to something that looks promising but may lack fruit.</note>.
Using now these, now those various windings and obscurities,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Like the <term>will-o'-the-wisps</term> <note>original: "fatuos ignes"; atmospheric ghost lights that lead travelers astray.</note> which are seen to wander off course.
Do you think anyone can comprehend all the circles and cycles
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Which the first Master-Magi established for their followers?
Who are you, the least of the crowd, who reads the works of the **Wise**,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;That you will perceive this book correctly and sufficiently?
Tell me, how many could have grasped the Stone of Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, a foundational figure in alchemy.</note>,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Or known the dogmas of the "Perfect Work" by Rhazes <note>An influential Persian physician and alchemist.</note>?
To whom could the true mind return after reading Plato,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Or for whom did the twin **bird** <note>Likely a reference to the "Hermetic Bird" or the volatile and fixed states of matter.</note> produce the material?
Whose ears does Raymond Lully <note>Major 13th-century philosopher and alchemist.</note> nourish? He is a fool,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;For whom so many deceptive "waters" are enumerated.
Shall Arnold of Villanova <note>A famous 13th-century physician and alchemist.</note> feed your eyes with something new?
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Far be it; what he reported is either sluggish or entirely for himself.

# THE INTERPRETER'S ADDRESS

Since our bark <note>The author uses the metaphor of a ship (carina) to describe his book or his intellectual journey.</note> now holds a safe course amidst these immense waves of Tethys <note>Tethys was a sea goddess; here the "waves" represent the vast and dangerous sea of knowledge or the world.</note>, it is right that the shining tiller—a heavy burden for the sailor—should be approached more swiftly and preferably. In every way similar to the *Argo* <note>The legendary ship of Jason and the Argonauts.</note>, both in its sail and its curved stern, this vessel is laden with the spoils of the golden-haired skin <note>A reference to the Golden Fleece.</note>. It bends and turns, never destined to perish in the deep, but rather to tame the winds within its linen sails.

But if the novelty of the breeze should cease to blow, the ship must be restored to our wing-footed God <note>Mercury (Hermes), the god of messages, commerce, and alchemy.</note>. From here it flies and flourishes, not to be destroyed in its first age, unless an empty poet should bring it to other printing presses. The Sun, Mars, the Moon, Venus, and Jupiter <note>These represent the seven metals of alchemy: Gold, Iron, Silver, Copper, and Tin.</note> will all liquefy in the air, and he will sooner allow lead to smoke upon the funeral pyre, and fugitive Mercury will remain in the fierce fire, before the vivid Nymph of golden Jupiter <note>Likely a poetic reference to the "Philosophical Gold" or the refined soul of the work.</note> shall fall.

But where do you slip, O tongue, ignorant of nursing fame, you who are often a jest in place of an extraordinary name? Yet, so that the discourse may return to the same point from which it started—so that you may be wise—take your place here beneath the stern-ornament. For in a short space, with light effort, in place of the unique wings of the Phoenix, here the journey is run and traveled in this stadium of study.

He who desires to carry away the longed-for hide from Colchis <note>The Golden Fleece</note>, here is the man rich in the fleece of the Gold-vomiting Sheep. Here is the daughter of God, the admirable glory of the world, than which that Craftsman <note>Referring to the Divine Creator or the Great Architect.</note> fashions nothing worthier or better. Hence, without deceit, my scribe sings with a good omen of that which comes from hands more powerful than human ones. Those individual things which other volumes contain only here and there, have here come together into one pure source. Here nothing is inserted except the face of Pallas <note>Athena/Minerva, goddess of wisdom.</note>; here nothing lies hidden except what the learned Thalia <note>The Muse of comedy and pastoral poetry.</note> hands down.

## The Argument of the Work,
-> TO <-
### Prevent rash judgments.

1. *I have thought it best, my follower of golden truth, to place the summary of this entire little work before your eyes here in an image, as if in a three-word motto, along with the destined spirit of the present matter and the value of the labor. I do this lest, being ignorant of our unusual way of proceeding and of our intention, you might prematurely judge the matter to be irrelevant, or pass an immature judgment upon it. Therefore, look upon my web; consider it well, and observe that it is divided into three principal threads: namely, the Prelude, the Sibylline Oracles, and the Unearthed Grain.*

# ARGUMENT

*...looking toward the [subject] itself, but contains only certain theoretical fragments of it, along with several sacred-profane philosophical lessons—or rather, documents of the Christian life and monuments of my own—yet all so intermingled that the primary reason, or the eye, always returns and turns back toward Chemistry <note>original: "Chymiam"; here referring to Alchemy, the "Spagyric Art"</note>.*

3. *The "Sibylline Oracles of the Magical Nights" <note>A poetic title for a section of the book</note> set forth the cause and circumstances of the business: namely, why and how it was begun. At the same time, they contribute something to the Art; for they very clearly and frequently proclaim and sing of the very Subject of the Philosophers <note>The "Subject" refers to the raw material used to create the Philosopher's Stone</note> according to its intention. However, they do so with such an artful tone of the vein <note>A metaphor for poetic style or "flow"</note> that not everyone will grasp it immediately, unless perhaps they read through everything with the greatest care.*

4. *Finally, the "Uprooted Grain of the Chemical Winnowing-Fan" <note>Latin: "Chymicæ Vanni Granum Erutum"</note> is the only part that embraces the whole matter in order and sharply extracts the marrow <note>i.e., explains the core essence</note> repeatedly. Therefore, he who does not wish nor desire to read anything here except what pertains precisely to the Art ought to skip over the prosimetric <note>A work written in a combination of prose and verse</note> Prelude along with the "Sibylline Oracles of the Magical Nights," and survey only the "Uprooted Grain of the Chemical Winnowing-Fan." But he will not need many hours for this; because once one ignores all the symbolic and hieroglyphic apparatus of parables, circumlocutions, and similes in which it is shadowed, the Art in itself is extremely brief, easy, linear, and simple.*

5. *Now, however, a question may arise against me: to what purpose does it serve to insert such a structure of repeated things? I will say: I did this because it is not the custom, nor is it possible, for a book or booklet to be composed of one single little page, and so that you might believe the truth to be true; and that you might hold the Nymph <note>A common alchemical personification of the "Secret Matter" or the soul of the stone</note> in a more worthy place, the more she is made lovely by the adornment of gems and studs. For truly weighty reasons, the Church employs ceremonies for sacred things and sacraments; for a thing proposed crudely and nakedly, however mystical or sacred, quickly becomes a joke and falls into contempt.*

6. *If a King were to walk through the streets alone without any pomp or royal retinue in an unknown dress, who would believe him to be a King? Who would defer royal honor to him? In the same way, if the Royal Art of the world <note>The "Ars Regia" or Alchemy</note> were naked and stripped of all its trappings and pompous clothing, by whom would it be held as such? How many would believe Gea <note>The Greek Goddess of the Earth</note> or Rhea <note>The Mother of the Gods in Greek mythology</note> to be a Goddess? Who would bend the knee of reverence to her? It was necessary, therefore, to sew an honorable tunic for our Nymph, so that she might frequent the public in a majestic manner and be able to enter the courts of Great Men.*

7. *And certainly, I do not doubt that, unless one is blinder than Tiresias <note>The famous blind prophet of Thebes in Greek mythology</note>, or alto-*

# OF THE WORK.

<margin>D 3</margin>

...so that it swells with the ink of the cuttlefish <note>original: "loligineo... succo"; a classical metaphor for writing ink or perhaps bitterness</note>, he will easily see how much labor I had to swallow in weaving together this little wig <note><term>galericulo</term>: literally a small cap or wig; here used metaphorically for the decorative or artificial structure of the text</note>, and in fashioning so many various jewels for the Goddess. # A Prelude in Verse and Prose

->To God<-

### *To the prepared sons of the art seeking to extract the heavy and pregnant Galena <note>Lead glance or lead ore, often used as a starting material in alchemy</note> of the Philosophers.*

->§. I.<-

That man, an alchemical Praxiteles <note>A reference to the famous Greek sculptor, here used to mean a master craftsman of the Great Work</note> with a triple and divine talent, constructed with wondrous effort a glass belly <note>A flask or cucurbit</note> warming with a gentle and steady heat; he had engendered within this all the systems of the heavens, and all the wandering labors of the stars in their order, with a diligence that seemed scarcely believable. For instance, the orbit of Saturn was completed in thirty years, that of Jupiter in twice six, and that of Mars in nearly two; the fiery torch of Phoebus <note>The Sun</note> in one year, but that of the Moon in twenty-seven days and twice four hours.

Just as it is accustomed to happen in that superior world, so it was brought down into this inferior one: Here were the predominant and recurring constellations; the wandering stars <note>planets</note> and the fixed stars. Here the risings and settings of the stars and the ethers, and here the eclipses of the Luminaries—the sun and the moon—were demonstrated to the eye. It was truly a miracle of abundant art, and no less a miracle of the artist. Does it please you? Pray, listen, so that I may play elegantly for you concerning this glass tomb of the Phoenix <note>The Phoenix here represents the philosopher's stone or the rejuvenated matter within the vessel</note>.

<summary>This page introduces a poetic and prose prelude describing a master alchemist who creates a "glass belly" (vessel) that perfectly mirrors the movements and cycles of the celestial bodies. It establishes the Hermetic principle of "as above, so below" by linking planetary orbits to the internal timing of the alchemical work.</summary>

<keywords>Praxiteles, alchemical vessel, planetary cycles, Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Sun, Moon, Phoenix, macrocosm and microcosm</keywords>

# PRELUDE

->Hermogenes, having observed the ages of our world,<-
->Paused, and with a clever tongue thus addressed the Gods:<-
"Has the industry of human practice <term>praxis: the practical application of knowledge</term> progressed so far?
Now the lowly duties of the earth shall utterly vanish.
The courses of the Sun in the Zodiac, and the paths of the Moon
Are governed by art; the very axis of the heavens is bent 
By mortal genius to move according to prescribed laws:
And scythe-bearing Diana <note>The Moon</note>, with her revived light,
Shines full in her time; how much and how often they labor,
The Governess of night and the Governor of day;
When each veils their head in dusky gloom <note>An allusion to solar and lunar eclipses</note>,
When the most welcome lights of Phoebus <note>The Sun</note> return to their state,
And pass through their changes—what Daedalus <note>A metaphor for a master craftsman or inventor</note> was set over the world,
Who might repair the losses of Cynthia <note>The Moon</note> with a swift return?
Why Delia <note>Another name for the Moon goddess</note> is now horned, now with a full face,
And why she now fails, deprived of her brother’s horses <note>original: "fraternis priva caballis" – referring to the Sun's chariot</note>,
What hinders the tortoise-like steps of Saturn,
What force of repeating nature might forge gold,
And from whence the four-horsed wheels take their beginnings,
*All these things we have witnessed within a glass nest.*"

A truly eloquent invention. Archimedes fashioned the first machine pregnant with the world—a portable heaven, a compendium of nature, a mirror of nature—arranged after the likeness of the ether with incomprehensible mobility. But truly, *you listeners of the wonders of magical nature*, has not God, that Supreme Architect of things, labored upon a work far more absolute, a thousand times more perfect, more admirable, and more subtle—namely, the human fabric? In which, evidently, like a certain mass of gold, [the virtues] of all...

<summary>This page uses poetic and mythological imagery to describe how human ingenuity has mastered the laws of astronomy, before arguing that God's greatest masterpiece is not the cosmos, but the human body.</summary>
<keywords>Hermogenes, Archimedes, astronomy, eclipses, alchemy, divine architect, microcosm, human anatomy</keywords>

# PROSIMETRICUM

Within the value of nature’s coinage, whatever perfection exists anywhere or in anyone beneath the vaults of heaven—the understanding of the Celestials, the senses of the beasts, the growth of plants—is contained in a certain preeminent way and knot. One might applaud this more fittingly than the carved work of Archimedes <note>original: "Archimedis anaglypho." Referring to Archimedes' famous planetarium or celestial globe.</note>.

> For he had enclosed the heavens within a small glass,
> Embracing the true spheres with simulated curves,
> But that fragile labor perished, and now no
> Fragments remain; yet You, Creator of the earth and high Olympus,

You have fashioned one work, Man, whose eternal excellence no antiquity will ever be able to admire enough. That mysterious Zoroaster <note>The ancient Persian prophet, often viewed in the Renaissance as a source of primordial wisdom.</note> seems to have hit the mark exactly—he who solidly tasted even the deepest and most subtle things with the sounding-lead of his genius—when, having deliberately contemplated the advancement and perfection of man through his Magic, he finally burst forth: *O man, wondrous follower of God, of a daring nature!* <note>original: "O homo audacis naturæ Deisequum mirificum!"</note> This is certainly a profound sentiment, as if to say: wise nature only then attempted a daring work when she began to think about the fabrication of man. This animal—provident, skillful, multifaceted, restless, acute, mindful, full of reason and counsel, whom we call man—was generated in a certain noble condition by the supreme God. For he alone, out of so many kinds and natures of living beings, is a participant in reason and thought, while all others are devoid of them. What is there, I will not say in man, but in all heaven and earth, more divine than reason? Which, when it has matured and been perfected, is rightly named wisdom.

Therefore, not without merit has it passed into the praise of the Sacred Writers <note>original: "Hierographorum."</note> that this king of the works and burdens of the Most High carries the boundary of the *Great World* <note>original: "Magni Mundi," referring to the Macrocosm.</note> within the structure of his own narrow vessel and palace. And for that reason, that most celebrated and beautiful verse and oracle of the prophetic mouth was once painted in large, golden characters—not on benches or tables, but upon the very threshold of Delphic Apollo:

<margin>Know Thyself</margin>

<meta>This page continues the introductory "Prelude," focusing on the philosophical and spiritual necessity of self-knowledge as the foundation for wisdom and divine connection.</meta>

# PRELUDE

->Consult yourself, know yourself, and walk from within:<-

As if this sentence were delivered from heaven and born divinely in the soul—being the beginning of all science and wisdom, and the entrance to God—it is rightly written in golden letters. For it is a golden eulogy, worth its weight in gold, which I wish would never be erased from the tablets of our hearts, but rather fixed there and pondered by a mindful breast. It is brief indeed, yet sufficient without anything else, even if all other things outside of this exist and profit little. Irradiated by this supreme torch, as it were, we are reminded to fix the face and sharp focus of our minds upon ourselves. We should strive most closely to arrive at the knowledge of no other thing sooner than that by which each person consults and recognizes themselves.

Indeed, he knows much who knows himself; he alone is wise, and all others are out of their minds. Therefore, we must enter the inner sanctuaries of the nature of things and see deeply what nature requires; otherwise, we cannot truly know ourselves. Because this precept was too great to be seen as uttered by a man, it was assigned to God <note>The author refers to the famous maxim "Know Thyself" (Gnothi Seauton), which was inscribed on the Temple of Apollo at Delphi and often attributed to divine origin rather than a human philosopher.</note>, who wishes for us to know ourselves. And since this knowledge is the most necessary of all, the Delphic oracle <note>original: "Delphica cortina," referring to the tripod or cauldron from which the priestess delivered prophecies.</note> is said to have delivered this fate to King Croesus <note>Croesus was the famously wealthy King of Lydia; the author cites a tradition where his happiness depended on self-knowledge.</note> when he once inquired by what means he might be happy: *if you know yourself*. This response is truly most worthy of the memory of all ages and nations; for to be able to know oneself is the little peak of the sciences, which embraces the summary of the entire Christian life in an ancient praise, just as that "walking tree," man, displays the evidence of all created things. Evangelus <note>Likely a reference to a specific author or a personification of "Gospel-like" wisdom.</note> has polished and exquisitely agreed with me on this point: that the first benefit granted by God to a sinner is to dart a ray of light into his heart, so that he may know himself more intimately. The first gift, he says, which is given to man in respect to the Light, is the knowledge of self.

> To know oneself, and what one's heavenly origin may be,
> This is the way which leads to the dwellings above.

These are noble verses, truly worthy of not being sung from the earth: for indeed, I do not see what could be more religious or more holy—

# PROSIMETRIC <note>original: "Prosimetricum" — a literary style mixing prose and verse</note>

What could be more wisely expressed in poetry? For to know this one thing is to be ignorant of nothing; to be ignorant of this is to know nothing at all. Even the Nations, though groping in the dark clouds of Heathenism <note>original: "coeno Gentilitatis" — literally 'the filth of paganism'</note>, have abundantly expressed their displeasure at such ignorance.

As the first witness of this truth, let that oracle of Philosophers and one of the seven Sages of Greece, **Solon**, step onto the stage. In order to restrain proud and Alexandrian <note>referring to the legendary ambition of Alexander the Great</note> spirits, to curb the insolent, and to recall the arrogant and stubborn back to the rule of reason, he employed a single means: he inscribed a famous verse upon the doors and both walls of the Delphic temple:

->Consult yourself, know yourself, and walk from within.<-

Walk with yourself, I say; dwell with yourself, consult yourself, and know yourself. Know, clearly, who you are and where you came from; for "nothingness" itself is your father, mud and dung are your nobility, and worms are your true heraldic crests.

Following him, dressed in no inferior toga, comes the leader of that same school, **Thales of Miletus**. According to the testimony of Laërtius <note>Diogenes Laërtius, a biographer of Greek philosophers</note>, when someone asked him what was the most difficult of all things, he replied: "To have known oneself." Oh, behold the transcripts from the Orchestra of the ancients! Oh, men utterly admirable in their learning! For what does it help to embrace the heaven and earth with one's intellect, yet fail to grasp one's own smallness and vileness? What use is it to skillfully search for the spots on the Sun, while meditating nothing on one's own stains? To what end does it serve to observe the eclipses of the Moon, and not see one's own failings? If you obtain the knowledge of all secrets and arts, what is this worth if you are ignorant of yourself? You are constantly walking abroad and wandering outside, thinking yourself well-advised and knowing much, when you know nothing of who and what you are. If you knew the height of heaven and the depth of the sea, and possessed all sciences at once, but did not know yourself, you would be like one who builds upon rubble without a foundation:

->For when the foundation collapses, all things fall.<-

Yet how very few follow and attain that goal! Because to their fellow—

# PRELUDE

In a similar fashion, Plato, the prince and father of philosophers, seems to have noted that in the marketplace, scarcely one in ten knows himself. Persius, however, finds not even one; wherefore, grazing the rumors of the age with biting Satire, he argues:

> No one attempts to descend into himself, no, not one,
> But every man stares at the pack on the back of the person before him.
> <note>Persius, Satire 4.24. The "pack" refers to a fable where people carry their own faults in a bag behind them, while seeing the faults of others in a bag hanging in front.</note>

Wisely, therefore, did Plato—though a pagan philosopher—crown the aforementioned motto when he said that the knowledge and memory of oneself is absolute and solid science. From this perfected verse:

->Consult your own self, know yourself, and walk from within.<-

All wisdom and justice of life sprout forth without dispute. Whence Tully <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero</note>, the torch and flower of Roman eloquence, says: "Thus it happens that wisdom is the mother of all good arts; from the love of which, by its Greek etymology <note>original: "etymo græco" referring to 'philosophia' as the love of wisdom</note>, philosophy found its name. Nothing more fruitful, nothing more flourishing, nothing more excellent has been given by the immortal Gods to the life of men. For this alone has taught us, among all other things, that which is most difficult: to know ourselves. So great is the force and meaning of this precept that it was attributed not to any mere man, but to the Delphic God <note>Apollo, at whose temple the phrase "Know Thyself" was inscribed.</note>. For he who knows himself will first feel that he possesses something divine, and will regard his own intellect as a kind of dedicated sacred image; he will always act and feel in a manner worthy of so great a gift from the Gods. When he has examined himself thoroughly and tested his whole being, he will understand how he came into the light furnished by nature, and what great instruments he possesses for obtaining and attaining wisdom. For in the beginning, he conceives in his soul and mind the shadowed outlines of all things; enlightened by these, with wisdom as his guide, he perceives that he will be a good man, and for that reason, a happy one."

But this consolation has been drawn from elsewhere; however, so that we may also emit an arrow from our own quiver: rightly it seems to me—

# PROSIMETRICUM
<note>original: "Prosimetricum" — a literary style that blends prose and verse.</note>

I seem to be able to see that the height of the knowledge of Christ consists in consultation, habitation, and the recognition and memory of oneself. In comparison to His sublime wisdom, whatever else exists is truly ignorance. What a remarkable and polished weapon it is, which suddenly transforms even the most foolish men into wise Priests! O, therefore, golden *three-word-motto* <note>original: "triverbium" — referring to the three-part command that follows</note>, ah, majestic song, which surely ought to be forged deep into the triangle of the human heart! For in this magnificence of things, and in this sight and knowledge of that unspeakable Word—immortal Gods!—how much will a man consult himself and discern his inner nature, just as the Pythian Apollo commanded! <note>Apollo’s temple at Delphi bore the famous inscription "Know Thyself."</note> How he will despise, how he will look down upon, and how he will count as nothing those things which are commonly called most grand!

But with other colors still, and with a new piece of charcoal, so to speak, I shall depict this same thing for you on a white tablet. That Antaeus, son of the Earth, born of the race of Giants, whenever he was thrown to the ground while wrestling with Hercules and kissed that most indulgent mother of his, his strength and vigor were perpetually restored. But soon, as he lifted his head high into the air, his muscles were weakened again, and he was overthrown by Alcides <note>Another name for Hercules, descendant of Alcaeus.</note>. But leaving behind the husk of the fable, let us extract the kernel of truth that lies hidden within it. It must be said, therefore, that the very same thing happens to us when we carry Giant-like spirits and presume some singular prerogative for ourselves as "Earth-born" <note>original: "Terrigenis" — mortals or those born of the earth</note>, and we forget ourselves. For as long as we hold to the earth and fix our eyes upon our own being, and simultaneously revolve that saying often in our minds:

> Consult yourself, Know yourself, and Walk from within.

And when we weigh what we are, where we have come from, and into what we are to be reduced, no enemy can be found, nothing so arduous or Herculean can exist that might defeat or overthrow us; nothing is so secret or suppressed that it could be hidden from us or pass us by. But indeed, if we allow ourselves to be carried away into elation and into the heights by some empty and vain wind of presumption and "wisdom," and if we chase after clouds and vanities and exhaust ourselves trying to raise ourselves upward—if, finally, we are ignorant of what our origin is and from whence we came, and if that fixed [goal] is not always...

He argues that true wisdom is found in recognizing one's earthly origins and internal nature through the "knowledge of Christ."</summary>

If we lose sight of this little verse, we are conquered, overcome, and we wander astray. Behold, an emphasis carved out, a lesson most worthy of being held for a very long time, which not only the unlearned but even the most learned should strive to emulate! Therefore, as many of you as go to gaze upon the Nymph of this highest wisdom, be continually driven and stirred toward her thesis and imitation, *O Pupils of our authentic and Golden Philosophy*.

->This is the way; this field shall be marked by our chariot,<-
->This is the boundary that shall be reached by the gilded Horse.<-
<note>The author uses chariot and horse imagery to describe the disciplined path of the alchemical Great Work.</note>

This is truly the deepest philosophy of all; this is the first, the lowest, and the chief little ray of that most splendid planet of the arts, Alchemy; this, I say, is a singular little branch of this most fertile Golden Tree; and this is the unique torch and light of this function, which, flowing from the springs of leaping water, is destined to illuminate the darkness of your intellect with its own incredible radiance.

->§. 2.<-

But truly, because life has given nothing to mortals without great labor, it behooves all who sacrifice to this Stone <note>original: "Litho," referring to the Philosopher's Stone</note> to sweat like athletes, to strive with all the wheels of their genius set in motion, and to rise up manfully with oars and sails in this winding Argo <note>A reference to the ship of Jason and the Argonauts, symbolizing a perilous but heroic quest.</note>,

> To turn the pages with a nightly hand, and turn them by day,
> No broad path of travel is given to the Magical Muses,
> Nor does Golden Wisdom recline on a soft bed,
> Just as roasted pigeons never come flying on the wind.
> <note>A proverbial expression meaning that success does not fall into one's lap without effort.</note>

For who that was ever sluggish or idle gathered trophies or prizes? What athlete, I ask, was ever crowned without sweat? Certainly, no one putting his hand to the plow and looking back is to be approved as fit, nor he who hides his Lord’s talent in a cloth and neglects to multiply it: for Philomagia <note>term: Philomagia (Love of Magic/Wisdom). A personification of the occult sciences as a mother or goddess.</note> has never embraced or kissed as her own sons those who are dull-witted, or those sleeping the sleep of Endymion or Epimenides <note>Legendary figures known for sleeping for decades; used here to condemn intellectual laziness.</note>, or those wasting away in idleness.
