# PROSIMETRICUM

Since, therefore, the reality of these mysteries is by no means of a secondary status, but clearly of the primary, then by necessity and the very nature of law, those who are shapeless and monstrous trunks <note>referring to spiritually undeveloped or "wooden" individuals</note> must never be permitted entrance to the **Philosophical Rose Garden** <note>original: "Philosophicum Rosetum"; a common alchemical metaphor for the secret garden of wisdom</note>. Nor should those who remain stretching and yawning, allowing their lives to grow wild in idleness, be allowed in. Rather, those who enter must be those who immediately set out with full sails and by a direct path—strenuous, diligent, and vigilant **Hermits** <note>original: "Anachoretæ"; those who withdraw from the world for spiritual labor</note>. These are the ones who, with the Moon as their witness, have endured wonderful and difficult labors in caves, in dens, and in the hidden vaults of the earth. They are those who, through trackless wastes and byways, through thorns and thickets, through the harshness of rocks and the broken crags of mountains, strive with hands and feet toward the palm of victory. They are those, I say, who seek to carry their vessels through the Syrtes <note>dangerous quicksands off the coast of Africa</note> and reefs, out of the turbulent storms and into a quiet, most peaceful harbor. They purchase wisdom at the cost of great poverty; and just as nothing in the nature of things is more excellent than this form of wisdom, so nothing is more outstanding, better, or worthier than this living imitation and likeness of it.

For what, by the Gods, could be more desirable than her? What more outstanding? What better for man? Those who seek her are therefore called **Philomagi** <note>literally "Lovers of Magic"</note>; nor is **Philomagia** anything else, if you wish to interpret it, than the study of the *Opulence and wisdom of the Divine Power of the Great World*. This, moreover, as defined by the assembly of the **Adepts** <note>original: "Adeptorum"; those who have mastered the secret arts</note>, is the knowledge of the most difficult things in nature and of the causes by which these things are sustained. Concerning this, I might rightly use that phrase about to sound from the mouth of Socrates: "O most beautiful and noble picture!" But it is by no means to be purchased by any man for a price—such as gold or silver—in the manner of fields, buildings, garments, and similar things. On the contrary, all riches grow filthy and become as nothing when compared to the symbolism of wisdom.

"We have preferred her," says **Solomon**, the wisest of the kings of mortal men, "above kingdoms and thrones, and we have not likened precious stones to her, because all gold in comparison to her is a little sand, and shall be accounted as clay in her sight." <note>A paraphrase of Wisdom of Solomon 7:8-9</note> Let it not grieve us to imitate this here, and to apply ourselves with all zeal to this end: how we may daily increase our mental inheritance, how we may grow from virtue to virtue, and how we may be able to accumulate the treasures of wisdom. For above all things, the treasure—

<meta>Continuity note: This page continues the introductory discourse on the value of wisdom, following the catchword 'Greece' from the previous page's conclusion.</meta>

# PRELUDE

Wisdom is the most precious thing, according to the oracle of the Easterners—specifically that most wealthy and powerful of men (whom some even believe to have been a King), the prophet Job. He found nothing to be its equal, saying: *Pure gold shall not be exchanged for it* <note>original: "Non commutabitur aurum obryzum pro eâ"; see Job 28:17</note>. For this reason, the "Omega of Orators" <note>likely referring to Marcus Tullius Cicero as the ultimate authority</note>, the prince of philosophers, and that torch of theologians and sun of doctors, Thomas Aquinas, reckon wisdom among the greatest goods of man. It is called the *Torch of the honorable mind*, by whose glory and splendor even the most upright men are captivated.

For so great is the innate love of cognition and knowledge in all people that no one can doubt that human nature is drawn to these things without being invited by any reward. We see how children cannot be deterred from contemplating and investigating things even by lashes; though driven away, they seek them out again and rejoice that they know something. They long to tell others, and are held fast by processions, games, and spectacles of that kind, enduring even hunger and thirst for that purpose. What then of those who delight in noble studies and arts? Do we not see them take no account of their health or domestic affairs? They endure all things, captivated by cognition and science itself, and they balance the greatest cares and labors against the pleasure they draw from learning. To me, indeed, Homer seems to have seen something of this kind in the stories he invented regarding the songs of the Sirens. For it was not by the sweetness of their voices, or by some itch for novelty and variety in singing, that they were accustomed to call back those who sailed past; rather, it was because they professed to know many things, so that men would cling to their rocks out of a desire for learning. For this is how they invite Ulysses:

> Stay your ship, O Ulysses, faithful pride of the Greeks,
> So that you may drink in our charms with your ears:
> For no man has ever sailed past this sea,
> Without first stopping, drawn by the sweetness of our voices;
> Having filled his heart with a longing for all Wisdom <note>original: "Minervis", referring to Minerva, the goddess of wisdom</note>,
> He always arrives at his fatherland more learned:
> We know the heavy burden of Mars, and the miserable slaughter...

<summary>This page discusses the inherent human drive for knowledge and wisdom, citing authorities like Job, Thomas Aquinas, and Homer's account of Ulysses and the Sirens to prove that the pursuit of learning is a natural, irresistible pleasure.</summary>

> Greece, which for so long carried the pledge of Troy,
> And all the traces of things from broad lands.

For Homer had weighed the matter, realizing that the story could not be proven true if so great a man <note>referring to Odysseus</note> were held ensnared by mere little songs; they promise knowledge, which it was no wonder was dearer than his fatherland to a man greedy for wisdom. Indeed, to desire to know all things, of whatever kind they may be, is the mark of the curious; but to be led to the desire for knowledge by the contemplation of greater things is to be considered the mark of the highest men. Nor will it be out of place here, but rather relevant to the matter, that elsewhere in *On Duties*, Cicero—the strength and dew of Roman eloquence—speaks concerning the loveliness and splendor of virtue. He relates that it is so lovely and excellent that, if only it could be discerned by human eyes, it would excite a wonderful longing for itself in the minds of men, and draw everyone into love for it;

> Virtue is an enticer; virtue is the most beautiful maiden,
> Who, once seen, has tormented everyone with love for her.

What that Orator said concerning the loveliness of virtue, the same may be more rightly uttered concerning wisdom. It must be said, therefore, that she contains so much beauty, so much grace, that no one has ever looked upon her closely who did not admire her, and was not incited by her form toward virtue and a more vigilant fruitfulness of life. Plato says that the sense of sight is the sharpest in us, yet with our eyes we do not discern wisdom; oh, how she would arouse burning loves for herself if she were seen!

I have read a beautiful and clever <term>apophthegm</term> <note>a concise, pointed saying or anecdote</note> on this matter: That famous Diogenes the Cynic (of whom it is well known that he spoke the truth while laughing, and most excellently set forth the condition of human affairs) was one day repulsed by Antisthenes. When Antisthenes finally threatened him with a staff to drive him away, Diogenes said to him: *Strike if you wish, but you will find no staff so wild or so hard that you can drive me away from you, so long as you teach me something.* O zeal and fervor for wisdom, uniquely to be emulated by everyone!

That which I remember reading concerning the Assyrians and Babylonians also serves this same purpose. They used to bring their daughters into a certain very large courtyard, as if into a public forum; and regarding them, they established three—

# PRELUDE

...arrangements <note>original: "syntagmata," referring to organized groups or classes</note>; The first was of those whom nature, with a more generous hand, had enriched with the beauty and grace of natural gifts. Indeed, the second group consisted of those who stood in the middle, being neither beautiful nor deformed. Consequently, when young men arrived eager to take a bride, they first wished to take the daughters of the first rank and beauty, but under this condition: that he who received them was compelled to provide a massive sum of money as a dowry. Now, those middle ones, who were neither beautiful nor ugly, were obtained without any profit or payment. Therefore, in their judgment, physical beauty and riches could not be possessed at the same time; they valued taking a beautiful woman so highly that not only was she to be obtained without a dowry, but a price even had to be paid in order to have her. # PRELUDE

It is truly ridiculous for anyone to claim for themselves something for which they were not the cause, or which they have not earned. Therefore, when you wish to see a true estimation of a man and to know what he is like, look upon him naked. Let him set aside his inheritance, set aside his social standing, set aside his honors and the other falsehoods of fortune; let him strip away the body itself and look upon the soul—what it is, how great it is, and of what quality; whether it is great by its own merit or by another’s. For he who praises his own lineage praises the achievements of others. Boasting aside, tell me: what are all men but men? Once possessions, the splendor of clothing, gold, gems, and the rest are removed, men are only men; they do not change except in outward appearance:

> Why do they boast of ancestors? If they look to their beginnings
> and to God their Author, then no one is base-born;
> the whole mortal race rises from an equal origin.
<note>original: "Quid Proavos jactent..." These verses are from Boethius, *The Consolation of Philosophy*, Book III, Meter 6.</note>

True and notable nobility consists in being distinguished by learning, according to Socrates. When he observed a man who was very wealthy and arrogant but endowed with no education, he said, *“This is a horse covered in silver.”* For horses are accustomed to being adorned all around with blankets, trappings, and silver studs, yet inside they are nothing other than horses. Therefore, reason and clarity itself declare that only the wise man is noble. For what does a distinguished birth profit him whom morals defile? Or what does a lowly birth hinder him whom morals adorn and ennoble?

> I would rather my father were Thersites <note>In Homer's Iliad, Thersites is depicted as the ugliest and most cowardly of the Greeks.</note>, provided that I am
> like the grandson of Aeacus <note>Referring to Achilles, the greatest Greek hero.</note> and can take up the arms of Vulcan,
> than that Achilles should produce me to be like Thersites.
<note>original: "Malo pater mihi sit..." From Juvenal, *Satires*, VIII.269-271.</note>

Whoever, therefore, is by his own nature inclined toward good things is noble, even if born of an Ethiopian mother. Most deservedly, then, I might sing:

->The nobility of man is the mind and the image of the Deity,<-
->The nobility of man is the bright offspring of virtues,<-
->The nobility of man is to relieve the wretched man lying low,<-
->The nobility of man is to restrain the raging mind.<-

<summary>This page argues that true nobility is derived from wisdom, virtue, and education rather than inherited wealth or social status. It utilizes classical references to Socrates, Boethius, and Juvenal to emphasize that the soul's quality is the only true measure of a human being.</summary>

The nobility of man is to uphold the laws of nature,
The nobility of man is to fear nothing except base deeds;
The nobility of man is to despise earthly bridges,
The nobility of man is to seek the celestial fountains;
True nobility is prepared neither by gems nor by gold,
Nobility demands to possess something greater,
For the things of wisdom are considered the only true ornaments,
Which fortune both gives and snatches away with her hands:
These things, therefore, are unable to make anyone noble,
For learning preserves the ancestors of nobility within itself.

->§. 3.<-

Indeed, these are charming rhythms and verses worthy of Apollo’s tripod <note>The tripod of the Pythia at Delphi, signifying prophetic or divine truth</note>; by which all of us, who are devoted to Christian Philosophy, are moved to realize that we must always hold a greater account of eternal things than of earthly ones. The things of the earth and of time are to be held as the least of matters. If this is so, we must certainly strive—with as much mental effort as we can muster and as much diligence as we can achieve—to ensure we are not separated from those whose proper lot it is to enjoy the everlasting and blessed life. Whoever wishes to accomplish this (and all who love themselves and wish to live in harmony with nature ought to so wish) will never allow themselves to pursue those things which they believe will be ruinous to others.

->For that would truly be a most mournful thing,<-

That any philosopher should arrive at such a point of rashness and insanity, that for the sake of a moment of shadowy and imaginary little joy <note>original: "gaudioli"</note>, he should not fear to subject himself, knowingly and willingly, to the most bitter tortures; that he should not dread to exchange lasting goods for a fleeting little pleasure; that he should not be terrified to be cast headlong into an abyss of all miseries for the sake of a fleeting, scarcely tasted little delight; that he should not shudder to be tormented by timeless fire forever on account of a single disordered little thought. *Who would not weep for such a fate?* To be excluded from eternal joys for the sake of a momentary little delectation <note>original: "delectatiunculam"</note>, *Who, in telling such things, could refrain from tear—* <note>The text cuts off mid-word "lacrymis" (tears) to match the catchword for the next page.</note>

This brought about the confused chaos of the world, and among the sons of Japheth <note>original: "Japetidas" — referring to the descendants of Japheth, often used to represent humanity or Europeans in early modern literature</note> it sowed the seeds of madness and misery through an unhappy lineage. > True love can be said to be blind.

The *first* is that it strikes all indiscriminately without any regard,

> Love blinds the minds of both the foolish and the wise;

The *second* is that, in the manner of a blind man, it does not see the defects and deformities of the beloved;

*Next*, Justice is similarly depicted as sightless, because she judges all without respect or partiality toward persons; *finally*, Death is blind because it shatters all things without any distinction and mows down whatever lies in its path.

# PRELUDE

> Shaking the huts of the poor with an equal outcry,

For Death is great, powerful, and terrible; she is no respecter of persons, nor does she accept bribes. She holds the poor and the rich alike. Just as a cloth merchant measures out both silk and coarse linen with the same forearm <term>ulna; a historical unit of measurement based on the length of the arm</term>, so Death drags both the master and the servant to the same mill. # PROSIMETRICUM
<note>A literary style mixing prose and verse.</note>

...destined for the uses and delights of the world; yet as soon as the ages have struck against them, and they are cast into the fire and reduced to ashes, who, I ask, could distinguish the bramble from the cedar, the broom-bush from the myrtle, or the sacred laurels from the wild heather? How many people of such sluggish and degenerate judgment would now deny that this abyss of tumults and assaults—the world—can be called a forest in the same way, and men indeed called plants? This is according to the ancient saying of our Theomagus <note>Literally "God-Magician," likely referring to Hermes Trismegistus or a similar mystical philosopher</note>: *man is an inverted tree;*

->And indeed man is called a plant turned upside down,<-

Since just as a tree has its roots at the bottom, so man has his at the top—that is, the hair, which veils the citadel of the entire body, the head. And truly this grove, as long as it flourishes, is distinguished by variegated colors. For some men can be discerned by the "foliage" of their words—are they not indeed slow and dull-witted? Others, however, are eloquent and expressive; some are even Philosophers, craftsmen, or creators of rare things. Others are known by their "flowers," for some are beautiful and others deformed, nor is the manner of their growth the same for all. Finally, it is given to recognize others by their "fruits"—that is to say, by their heroic works or deeds. We see some who are spirited and noble; others wealthy; others still fearful, timid, and daring to attempt nothing because of their poverty. But as soon as that fierce and violent Megaera <note>One of the Furies, here personifying Death</note>, Death, begins to make her incision and hurls the darts of her wrath into them, reducing them all to dust and decay, no distinction is observed any longer. All undergo an equal lot; no mention is then made of difference:

->But all are equally hewn down by the same funeral cord.<-

Choose then, if you can, the heads which you once saw encircled with golden diadems; select then the corpses of bodies once covered in purple and scarlet; pick out, I say, the tongues of such excellent philosophers, of such eloquent Orators of old; point out then the faces of the graceful Nymphs, the Dianas, and the Helens, for whose adornment the gems of the East and all the groves of Arabia...

# PRELUDE

->Striking the huts of the poor with an equal clamor,<-
->As the royal halls, leveling the crown and the diadem;<-
<note>This is a paraphrase of Horace’s Odes (1.4.13), emphasizing that death does not discriminate between social classes.</note>

For Death is great, powerful, and terrible; she is no respecter of persons, nor does she accept bribes. She holds the poor and the rich in the same regard. Just as a cloth merchant measures both fine silk and a coarse shroud with the same forearm-length <term>ulna<note>A traditional unit of measurement, roughly equivalent to an English ell or a cubit.</note></term>, so too does she drag the master and the servant to the same grinding-mill. Death by no means tolerates modest manners; she shows herself no more kind to Barons, Counts, Princes, Dukes, Kings, or Emperors than to the lowest of peasants or beggars. Indeed, with the same foot she strikes the peoples of the North:

> Shriveled by the Arctic frost, and those scorched by a closer sun,
> Those whom the rising Sun <note>original: "Phœbus"</note> beholds, and those he sees when hidden in the sea,
> Those whom his radiance wanders over for a short time, or for a long time from his glowing axis.
> This is the law: here comes the King, and here the flock; here the first and the last rank.
> It is a bitter path, but this mournful way must be trodden by all.
> The ever-watchful gatekeeper of the infernal cave <note>A reference to Cerberus, the three-headed dog of the underworld.</note> must be soothed,
> And the public skiff of the squalid Old Man <note>Charon, the ferryman of the Styx.</note> must be boarded,
> Which carries everyone across with no distinction made.
> Death rushes on, and like a reaper among the ripe ears of grain,
> She cuts down all things, bloodied by her wound-inflicting scythe.
> She does not spare the fortunate, nor the blessed;
> Codrus <note>A legendary figure representing the poor man.</note> descends beneath the underworld <note>original: "Tartara"</note> alongside the wealthy Crassus <note>A Roman general famous for his immense wealth.</note>.

Therefore, just as in a thick-leafed and scattered forest, as long as it flourishes, we see many diverse kinds of trees: acorn-bearing oaks, shade-giving beeches, knotty junipers, prickly hollies, loftily swaying poplars, and the pines that are perpetually green and thick, and other trees infinite in both mass and number, manifold in color and vigor. Among these, some creep along the ground, while others hide their foliage and hair within the clouds. Some are praised for their flowers, others for their leaves, and still others for their fruit. Among them, some are common and lowly, while others are singular and nobler... <insert>nobler</insert>

# PROSIMETRICUM

<margin>G 2</margin>

destined for the uses and delights of the world; yet as soon as the ages have struck against them, and they are cast into the fire and reduced to ashes, who, I ask, could distinguish the bramble from the cedar, the broom-bush from the myrtle, or the sacred laurels from the wild heather? How many people of such lazy and degenerate judgment would deny that this world—this abyss of tumults and supports—can be called a forest in the same way, and men indeed called plants? This is according to the ancient saying of our *Theomagus* <note>original: "Theomagi nostri"; likely referring to Hermes Trismegistus or a similar "divine magician" of the Hermetic tradition</note>; *man is an inverted tree*,

->And indeed man is called a turned-about little plant,<-

Since just as a tree has its roots at the bottom, so man has his in the heights—that is, his hair, which veils the citadel of the entire body, the head. And truly this grove, as long as it flourishes, is distinguished by variegated colors. For some can be discerned by the "foliage" of their words—are not some men indeed slow and dull-witted, while others are eloquent and fluent, and some even philosophers, craftsmen, or creators of rare things? Others are known by their "flowers," for these are beautiful and those are deformed, nor is the manner of growing up the same for everyone. Finally, it is given to distinguish others by their "fruits"—that is to say, by their heroic works or deeds. We see some who are spirited and noble; others wealthy; others still fearful, timid, and daring to attempt nothing because of their poverty. But as soon as that grim and violent *Megaera* <note>One of the Furies, here personifying a cruel and relentless Death</note>, Death, begins to make her incision, and hurls the darts of her wrath against them, reducing them all to dust and rot, no distinction is observed any longer. All meet an equal fate; no mention is then made of difference:

->But all are equally hewn by one and the same cord.<-

Choose then, if you can, the heads which you once saw encircled with golden diadems; select then the corpses of bodies once covered in purple and scarlet; pick out, I say, the tongues of such excellent philosophers, of such eloquent Orators of old; point out then the faces of the lovely Nymphs, the Dianas, and the Helens, for whose adornment the gems of the East and all the groves of Arabia <note>A reference to expensive perfumes and spices imported from the Near East</note> were once sought...

# PRELUDE

Words were not enough; cast out then those cheeks, which formerly consumed so much antimony <note>stibium: a dark mineral used as eyeliner since antiquity</note>, oil of myrrh, mercury sublimate, and purple pigment. Point out then, just once, that beautiful Juno <note>A reference to the queen of the Roman gods, used here to represent a woman of supreme beauty and status</note>, whose elegance drew everyone into admiration and envy, for whom so many suitors perished, and who was always laden with gems, stiff with gold embroidery, and covered in fine linen.

On this occasion, it pleased a certain Cynic philosopher <note>Diogenes of Sinope, known for his eccentric behavior and rejection of social norms</note>, through a humorous deed, to mock the pride of Alexander. For as Alexander was walking past a certain shrine, Diogenes was rummaging through the skulls in a graveyard among the bone-houses of the dead. He contemplated now one, now another; now snatching one up and casting it aside, now seizing another. Alexander, observing him, asked what he, a living man, was doing there among the dead? The Satiric philosopher replied that he was searching for the skull of Philip of Macedon, Alexander's father, but so far he had been unable to find it, because there was no distinction among them.

For just as various kinds of herbs and flowers come to life and flourish in sunny places during the beautiful springtime—what a diversity of colors, brilliance, scents, and fragrances! What variety in width and length! What inequality in vigor and greenery! But as soon as the reaper has cast in his sickle, and the flowers and herbs are cut down to the earth, no further distinction is discerned; instead, all have undergone the same fate, the great and the small together, the beautiful no differently than the lowly. Is not this world, under the monarchy of death, like a certain meadow or greenery? In which humans play the part of flowers and herbs; they all differ and vary among themselves in size, and are unequal in honors and fortunes: but truly, as soon as the Gorgon-like Libitina <note>Libitina: the ancient Roman goddess of funerals and burials; "Gorgon-like" refers to her terrifying, inescapable nature</note> has cast in her small sickle, all very swiftly become peers and equals:

> For rapid death levels all things with a cruel sickle,
> It is the fate to die; death spares no honor,
> The weak and the strong come under the arrows of death.
> The great and the small, the rich, the young and the old,
> Trembling death captures, grim death snatches away.

# PROSIMETRICUM
<note>A work combining prose and verse.</note>

Tell me, where now are the Samsons and Gideons? Where are Hercules and Achilles?

> They have all been swept away by the wind, carried off by the whirlwind.
> O heavenly glory, Apollo <note>The sun god</note> of the radiant world,
> Whose wandering moon, exhausted by the evening vapors,
> Lifts the horns of her nocturnal chariot;
> Record that Alcides <note>Hercules</note> has traveled to the eternal Spirits,
> And to the kingdom of the dog <note>Cerberus</note> reclining at the Stygian court,
> From whence no one is ever said to return:
> O death, death most cruel, tyrannical, and bitter!
> O death, how harsh and how sorrowful are your laws!
> As great a multitude as gathers throughout the city,
> Eager to watch the games of the new theater;
> As great as the crowd that runs to the divinity of Lenaean Iacchus <note>Bacchus/Dionysus, god of wine and theater</note>,
> When the fifth summer has crowned the Sacred Rite with flowers;
> As great a throng as attends the secret rites of the Goddess Ceres <note>Demeter, goddess of the harvest</note>,
> When the holy hour of the long night is reborn;
> So great a multitude grows numb throughout the sluggish marshes <note>The underworld swamps</note>,
> One part walking sadly, vanished after a long life,
> And another part still running, suited to the greenness of spring;
> Corinnas <note>A poetic name for young women</note> not yet despoiled of their maidenly flower,
> And youths whose hair has not yet been cut from their heads,
> And the tiny child who has only just learned his mother's name;
> As if these alone, being cautious in their youth, did not fear
> To drive away the gloomy night with a light held before them,
> The rest wander through the shadows in mournful form,
> Just as our mind is, when the light is removed
> And each person feels in their sorrow that their head is filled
> With the whole earth; the empty clouds stand in a whirlwind,
> Along with dense chaos, and foul, hideous darkness,
> And the rest of the world joined with the blind color of night,
> Until a late and heavy age demolishes us there.

<term>Alcides</term>: A patronymic name for Hercules, referring to his strength and lineage.
<term>Stygian</term>: Relating to the River Styx, the boundary between Earth and the Underworld.

# PRELUDE

> No one comes to this too late, but arrives in due time, from whence
> Once he has turned toward it, he could never depart.
> What use is it to outrun a harsh and wretched fate?
> All this wandering crowd of the world shall depart from the earth
> To the Shades <note>original: "Manes," the spirits of the dead in Roman mythology</note>, and shall set sail upon the quiet waters of Lethe <note>the river of forgetfulness in the underworld</note>.
> Everything that the Evening and the Rising Sun survey shall grow for you;
> Spare those who are to come, O Libitina <note>the Roman goddess of funerals and death</note>, for we are being prepared for you.
> Although you are slow, we ourselves break the threads of life;
> The final hour, which gave us life, has taken it away.

Since, therefore, in natural things, so great a necessity is assigned to this "end" that the <term>Physicists</term> <note>natural philosophers or scientists of the physical world</note> do not fear to establish it as the first principle in every matter—so that, although it is last in the execution of a work, it is nevertheless first in intention and mind—it is necessary then that death, since it is the end and the final line of all things, should be first in all our actions and hold the chief place in all our labors. For just as a mariner, while he steers his ship amidst the necessities of the waves, sits in the stern, which is the hindmost part of the ship; in no different way the <term>Philomagus</term> <note>a "lover of magic" or seeker of hidden wisdom, likely referring to an alchemist or hermetic philosopher</note>, who sails through the ocean of this world's most occult difficulties, must not trust in the prow or the condition of his office to direct the ship of his life and his portion rightly. That is to say, he should not admire his own prerogative because he was pre-elected to secrets before others (for can the clay boast of itself, and say "Aha!" to the vessels, because it was rotated under the potter's wheel into a cup of more fortunate shape?). Nor should he trust in the mid-deck, by flattering himself in the mid-summer of life, counting his honors, dignities, and the abundance of his riches; but rather in the stern, *by recalling to mind the night of death and the very last things.*

This, this is what the prince of genius and learning, <term>Plato</term> (whom I am commanded to call divine, most wise, most holy, and the Homer of the Philomagi), was accustomed to say: namely, that the prudent and the wise establish for themselves a certain school in which nothing else is taught but the brevity of life and the swiftness of death.

<summary>This preface establishes death as the primary focus for the seeker of wisdom, arguing that one must steer life from its "stern" (the end) rather than its "prow" (the beginning). It invokes classical imagery and Platonic philosophy to frame the study of hidden secrets as a preparation for the inevitable end of life.</summary>

# PROSIMETRIC <note>original: "PROSIMETRICUM" — a literary style mixing prose and verse</note>

...and that the meditation upon death is a certain kind of true and upright philosophy. On the other hand, the dull and the foolish inhabit an "Academy of Forgetfulness," because they never remember Libitina <note>The Roman goddess of funerals; here used as a metaphor for death</note> or their final moments, and at all times they deliberate only on how to prolong their years. For it is well established that the wise, the simple, and those who strive for virtue and wisdom die gradually while living <note>meaning they detach themselves from worldly desires while still alive</note>; whereas the wicked, the haughty, and the nefarious live while dying, and by always promising themselves more life, they trample death underfoot. For this reason, it is now clearly evident that he who shapes and devotes his mind to the studies of this gymnasium <note>metaphor for a place of intellectual or spiritual struggle</note> ought to be greedy for nothing else but sacred wisdom alone.

> Though you be master of great houses and much land,
> Your empty shade shall carry nothing to its Spirits. <note>original: "Manibus" — the Manes or ancestral spirits of the underworld</note>

All things will remain here, for all your kin; and whatever you were able to desire in this life, once deprived of it, you shall enter a vile and narrow tomb.

> Bearing no riches at all to the waves of Acheron, <note>A river in the underworld</note>
> You shall stand naked on the tragic shore of Cocytus. <note>The "river of wailing" in the underworld</note>

Kings, the powerful, Princes, and the wealthy are appointed as Gods only upon the earth. Hence the true lover of wisdom—even if he has only tasted wisdom "with books or lips" <note>original: "libris labris" — a wordplay suggesting either superficial study or deep devotion</note> as the saying goes—never pursues gold or the vain breeze of honor. Instead, he clings to the "Galena of the Philosophers" <note>A technical term in alchemy and philosophy; galena is lead ore, but here refers to a foundational or hidden essence</note> which, according to the sound of Holy Scripture, is the storehouse of nature. Indeed, having acquired the value not just of one empire, but of all things and the entire world, he can carry it about in his own pockets; as the Master of the whole fabric of the world, he possesses all things and can rightly say, *I carry all my things with me.*

> Our riches shall fear no thief;
> Let others mock, let the fool mix his wit.

For what use is it, as the Writer of Proverbs <note>original: "Paræmiographo" — likely referring to Solomon or a collector of adages</note> interprets, for a fool to have riches when he cannot buy wisdom?

<summary>This page contrasts the "Academy of Forgetfulness" inhabited by the foolish with the life of the philosopher, arguing that material wealth is lost at death while wisdom is a portable and eternal treasure. It uses classical underworld imagery (Acheron, Cocytus) to emphasize that one enters the grave naked of all but their character.</summary>

### §. 4.

Therefore, I have committed myself to you in the theater of this prelude—provided that my Evangelist <note>The author likely refers to a guiding spirit or divine inspiration, here personified as "Evangelus"</note> does not disdain to steer my small boat through this stormy sea by the most majestic breath of his help—to apply the spur and to point out the rare and clear path to the highest honors and wealth. Behold, Socrates, the god and glory of philosophers, shines a torch for you from the open valley; having attained both human and divine glory <note>original: "Adoream," a Roman term for military glory or a reward of grain</note>, and known by fame even above the heavens, he exhorts you to follow him in this way:

For once, when he had met the young Xenophon <note>original: "Zenophontem"</note> in the street one day, as is noted in the *Apophthegms* <note>A collection of concise sayings or anecdotes</note>, he gazed upon him and noticed from his physiognomy <note>The practice of judging character from facial features</note> that he was naturally inclined and most fit for acquiring wisdom. Extending the staff he carried on his shoulders, he immediately detained him, uttering such words as: "Hey there, young man, where do you come from? Where is bread sold? Where are fish sold?" and other things of that sort. When the physiognomist <note>Referring here to Socrates</note> perceived that the youth had answered the questions in an orderly fashion, he soon added: "In what place, then, do the wise dwell?" The youth gave his answer, saying he did not know. Then Socrates said: "Follow me, and I will instruct you, because it is a shame for you to be ignorant of that which is most worthy of being known, after you have learned other less necessary things." Truly a lesson worthy of the Socratic mouth! But adapting that to my own purpose, I say:

That merchant of wisdom, my Mercury <note>The Roman messenger god, associated here with the transmission of knowledge</note>, continually runs through the streets with his caduceus <note>The staff carried by Mercury, a symbol of commerce and negotiation</note>; if he were to meet you and ask about nuts, or such trifles and less necessary things, you would undoubtedly know how to answer him most exquisitely at once. But if he began to inquire of any of you about the things most vital to be known—namely, where on earth simple and upright philosophy, or the records containing it, might lie hidden or be found:

->Certainly the water would fail you, and your tongue would stick<-
->To your palate; you would be mute, with exhausted and strained brains.<-

<summary>The author uses a famous anecdote of Socrates meeting Xenophon to argue that people often master trivial knowledge while remaining ignorant of where to find true wisdom. He challenges the reader to seek "upright philosophy" rather than being distracted by the "less necessary" details of life.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Xenophon, physiognomy, wisdom, Mercury, philosophy, Apophthegms, education, pursuit of knowledge</keywords>

# PROSIMETRICUM
<note>A work written in a combination of prose and verse.</note>

And indeed, under my own auspices—so that I do not remain stubborn in this regard (since, alas, so many diverse and fraudulent little retreats have been sent out and filled everywhere)—you and the entire court might cry out that this too has passed you by. Oh, what a deplorable art! And oh, our most desperate affairs! But look, hurrah! Be of good cheer even now; to me and to you, *gilded offspring of wisdom* <note>original: "sapientiæ soboles deauratæ"</note>—not mere coin-collectors, nor sophists suffering from a hunger for gold—it has been granted to study nature in the Socratic manner. Follow me:

->I shall lead you into a broad land, and one greatly esteemed,<-

I shall be your future herald, leader, and teacher, you who strive with me to enter the shrines of Apollo, to ascend like a sublime eagle to the highest Cedar of Lebanon, and to climb the "Golden-Born" <note>original: "Chrysogonum"</note> Atlas of Alchemy. Hasten to this asylum and oaken citadel, more impregnable than the Roman Capitol, as if intoxicated by the harmonic tone of the lute-players of this Temple of Song <note>original: "Odei"</note>, as if by a broth from the cup of Lethe <note>The river of forgetfulness in Greek mythology.</note>. These magical grains <note>original: "coccos"</note> plucked from the chaff, these vintages of my harvest scraped from the dross and weeds—these little "Fruits of the Night," I say, or the Phrygian <note>Likely a reference to intricate embroidery or complex craftsmanship.</note> offspring of my spirit and genius, approved by a solemn and Ambrosial choir—I contemplate them with whatever small desire I have, or rather, I embrace them with both arms.

For we are not those "smokes" <note>A play on "puffers," a derisive term for failed alchemists.</note> to whom nothing seems to be true, but rather those who say that certain falsehoods are joined to all truths with such similarity and such rivalry that there is no certain mark in them for judging or giving assent. For the inquiries of the Philosophers, because they are utterly rugged and hieroglyphic, and darkened by the misty perplexities of riddles and opinions, cannot be understood through themselves except by a divinely illuminated man, or an Adept Philosopher <term>Adeptus philosophus: a master who has successfully achieved the "Great Work" of alchemy</term>.

> If only it will please you to listen to me a little,
> From the very cradles of nascent Magic
> (If it is permitted to use small examples for great things)
> I shall repeat the matter for you from deeper down, and I shall provide a paradigm:
> I shall sing of deeds done, though there will be those who say I have made them up.

# PROSIMETRICUM

And indeed, under my auspices—so that I do not remain stubborn in this regard (since, alas, so many diverse and fraudulent little retreats have been sent out and filled everywhere)—you and the whole court might cry out that this too should be passed over. Oh, what a deplorable art! And oh, how desperate our affairs have become! But look, ah, rejoice! Be honored even now, you *gilded offspring of wisdom* <note>Latin: sapientiæ soboles deauratæ; a metaphor for students of alchemy who have been "refined" like gold</note>, you who are not mere money-grubbers nor sophists suffering from a hunger for gold. It has been entrusted to me to philosophize in the Socratic manner <note>original: Socraticè physiculare; to study nature through the dialectic method of Socrates</note> for you; follow me:

->I shall lead you into a broad land, and one greatly esteemed,<-

I shall be your herald, leader, and teacher—you who strive with me to enter the shrines of Apollo, to ascend like a sublime eagle to the highest Cedar of Lebanon, and to climb the "Gold-Born" <note>original: Chrysogonúmque; likely a reference to the mythological or alchemical "birth of gold"</note> Atlas of Alchemy <term>Alchymia: the art of transmuting metals and the soul</term>. Hasten to this asylum and oaken citadel, more impregnable than the Roman Capitol, as if intoxicated by the broth of a Lethean cup <note>A drink from the river Lethe, causing forgetfulness of the mundane world</note> by the harmonic tone of the lute-players of this Temple of Song. These Magical grains <note>original: coccos; likely referring to kermes grains or seeds of knowledge</note> plucked from the chaff, these vintages of my harvest scraped from the dross and weeds—these "Night-fruits," I say, or the Phrygian <note>Phrygian embroidery was famous for its intricacy; here it refers to complex intellectual works</note> offspring of my spirit and genius, approved by a solemn and Ambrosial choir—I contemplate with whatever small desire I have, or rather, I embrace them with open arms.

For we are not those "smokes" <note>original: fumus; likely a play on "puffers," a derogatory term for false alchemists</note> to whom nothing seems to be true, but rather those who say that certain falsehoods are joined to all truths with such similarity and such rivalry that there is no certain mark in them for judging or giving assent. For the inquiries of the Philosophers, because they are utterly rugged and hieroglyphic <note>original: hieroglyphica; meaning symbolic or encoded</note>, and darkened by the misty perplexities of riddles and opinions, cannot be understood in themselves except by a divinely illuminated man, or an Adept philosopher <term>Adeptus: one who has attained the "Great Work" of alchemy</term>.

> If only it will please you to listen to me a little,
> From the very cradles of nascent Magic <term>Magia: the study of the hidden forces of nature</term>
> (If it is permitted to use small examples for great things)
> I shall repeat the matter for you from deeper down, and I shall provide a paradigm:
> I shall sing of deeds done, though there will be those who say I have made them up.

# PRELUDE

By gathering ancient symbols and the "song of the cuckoo" <note>original: "cuculi cantum"; likely a reference to repetitive or derivative knowledge</note> into these new centuries of thought.

Fashion a round circle from the man and the woman, and from that extract a square, and from the square a triangle, and from the triangle likewise make a cyclic circle, and you shall have completed the <term>Mastery</term> <note>original: "magisterium"; the successful completion of the alchemical process or the creation of the Philosopher's Stone</note>; for this is a thing of craftsmanship whose head is of Carbuncle <note>a deep red gemstone</note>, whose eyes are of Jet, and whose feet are of Diamond; and a thousand other things of this kind occur everywhere. Let this be the last of them, serving as a supplement to the rest (to walk in the shoes of the Stoics, who are accustomed to tightening their arguments to a summary):

Purple-haired Phoebus <note>the Sun</note> fathered a little son in the lower world, whom the son of Maia <note>Mercury/Hermes</note> gave to Mulciber <note>Vulcan/Fire</note> to be nourished, and to the son of Philyra <note>Chiron the Centaur</note> to be instructed. We command all posterity to first take this son with the blood of the Eastern Lion (which was conceived from the heavenly frost and earthly warmth, and brought forth in the streams of the Mediterranean Sea by Lucina <note>goddess of childbirth</note> with Aeolus <note>god of wind</note> and the Earth-Shaker <note>Neptune/Poseidon</note> acting as midwives). For this represents the <term>Mercury of the Philosophers</term> <note>the essential "First Matter" of alchemy, not common quicksilver</note>, that secret <term>Spirit of the World</term> <note>spiritus mundi</note>, and the Syrian dew; for his spirit has surrounded the face of the earth, and from its inward parts the "twisted serpent" shall be led forth.

Afterward, separate it from useless decay by the brine of Amphitrite <note>the sea</note>, and purge it with a lye—not one composed of beech or oak ashes and their salt, but a metallic one, which is more durable than the others. Nor should this be done with common water, but with that which is sought from the bubbling spring of Parnassus (differing from the nature of other fountains, existing at the mountain's peak and generated by the hoof of the Medusan Steed <note>Pegasus</note>). This water turned into ice and crystal under the young Trojan <note>Ganymede</note>, because it is of finer parts than stagnant waters or marshy pools; for this reason, it can penetrate more deeply into the innermost parts of the black and foul "philosophical body" to wash it clean.

Finally, cherish the pregnant Goddess who bears twins with a gentle warmth and a kind fire for so long, until—through the wheels of the elemental world and the stratagem of art and nature—the flower of the Sun-god <note>Cynthius/Apollo</note> and the dew of the Moon-goddess <note>Cynthia/Artemis</note> rise up into a certain undivided little body in the form of a hexagon.

# PROSIMETRICUM
<note>original: "Prosimetricum" — a composition written in a mixture of prose and verse.</note>

...and having brought forth a male and a female—a marvel and a doubling of stupendous powers—one must then immediately nourish each separately and fittingly according to their individual nature. They must be whitened with the **soap of the wise** <note>A term for a purifying chemical agent, often alkaline, used to "cleanse" the base matter.</note> and refreshed with **Virgin’s milk** <note>A common alchemical metaphor for a white, nourishing liquid or mercurial water used in the process.</note> until they reach a solid age. Then, she must be betrothed to her own brother, **Paean** <note>An epithet for Apollo or the Sun; here representing the solar/sulfuric principle.</note>, who is clothed in a **cinnabar robe** and attended by a rough **coralline guard**, and joined to him by the wedding torch. For once she is made pregnant by his prolific seed—when, after the passing of the required days, **Vulcan** <note>Fire.</note> returns to reconciliation with **Neptune** <note>Water or the liquid solvent.</note>, and when **Jupiter**, by the help of **Ops** <note>The Earth.</note>, the parent or nurse of **Phoebus** <note>The Sun.</note> and **Phoebe** <note>The Moon.</note>, has fathered **Apollo** and **Diana**—she will bring forth that **Phoenix**, so long desired through many prayers and great costs. This Phoenix is able not only to perpetuate its own life, but also to prolong human health and truly recall the **Golden Age**.

By Hercules, this is a very deep sea, a tangled thing, unnavigable even to the most learned! What whirlpools and abysses are here! Oh, what depth!

> Here is the Charybdis of Zancle, here Scylla and the Capharean rocks;
> Here are the Cyclopean cliffs with a thousand meanders;

And I know not what could be more inextricable than this labyrinth itself. How can the understanding of beginners cross over such rising waves of entanglement, where even the mind of an **Oedipus** <note>The legendary solver of the Sphinx's riddle.</note> is almost suspended and comes to a halt? How, I ask, shall the sails of mortal intelligence be spread, where even immortal things are weakened and drawn in? Alas, the labor of labors, supreme and final beyond all those of **Hercules**! Oh, the steep crags! Oh, the shipwrecking bends! O Labyrinthine windings expressed in imperceptible circumlocution! Everything in this great monument is subjected to crosses, snares, and hazards; nothing here is intelligible, but everywhere we see inhospitable mountains. Oh, how many altars of transposed meanings, how many images and echoes! Oh, how many benches are built in this courtyard, how many emblems marked here and there with fictitious and invented letters! *Who shall read these things?* Oh, what a knot! Truly more indissoluble than the **Gordian knot** itself; by Pollux, it is difficult and in every way like the Herculean knot, in which neither beginning nor end appeared—just as the Gordian knot was said to be, which Alexander, when he could not untie it, cut with his sword. By the experience of poly- <note>The text cuts off mid-word; the catchword "poly-" likely leads to "polychresta" (many-uses) or "polymathia" (great learning) on the next page.</note>

# PRELUDE

Will there be a need for many-layered skill, or the hundred eyes of Argus <note>In Greek mythology, a giant with a hundred eyes; used here to mean extreme vigilance</note>, or even the Delphic sword itself <note>original: "rhomphæâ Delphicâ" – a reference to a versatile tool or a sharp, decisive solution</note> to undo these Vulcanian chains <note>Unbreakable bonds forged by the god of fire</note> and solve these riddles? So deeply are the mysteries of secret things shrouded by the ancients in fabulous and winding sentences and words; the books of the philosophers are full of them, and almost every page is stuffed with allegories and distended with parables—indeed, with such a great abundance of metaphors that nothing could be more crowded.

I, therefore, lest anyone should brand me with a similar mark of envy <note>The "envy" of ancient masters who hid their knowledge from the public</note>, will not entangle the Decrees of Past Lovers of Magic <term>Philomagi: those who love or study the wisdom of the Magi</term> in such repetitions of circumlocution and complexity. Instead, having broken the Pythagorean silence <note>The vow of secrecy required by the followers of Pythagoras</note>, I shall declare the whole matter to honest and chosen disciples in a few plain words. I will fulfill this neglected task without the help of anyone else but, as they say, by my own Mars <note>original: "Marte proprio" – by my own strength or effort</note>; for nothing strictly published on this subject among those works that have come into my hands has met with my approval. Since, therefore, a new kind of usefulness has presented itself, I felt compelled to act. Truly, I have not undertaken the defense of things that are utterly abandoned; for arts do not perish with the death of men, but merely long for the light of an Author. 

You will therefore receive this Little Work of True Magic <term>Orthomagiopusculum: from 'orthos' (true/right) and 'magia' (magic)</term>, composed during these now-shortening nights, since that greater labor of my long vigils will be published later under our auspices. You will rejoice at the opening of this treasury of my Verses, which I have composed with strength; for those things which are treated scatteredly by others—rare and excellent as they may be—I shall transfer all alike into my own concise and Metric style of writing. It will indeed seem incredible how many great things I intend to sing to you here: to prophesy the very pinnacle of human desires, and to offer the most hidden treasure of all the secrets of this world, not in a rambling way, but nakedly and briefly. This shall be my rule, or rather a linear and certain token, by which you may walk as if guided by a thread. O, what elegant love of learning <term>philomathia: the passion for acquiring knowledge</term> I shall bring forth into the midst! With it, as if with the jawbone of an ass <note>A biblical reference to Samson defeating his enemies</note>, you will be able to put the Philistines to flight and lift the gates of the treasury. I shall provide, I believe, a most brilliant guarantee of my promise; therefore, it is fitting that you offer me such faithfulness in your attention as the lot of knowledge I here offer you in this introduction.

<summary>The author critiques the intentional obscurity of previous philosophers and vows to break the tradition of secrecy by explaining the "treasures of the world" through a clear, poetic, and systematic method. He introduces his work as a "Little Work of True Magic" (Orthomagiopusculum) intended to guide the student plainly where others have used riddles.</summary>

# PROSIMETRICUM

Nevertheless, to enjoy these golden feasts, it is necessary above all else for those who wish to labor in this dust with the highest glory, and to cast a similar die of fortune, to have the spirit to act as Leaders <note>original: "Archimandritas," a term for heads of monasteries, here used to mean spiritual or intellectual leaders</note>, and not to slacken their pace with Diogenes running in the stadium. It is told that even amidst the business of public upheaval, having cast aside his little cloak, he began most ardently to roll his tub—his versatile roof—hither and thither without delay. In this tub, like a snail carrying its home <note>original: "domiporta"</note>, he was perpetually enclosed, leading a life of the mind rather than mere existence, not unlike a mind fixed to a wooden heaven. Here he would sweat; here he would be diligently occupied in leisure; here, by acting much, he would achieve nothing, treating everything as such a serious game that the safety of Greece seemed to be enclosed in the tub as if in the Trojan Horse. Indeed, many citizens began to wonder and feel indignant at these actions; when they asked him what he finally intended by it, he explained: "I am moving my tub so that, while everyone else is busy, you might see me being active too; *for he who does nothing, seems to be nothing.*"

Truly a magnificent and divine saying of Diogenes! By which that clever philosopher seems to have wished to indicate obscurely that if nature did not produce "Anacharsides" <note>referring to Anacharsis, the Scythian philosopher known for his wisdom and outsider perspective</note> at home, many are still possible through art and much exercise—men even more Hermetic than the Egyptian Hermeses themselves <note>referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary father of alchemy and philosophy</note>, and more Platonic than the very Platos. These men, broken by no labors and sparing no expense, regretted no wicked deed <note>likely referring to the social transgressions or "madness" associated with deep philosophical pursuit</note> if only their undertaking might succeed according to their heart's desire, so great an ardor for this philosophy had arisen in them.

There are found three animals (says Solomon, the wisest of the sons of Adam, who had indeed obtained wisdom from above) which are the smallest living things on earth, yet are wiser than the wise: these are the ant, the rabbit, the locust, and the lizard <note>original: "stellio," a spotted lizard</note>. Concerning this last one, a small verse exists: *the lizard leans on its hands, and dwells in palaces.*

However, the commentators on the Proverbs of Solomon hold from the Hebrew: *the spider leans on its hands*; which forms roughly this sense: The spider prepares its livelihood with the busy webs of its tiny hands, nor, as the writer of Proverbs says, should we overlook these four...

# PRELUDE

...that these animals can challenge even the most prudent men to a contest, and can prove the ignorance of even those who wish to be seen and heard as the wisest; *and they themselves are wiser than the wise.* <note>original: "et ipsa sunt sapientiora sapientibus"</note>

In what does the wisdom and art of the spider—that cheap and slender little beast—consist? In this: that although she dwells in the courts of Kings, she uses nothing at all except the labor of her own hands to prolong her life for many years. Indeed, she might seem to fall under the judgment of imprudence because, while living in the houses of Kings where there is such a great abundance of food and plenty of every provision, she nevertheless always works anxiously, tirelessly, and industriously within the workshop of her own bowels to weave nets. With these she catches careless flies, so that she may preserve her own life with their blood. If this is so, why did the wisest Writer of Proverbs <note>The "Paraemiastes" refers to Solomon, the traditional author of the Book of Proverbs.</note> attribute such a title of wisdom to this tiny creature? This little animal perfectly deserves the august praise of the prudent and the glorious epithet of the wise because of its natural genius for action, by which it fruitfully instructs men in Spagyria <term>Spagyria: the art of separating and recombining natural substances, often used as a synonym for alchemy</term> and teaches the Wise Chemists. <note>original: "Sophochymicos"</note>

*For the spider leans upon her hands, and dwells in the palaces of Kings:* <note>A reference to Proverbs 30:28.</note> as if to say: what does it matter that the palace abounds in finery, flows with delights, and has storehouses where one thing overflows into another, if I do not seek my food with my own hands? I would promise myself that luxury of the court in vain if I did not eviscerate myself <note>The author uses "eviscerate" to describe the spider spinning silk from its own body.</note> and spend every night and day drawing out threads, weaving nets, and hunting flies, seeking my nourishment through equal labors and cares.

This very thing, by the silent example of its own genius, the spider cries out and teaches to those industrious souls consecrated to *Golden Wisdom.* Even if they have obtained, by the grace of God, a victorious seat and a fortunate home in the opulent kingdom of Alchemy <note>original: "Alchymia"</note>—where the Supreme Operator distributes such magnificent delights and singular favors, where there are so many masterworks <term>magisteria: high-level alchemical preparations or "masteries"</term>, such a harvest of tinctures <term>tinctura: a potent alchemical liquid capable of transforming or healing</term>, and such a superabundant Manna of the sublime art—they will nevertheless receive very little profit from it unless, after the fashion of the spider, they take initiative,

# PRELUDE

Others have handed down their works; I, however, shall here split open the wide wood <note>A metaphor for opening up a difficult subject or "breaking the ice."</note>,

> Let one oar strike the waters, while the other scrapes the sands,

By following only those things from the more celebrated authors which precisely concern the matter itself or the practical application <note>original: "praxin"</note>:

->To have pleased the leading men will be a difficult glory.<-

Namely, so that I may be able to strengthen blinded minds, and soothe with a mitigating doctrine those who have been long and greatly agitated, and rouse them to prompt experimentation (insofar as they may fulfill their certain destiny through suitable paths); yet not with the intent that I should immediately discourse on every subject in the manner of monks, or bring everything into the open by the strength of a small body and a tiny voice: for that would be to commit the fragile little boat of my genius to the abrupt waves of Amphitrite <note>A goddess of the sea</note>,

> To furrow the immense ocean with a modest keel,
> And to fly through the empty heavens on a small wing;
> Is the encounter of Troilus not unequal to Achilles? <note>A reference to the lopsided battle in the Iliad, suggesting the author's humility in the face of great philosophical mysteries.</note>

# PROSIMETRIC VERSE

A Pygmy or a Satyr compared to a Giant, a man of Chios compared to one of Cos, or Dares compared to Entellus <note>original: "Chius ad Coum, Darus ad Entellum" — classical metaphors for a weak or inferior person challenging a superior master</note>: for what can a little lamb do among wolves, or a tiny boy hiding in the midst of hounds, if a mother or nurse does not protect him? Truly, this would be like attacking the Lernaean Hydra <note>original: "Echidnam Lernæam"</note> without the strength of Hercules; for when one of its heads is cut off, ten others immediately spring up. My own poor reasoning, while I attempt to sail through all these hidden mysteries, is nothing other than a narrow and flimsy skiff tossed by the vast whirlpools of a most stormy ocean. The preparation of my meager talent, I say, while I long to reconcile these disorganized matters, is nothing but the bold flight of a tiny gnat or stinging fly which, striving to raise itself higher than usual, is caught by the bellows of the winds, cast down to the earth, and weakened.

Therefore, I shall strive to touch only upon mechanical matters, whispered through the aid of Hermogenes <note>likely a reference to the Greek rhetorician or a symbolic figure of communication</note>, by joining our own smallness to the sublimity of the Giants who were our ancestors; for *it is easy to add to things already invented.* I have understood more than the ancients <note>original: "super senes intellexi" — a common scholarly boast derived from the Psalms</note>. I would be here forever if I wished to match every single thing that can be sketched in the wide field of this subject with the clear truth of the matter and experience, according to the sense of the Authors and interpreters. It shall suffice that we pursue our purpose: to explain more fully for our benefit the fated and inward lines which the finger of God has inscribed upon the Earth.

For it is no concern of mine to know whether fish breathe under water or not, or whether the herring or the whale is the King of the scaly flock; whether the sun is a fiery stone or truly a fiery chariot; whether there is a real face in the lamp of the moon, and why; and six hundred other things of this sort, from which there is no fruit but labor and affliction of the spirit, and a mere waste of precious time. For lost things matter little, but "worn-out time" is a name that cannot be recalled, as Acacesius the Poet <note>original: "Acacesio Metrico"</note> bears witness:

> The loss of things is nothing, but the loss of days is greater,
> For things can always aid things, but nothing can aid the days.

It is told that Diogenes the Cynic once mockingly asked a man who was speaking most subtly and at great length about the stars, how long ago he had arrived from the heavenly regions, seeing as he was so well-acquainted with the celestial government <note>original: "politia cœlestis"</note>. In such a way, Thales...

<summary>The author humbles himself before the "Giants" of the past while arguing that scholars should focus on the "finger of God" inscribed on Earth rather than useless astronomical or biological speculations. He emphasizes the value of time over abstract curiosity.</summary>

# PRELUDE

<margin>I</margin>

Thales of Miletus <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher (c. 624–548 BCE) often cited as the first philosopher in the Greek tradition.</note>, one of the most illustrious among the Seven Sages of Greece, was once absorbed in contemplation. Having fixed his eyes upon the "summit of the world" <note>original: "cosmocolophonem"</note> and the wandering paths of the planets, as well as that glittering army of stars, he sought to foretell something of the future from them, should the Gods only grant a sign. As he gazed with a searching eye, he moved his feet incautiously and fell into a muddy pit that lay right before him. Having broken his legs, so the story goes, he returned home a laughingstock. For this reason, he was deservedly mocked by a sharp-witted old woman standing nearby; she rightly said he deserved to suffer this, for while he was blind to what lay at his very feet, he wished to explore the heavens. Does it please you to hear how that swift-footed poetaster <note>A term for an inferior or pretentious poet.</note> acutely thinned out the tale in verse?

> By chance, while Thales views the fires of the high ether,
> With stumbling foot he slips into a muddy pit;
> When a certain little woman saw him fallen there,
> Who happened to be coming to fetch water with her jar,
> Thus insulting him, when she had reached his side,
> She addressed that trembling head with a mocking voice:
> "Fool, why do you traverse the celestial stars with your eyes,
> When you do not see enough of the earthly things before you?
> And while you strive to predict the future fates of others,
> Can you not see the ditch that lies before your own feet?"

Thus, many "big-nosed" <note>A Latin idiom for those who are overly critical or pretentious.</note> critics still contemplate the heavens and a thousand trifling subtleties; one gapes at omens, while another hungrily pursues quarrels over names:

> Another often brawls over "goat's wool," <note>original: "lana caprina" – a Latin proverb referring to an argument over something completely worthless or non-existent.</note>
> Armed with trifles he fights, as if to say:
> "Let my word not be the first believed, and let me not
> Bark out fiercely what truly pleases me, but let him
> Become learned against all others;"

And meanwhile, they pay no heed to the pit of errors in which they are continually blinded, until at last they are driven to madness as their end. For while this man searches too accurately into the labors of the stars and the turnings of the heavens...

# PROSIMETRICUM

->By surveying his own genius, he feels his mind being twisted.<-
Both that man and this one turn their minds toward murmuring verses, and fall into a madness:

Therefore, Pythagoras—that Old Man of Samos and noble lawgiver <note>original: "nomotheta"</note>—spoke more prudently:

->Those things which, by their own loftiness, are above us, are nothing to us.<-

The same thing can quite aptly be applied here to that famous passage of Esdras <note>referring to the apocryphal book 2 Esdras/4 Ezra</note>; for to him the Angel said: if I were to ask you how many dwellings are found in the heart of the sea, or how many veins are at the source of the abyss, perhaps you would say to me, "I have not traveled the blue waves, nor have I descended into the dark abyss." But now, I have not even asked you except about those things from which you are inseparable, and you have answered me nothing regarding them; how much less, then, can you perceive the wings of the Most High?

In the same way, I refer those "all-wise" men <note>original: "pansophos," a term for those claiming universal knowledge</note>—who argue and dispute so sharply and cunningly about every kind of vacuum—to the spiders and the water-creatures. I say: come now, you who so curiously and scrupulously scrutinize and chase after the emptiness of the stars, the wandering paths of the heavens, the courses of the stars, and the constellations—tell me how a bird so beautifully feathered is made from an egg? And what of the bird for whom iron is a feast <note>a reference to the common early modern belief that ostriches could digest iron</note>? Why do the hands grow numb as soon as the Torpedo fish <note>original: "Narcus," the electric ray</note> falls into the nets, and why can that numbness be prevented even for those carrying something in their hand? And countless other things of that kind; if you cannot perceive these by chance, how will you comprehend the things above? Will you, who claim for yourself an all-encompassing and circular wisdom <note>original: "encycliam," the root of encyclopedia</note>, be able to answer how the earth—which hangs downward by the whirling mass of its own weight—sustains itself in a balanced weight in the midst of the waters? Or how bees weave their honey, spiders their webs, or silkworms <note>original: "bombyces"</note> their threads? But if you do not grasp the little works of tiny animals and worms, how can you grant yourself so much as to presume that the most admirable works of the Divine hand can be known by you? Truly, that glorious wisdom is not to be valued highly; indeed, it differs little from insanity.

They scarcely ever reach the summit of glory because they grow weary under the small but heavy burden of want. Furthermore, due to the rarity of Maecenases <note>Patrons of the arts, named after the Roman advisor to Augustus.</note>, they are held back like ships by the Remora fish <note>original: "Remeliginibus"; a reference to the sucking-fish believed in antiquity to stop ships in their tracks.</note>, which would otherwise travel most swiftly with sails and oars. Truly, a most difficult birth—oh, heavy and calamitous poverty!

Behold Cleanthes—or rather "Phreantes" <note>A play on words: Cleanthes was a Stoic philosopher who worked as a water-carrier (Phreantlos) to support his studies.</note>—that Stoic philosopher; was he not forced, by a lack of money to spend on buying paper, to write down the things he heard from Zeno <note>The founder of Stoicism.</note> upon the bones of oxen and pieces of broken pottery?

Similarly, Plautus, that most festive comic poet, honored with every praise for his wit; was he not also, on account of poverty, bound to an ass-mill <note>A mill turned by a donkey; Plautus reportedly worked as a manual laborer in a grain mill when his business ventures failed.</note>? And when he was free from that work, without any interval of time, he composed the plays which he sold. The same was true for me—*I am becoming stiff with cold* <note>original: "obstrigisco"</note>—and it was much more truly in me, so that I might most deservedly sing:

> I am a teacher to the poor, because I studied as a poor man,
> When coins were lacking, I put my tunics up for sale.

I say, these same examples were much more evident in me, who—*I am turning black* <note>original: "nigresiam"</note>—unless I had continually, through all the adolescent years of my life, endured many and incredible adversities and hardships for the zeal of the Muses. I have had innumerable heartaches, and was as if entirely swallowed by the waters of tribulation. With my eyes clouded by a heap of calamities and the sadness of full affliction, I was in the depths of Pimpla <note>A hill or fountain in Pieria sacred to the Muses; here used metaphorically for deep, perhaps drowning, immersion in study.</note> night and day. I wandered alone in foreign lands, withdrawing into the fields and living under tents <note>original: "Papilionibus"</note>, without property or money, and without any eloquent companion on the road to serve as a vehicle <note>A reference to the proverb that a pleasant companion on the road is as good as a carriage.</note>, even though it is a solace to the wretched to have companions in their pains.

Indeed, if it is now permitted to report it: by that little teaching of Antisthenes' disciple...

# PROSIMETRICUM

I was once far more miserable than that man who lacked all things <note>Referring to Diogenes the Cynic</note>; for he at least always had his rounded tub, which he turned about like a sunflower following the throne of the sun. But for me—oh, the grief!—because of my frequent and excessive beggary, there was scarcely even a wicker basket available under which a hen might crouch with her chicks. He had a tunic and a small cloak which he spread over himself, the meager furniture of beggars, a staff, and a bread-bag; but I frequently had none of these things. I was not only less provided for than Diogenes, but poorer than any tattered little beggar. After a little while, though wise too late <note>original: "cum Phrygibus" (with the Phrygians); a Latin proverb referring to those who only become wise after disaster has struck</note>, I began to groan deeply over my status and misfortunes. I often clapped my empty palms together and shook my feet with uncertain steps; I scratched now this part of my head, now that (though nothing itched), and sobbing with a half-closed mouth, I stammered out I know not what complaints. Weary in the day of my anguish, groaning frequently with a heavy soul, I cried out to myself:

> Woe is me! Why did I ever learn, or unroll a book,
> And why did any letter ever delay my eyes!
> Why should I, a fool, attempt the useless study of Alchemy?
> No wealth of a fine household <note>original: "Res Laris," referring to the Lares or household gods/home</note> is left to me.

I am a tiller of parched earth; why do I torture myself? I would hardly dare to say that Hercules <note>original: "Alcmenades," the son of Alcmena</note>, driven by the hatred of Juno, was subjected to as many assaults of persecution as I have been by these various impetuous storms of affliction. Added to this is the fact that my pious and elderly parents both departed to the many <note>original: "ad plures profecti," a classical euphemism for dying</note> this year. Having been at one time ill-informed, they drew forth streams of burning tears from my reddened and moist eyes with their mournful appearance and their wailing sighs throughout the town. Oh, if only speech were granted to the trees and fields! They would surely testify that, as the stings of my sorrows grew heavier every day, I was harassed and tormented more sharply than the Romans <note>original: "Romulidas"</note> were by Juno <note>original: "Saturnia," daughter of Saturn</note> on account of the rape of the Phrygian Ganymede—treated like a most despised vagabond, the lowest of men, or a common barbarian <note>original: "Allobrogem," referring to the Allobroges, a Celtic tribe</note>.

Unless they wish at some time to be a laughingstock and a slave to others with ignominy—just as I am now, I who have clearly borne the burden and heat of the day, and worked diligently in the vineyard, and now another shall reap, and indeed bountifully, where he sowed nothing, or at least very little, and shall enter into my labors. And yet, I foresee that someone here perhaps will quietly consider within himself that there are always those who easily could and would be willing to help, provided that there is candid communication on this matter between those who love Fortune <note>wealth</note> and those who love Minerva <note>wisdom/the arts</note>. I agree that the Philosophers (who carry all their possessions with them wherever they go,

> And to whom every soil is a fatherland, as the wave is to the fish,
> And as whatever lies open in the empty world is to the birds)

could move forward in such an instance requiring so little. This is according to the saying of the philosopher Aristippus; when he had one day demanded a talent of gold from King Dionysius of Sicily as a reward for his labor, the King said: "How is it that you, since you are a philosopher, demand gold from me? Nature herself makes wise men rich; you do not seem to imitate the others who, by despising gold and riches, preach that philosophers and wise men can never lack anything." He replied: "Give me first the coin <note>original: "tinni mihi," literally "clink for me"</note> which I seek from you..."

> Behold, the wealthy knight goes forth in wagons and chariots of state,
> While behind him, Plato drags the foot-soldier Aristotle.
<note>original: "En it dives eques plaustris rhedísque curûlis, Ponè Plato peditem raptat Aristotelem." The author uses the great Greek philosophers as symbols of wisdom being subservient to mere material wealth.</note>

In the houses of the opulent Glutton <note>Latin: Epulo; a reference to the "Rich Man" from the biblical parable</note>, the dogs and other beasts were feasting sumptuously, while the wretched and torn Lazarus—a most innocent man and a singular delight of God—was dying of hunger before his gate. Truly, matters are conducted even worse in the house of this World today than they once were in the palace of the Glutton. For the cruel, the wicked, and the impious, who live in the manner of dogs and beasts, overflow with delicacies and delights; they gluttonize and feast. Yet the merciful, the servants of God, the poor, and the humble almost perish from hunger and are oppressed by extreme necessity. 

Alas, what <term>ataxia</term> <note>disorder or confusion</note> and <term>dyspraxia</term> <note>malpractice or ill-functioning</note> this is in the world! What abuse, what disturbance, what chaos! *Fortune favors fools:* the inept take possession of honors, the dull-witted are elevated and appointed to high dignities, while the authentic live in infamy and reproach. The wise are rejected and thrust down from their duties; the ignorant and unskilled are presented with the laurels of victory. The dullards and pimps are enriched, while the "Daedaluses" <note>skilled craftsmen or inventors, after the mythical Daedalus</note> are left at the mercy of hats and feet <note>likely meaning they are reduced to menial service or wandering</note>, and the wise fall into extreme poverty. 

Horses <note>metaphor for the noble or swift</note> solicit for favors, yet promises are made to donkeys; the worthy are neglected, and the unworthy are judged as capable. The inventions of the learned and the upright are laughed at as trifles or old wives' tales, while the counsels of fools are embraced as oracles. Therefore, can the World not be best baptized as a <term>democracy</term> <note>The author uses this term pejoratively to mean a "rule of the masses" or "mob rule" where hierarchy is lost</note>, in which everyone wishes to be supreme and to be in charge? Is it not a poorly ordered kingdom, devoid of <term>sophia</term> <note>wisdom</note> and <term>politia</term> <note>organized government or civil order</note>, in which brutal men—who follow their appetites like beasts—command, govern, and prescribe laws to the wise? Is it not, I ask, to touch the quick and bind it in a word, a brothel?

> In which all things are done for the sake of hellish coins,
> Where you can scarcely see one who is not touched by the love [of money]
