# PROSIMETRICUM

...indeed, who shall escape? For truly, the human heart is full of diversions and windings; who can know it, depraved and inscrutable as it is? <note>A reference to Jeremiah 17:9: "The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?"</note> Who then can penetrate it with thought, or who can see through it clearly? Who would dare to claim it is free from any error? And what is even worse, the very signs established to direct our way often lead and mislead us, drawing us away from the right path. For a beautiful and gracious face surely suggests a kind and lovable heart, but it is a deceitful sign, because grace is deceptive and beauty is vain. <note>original: "fallax gratia, & vana eft pulchritudo," referencing Proverbs 31:30.</note>

->Under the skin of a lamb, a wolfish mind often lurks.<-

The tongue, indeed, offers itself as a guide for this path, but it weaves together and prepares various deceits;

->Not so many monsters dwell in the wind-swept sea,<-
->As the wicked tongue frequently encounters in its deceits.<-

Now truly, of all the inventions of the heart, the evil ones are recognized with the greatest difficulty; for a man, as much as he is able, seeks always to hide and cloak them. Fish but once for his failings, and reproach this or that man for his evil mind; soon a thousand shadows of reasons, causes, hiding places, arguments, and mantles are ready at hand, with which the depraved intention and the foxy soul may be most honorably clothed. For no perversity and no cunning lacks its reasons; scarcely any vice lacks its little cloak <term>palliolum: a small cloak or cover used metaphorically for an excuse</term>; almost no wickedness or fallacy is not excused by a beautiful pretext; none are left without their hiding place; everyone offers some argument for why they have gone astray. Truly, for every vessel its own lid is found; in the very midst of noon, in the clear light, the thickest shadows are drawn over, and the day is often wrapped in such an ingenious semblance of night that you would swear it was a most certain eclipse. How many eclipses of this kind, *O God*, are to be seen in this day and age!

# PRELUDE

I might still pluck flowers from there, since that noble pair of friends once saw the most hidden sea of Spagyric philosophy <note>Spagyric refers to alchemy, specifically the art of separating and recombining natural elements, often associated with Paracelsus.</note>. Theophrastus <note>Likely referring to Paracelsus, whose given name was Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim.</note>, seeing that one of them overflowed with wealth while the other was afflicted by a scarcity of means, said jokingly: *If they are friends, why then is one so rich and the other so destitute?* He wished to show that where sincere friendship is sealed, adversities and prosperities ought to be shared in common; it is not right, but rather against the laws of friendship, for a poor and needy friend to be deserted by a wealthy one.

->True love will never abandon a wretched friend.<-

Let us enter more deeply into this rose garden and see what our Plato—who is like a certain divine philosopher—says concerning love. In his dialogue on love <note>Referring to the *Symposium* or *Phaedrus*.</note>, he says: *Love is the parent of excess and of will.* Truly, I do not quite grasp what he said here; if it is the parent of *excess*, why does he immediately say it is also the parent *of will*? I, on the contrary, would rather say: *Love is the parent of will and of excess.* But far be it from me! The divine Plato spoke divinely here when he said, *Love is the parent of excess and of will*, which is as much as if he had put forward that for one who truly loves—after everything has been poured out for the one he loves, after everything has been spent and paid out for that person's honor and reputation—there remains only the desire to pour out, spend, and pay out even more. This desire is so great and so pure, as if he had poured out, spent, and paid out nothing at all: *the parent of excess and of will.* This, this is the Lydian stone <note>A touchstone used to test the purity of gold; here meaning a "true test" or "criterion."</note> of true and genuine love.

But I shall pluck only one more flower as I am about to exit this Rose Garden, as a conclusion and a sort of crowning gift. From dawn to dusk, from the first rising until the setting, it never ceases to watch the Sun with greedy eyes, as if its whole life depends on the sight of the Sun, and as if to live, for it, is to see that most serene and illustrious planet. # PROSIMETRICUM

...pious, when it is clothed by him in the most beautiful light of starry rays? By no means, says Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), a Roman author and natural philosopher famous for his "Natural History."</note>, that curious and studious observer of nature's secrets; for how small a kindness would this be, if it only worshipped the shining Phoebus <note>A common poetic name for the Sun or the god Apollo.</note> with a bowed head?

We have many times mentioned the miracle of the Heliotrope <note>The "sun-turner" flower, likely a marigold or sunflower variety in this historical context.</note> turning itself with the sun, even on a cloudy day: although a cloud may place itself in the middle and hide the sight of that most pleasing and bright star—as if through the greatest envy—so that the flower, most desirous of seeing it, cannot look upon it, it nevertheless does not cease to follow. Even on a cloudy day, when the wind mixes everything together, amidst these injuries, it turns toward its friendly planet. Why so? How is this? Pliny responds, *so great is the love for the star*, from which it happens that it follows the cloudy sky no less than the serene. If the admirable plant followed the glowing planet only when it smiled upon it brightly, it would give no proof of arising friendship; but because even on a cloudy day, as if with a head lowered in reverence, it inclines toward it in every direction—even though the storm prevents sight by the intervention of clouds—that is the most brilliant proof of true and sincere love, *because so great is the love for the star*: and so, by the silent warning of this flower,

> A true friend ought to be known by the pulse;

Not by the pulse of the *right hand* <note>The "right hand" symbolizes prosperity and good fortune.</note>, of prosperities and happiness, while one possesses favorable fortune and good health, and abounds in all things of this life under a generous God; but by the pulse of the *left hand* <note>The "left hand" symbolizes adversity or ill-fortune.</note>, and by this: if someone has loved a friend constantly, even when fortune has turned away from him, stripped him of all goods, reduced him to want, and cast him down into the rank of beggars. This is the most upright friendship, this is sincere love that deserves great praise; this is the smooth Lydian stone <note>A "touchstone" used to test the purity of gold; here, a metaphor for a test of character.</note>.

> Just as we test yellow gold in the fires,
> So must faith be tried in hard times.

Everything everywhere is most foully filled with simulation, deceit, hypocrisy, frauds, lies, masks, and flocks of masked swindlers. Everywhere there is an abundance of words and ceremonies, but little charity or faith. The words are beautiful and the ceremonies are charming, but the heart swims in bitter gall. Therefore, not without merit is this workshop of hypocrisies—the world—baptized in Holy Scripture as a dissembler, a liar, and an impostor; for on its exterior face it displays everything as truly beautiful, charming, and sincere, yet it cheats the buyer, since within it hides filth, loathing, pretense, and lies. *Oh, what a crafty world!* And certainly, has this not happened to me in reality more than once, as I have experienced? # PRELUDE

2. Following, therefore, in the footsteps of my predecessors and our elders, I wished to make it known through this simple observation that I intend to interpret the sayings of the ancient Magi <note>original: "Magorum"; refers to the ancient wise men or practitioners of the Hermetic arts</note> for orthodox and well-read minds. I seek to explain their mystical, yet most true, meaning, which they went about covering and veiling with eternal types, allegories, parables, and circumlocutions. This meaning concerns that **tempered substance** which the violence of fire cannot separate, nor the dross of the earth defile, nor the muddiness of water alter, nor the touch of air overshadow. By this substance, every hard body becomes soft, and the soft becomes hard; the fleeting is fixed, and the foul is illuminated with a marvelous brightness. This was called by the father and prophet of philosophers the *strong strength of all strength* <note>original: "totius fortitudinis fortitudo fortis"; a famous phrase from the Emerald Tablet of Hermes Trismegistus</note>. This is likewise that truth hidden by the poets, specifically in the fables of the Gorgon, and of Jason and Medea concerning the Golden Fleece. It is of the nature of the Sun—the heart, the form, and the flower of the Sun, and the Golden Tree from which, if the fruits are plucked, new ones immediately grow back. And this is that clay figure which always hardens in the fire, and this is that waxen image which melts in the same:

->As the clay hardens, and the scented wax melts<-
<note>A poetic reference to the dual action of the "philosopher's fire" which can produce opposite effects on different materials simultaneously.</note>

In short, by one and the same fire, this is that strong and strongest thing which conquers all and draws all to itself; and this is that which is separated from its own body, about which the philosophers, prophets, poets, and others have sung such wonders.

# PRELUDE

2. Just as it is customary among locals, or those who are well-known in a city, to rarely seek profit through writing or small pamphlets, nor to begin their business by displaying its location on strips of bark <note>original: "philyraceis indiciis"; referring to early writing materials or signage</note>—partly because everyone knows their business well enough, and partly due to a reluctance, or rather a swelling of a modest mind, because what is welcomed by a stranger or foreigner always sounds harsh in one's own fatherland—so, on the other hand, it is the custom of arriving foreigners that as soon as they have touched the threshold and reached the hearth or the place toward which they were sailing, they immediately signal the roles of their lives through various consultations or undertakings. Some do this with theatrical displays or garlands; some with doors or small boxes; and many others (those, evidently, whom the Deity of Fortune has favored more generously) finally do so with letters of recommendation to friends and old acquaintances. In short, everyone strives as contentedly as possible to advance the gamble of their own status.

3. Therefore, since I have recently arrived here—under a favorable omen, yet with a sinister catching of the breeze, I fear—and as a complete stranger, and since the condition of my trade forbids me from bargaining in the manner of the common people, and since I conversely lack patrons and have no supporters to make my cause flourish, I use these papers <note>original: "schedulis"; small sheets or handbills</note> not unseasonably, yet not by my own choice, but rather as if bound by fate, in the place of Maecenases <note>A reference to Gaius Maecenas, the famous Roman patron of the arts; here meaning wealthy protectors</note>, and I substitute these sheets as a pledge for them.

4. > We have borne in our age as many Lernaean hydras of evils <note>The Hydra of Lerna was a many-headed monster slain by Hercules; here it represents multiplying problems</note>,
> As the fiery stars that shine in the star-bearing heavens:
> And I have suffered as many mockeries as there are species swimming in the sea,
> And as many as the brooks and rivers that flow toward the Ocean;

If these things happen in the green wood, what will happen in the dry? <note>A biblical allusion to Luke 23:31, suggesting that if the innocent suffer, the fate of the wicked will be worse</note> Truly the hand of the Lord has touched me, chastened me, and tamed me; and I have been instructed like an untamed bullock.

> An age shaken by adverse events brings enlightenment,

> And that which is pressed shines more brightly with a cleansed face,

Yet, *may I perish*—believe me in this—even if perhaps I desired it before, I speak now from the depths of my heart: I do not seek it now.

> I am not now greedy to prepare *wealth without end*,
> Nor do I plow the hidden sea with the fires of Chemistry <term>Alchemy: the art of transmuting base metals and seeking spiritual perfection</term>;

> *I am no longer the "I" who I once was.*

> The crown woven from green linden-bark lies cast aside.

# PROSIMETRIC <note>original: "Prosimetricum" - a literary style mixing prose and verse</note>

I am now acting entirely like Diogenes <note>original: "Diogenizo" - to imitate the Cynic philosopher Diogenes of Sinope</note>, and I laugh at everything, holding it all in indifference. I am like Diogenes, who, when asked by Alexander the Great if he wanted anything from him, said nothing else except: "Only that you step back a little from the sun," for Alexander was casting an annoying shadow while Diogenes was sunning himself. They say Alexander was so delighted by this response that, returning to his followers, he said he would wish to be Diogenes if he were not Alexander. Thus, it seemed a complete paradox—even unintelligible—to many when I responded to those offering the most lavish conditions with nothing other than *that they should stay a little away from my light*. By this, I mean that it pleases me to live in my own way.

I do this especially because I know there is nothing—however useful, glorious, or pleasant it may be—in which the heart of man may find rest, except in God alone. From this, I feel I can rightly take the opportunity to propose a very pious question: namely, why did God, having established all other things, then create man? He had created the heavens and filled them with angels; the earth also, into which He sent the animals; and the air, which He assigned to the birds. When He had already established all these things, only then did He finally create man. But why, I beseech you, Lord, do You create a part so noble and of such great dignity now, when no place remains among the created things to assign to him or in which he may dwell? Where then will You place man? What space will he occupy? Which element will he enter? Will You bring him into heaven? But the angels will resist, crying out that heaven was destined for them. Will You move him into the air? But the birds will struggle against it. Shall he live in the sea? But the fish will not endure it. Shall he inhabit the earth? But the animals will stand in his way. Tell me then, disinherited man, what is to become of you? But let us not go too far; wait a moment, and you shall hear the reason.

The Creator of all, God, wished—once all other things were established and placed in their locations—to create man at the very end to show that He Himself is man's sole inheritance and possession. He alone is the center of man, in whom man must find his rest if he wishes to find peace for his soul. But why is this so? How...

# PRELUDE

What is this? What kind of philosophy is this? What does a thing hold within its center? My teacher <note>original: "meus ab auribus," literally "the one at my ears"</note> responds with three things: rest, preservation, and union. For truly, all things rest, are kept safe, and are united in their own center. Hence, that delight of God and glory of the Doctors <note>St. Augustine of Hippo</note> cries out with a full throat: *Lord, You have made me for Yourself, and my heart is restless until it rests in You!* These are truly emphatic words, swelling with a spiritual vein; while we weigh the occasion of these words with the examination of a keen mind, we see that every thing takes its leisure only in its own center, and nothing is content until it obtains its appointed end. For all the works of Divine Goodness are circular and perfect, rotated like a sphere toward the very One from whom they came forth.

From the beginning, before the first dawn of His creation, God—placing nature before all things—made four simple bodies <note>the four elements: earth, air, fire, and water</note>, from which He later constituted all mixed bodies. Of these mixed things, He made some intellectual, some sensitive and vegetable, and some purely intellectual. Some, however, He created solely from the rarity <note>fineness or lack of density</note> of the elements, and for this reason, our heart is restless until we come to Him. For the rarity of all elements ascends toward the fire which is above the stars; therefore, we also, being fashioned from that same substance, rightly stretch upward toward God as toward our single principle. 

However, all sensitive and vegetable things, being made from the thickness <note>density</note> of the elements, are distinguished by their different species; when they are dissolved through death, they are—not without reason—returned to the earth and water as if to their own mother. Indeed, the thickness of the elements naturally and continually tends downward toward its center, namely the earth, just as our fire here below always creeps upward until it reaches the elemental fire to which it is kin. Thus the philosopher applies himself entirely to his studies until he obtains knowledge; the sun hastens assiduously until it arrives from the East to the West. The winding rivers go until they reach the Ocean, to which they are tributaries. In short, every thing naturally inclines toward its own goal; once this is held, it rests within it. Therefore, since the center of our heart is only that eternal Creator of the whole universe,

# PROSIMETRICUM

Eternal and most excellent God, since our heart is the image of the most holy Trinity <note>original: "Triados"</note> and is capable of the infinite good for which it was created, why should it not be restless until it returns to Him who made it for Himself? Why, furthermore, should we not offer up every affection, every love, and our whole heart as a most noble votive offering <term>anathema: here used in the ancient sense of a gift dedicated to a god</term>, as a monument and pledge of love? In the temple of Faunus <note>The Roman god of the wild and fertility</note>, not far from the river Lethe <note>The river of forgetfulness in the underworld</note>, I remember reading this enigmatic inscription:

> The Divine Creator of the world demands from us
> A semicircle, a sphere, and the first letter in the name of Rome.
> <note>This is a word-puzzle: a semicircle (C), a sphere (O), and the first letter of Rome (R) spell "COR," the Latin word for heart.</note>

I have read the same thing elsewhere in another way, like this:

> Take the head of a dog, and of a sheep, but the entrails of a deer;
> Offer these to God, and then you shall be blessed.
> <note>Another word-puzzle: the head of a dog (C, from *Canis*), the head of a sheep (O, from *Ovis*), and the middle/entrails of a deer (R, from *ceRvus*) again spell "COR" (heart).</note>

These things denote nothing else, at least by my interpretation, than that God demands our heart for Himself; for as many desirable things as this whirlpool of sailors and this labyrinth of shifting sands <note>original: "Syrtium"</note>—the World—possesses, just as many things are found to be unsatisfying.

> You are a witness, Midas, who with insatiable throat
> Desired gold with too much cleverness.
> A witness is Euclio <note>A miserly character from the plays of Plautus</note>, who, while crying out for the double years of Nestor <note>The long-lived hero of the Iliad</note>,
> Grunted amidst his heaped-up wealth.

For just as a horse is not satisfied if we put a wagon-load of bones in its manger, nor a dog if we assign it a wide meadow of hay—because bones are not the proper food for a horse, nor hay for a dog—so in exactly the same way, the mind of man will never be satisfied by any created thing. This is because no created thing is its proper food, but God alone. For our soul, or our heart, is trigonal or triangular <note>A common medieval and Renaissance metaphor: the heart is triangular to represent the Trinity, while the world is a sphere; a sphere cannot fill the corners of a triangle</note>, and therefore it cannot be satisfied by the spherical world, but only by the Trinity which is its equal and like unto it. This I shall explain with this decisive, though well-worn, little story.

# PRELUDE

Among the Nobles, several philosophers renowned for their intellect and learning were summoned so that he <note>likely referring to a patron or prince mentioned on the previous page</note> might delight his mind for a little while and fish out the depths of their knowledge. He set before them this question, or problem, to be debated and discussed: *What, of all things in nature, is the greatest?* At this, with everyone’s ears and minds alert, *some* said Mount Olympus, which they claim is ten stadia <note>an ancient Greek unit of length; ten stadia is roughly 1.1 miles</note> high:

->Lofty Olympus transcends the ethereal clouds:<-

To which *another* added that if the controversy concerns the height of mountains, Atlas far surpasses it; for Atlas surely rises not only above the first

->Region of the air, but with its entire peak reaches<-
->Into the neighborhood of the Lunar circle, and<-
->Seems to prop up the very Heaven of the firmament,<-
->And continually touch the stars, because greatest Atlas<-
->Turns the axis on his shoulders, fitted with burning stars.<-

A *third* had devised something greater than the whole earth, namely water, which originally surrounded and encircled the entire globe. A *fourth*, thinking he would hit the mark <note>original: "papagallum jaculaturum," literally "to shoot the parrot," a Renaissance idiom for hitting the bullseye</note>, pronounced the sun the greatest of all things, inasmuch as it exceeds the entire world in size one hundred and sixty-six times. But truly, the *fifth* spoke closest to the truth when he proposed that the human heart is the greatest and most capable of all things. He proved this in the case of that "chick of Mars," Alexander <note>Alexander the Great</note>, the son of Philip. For when Alexander once heard Aristarchus <note>likely referring to Anaxarchus, the philosopher who taught the plurality of worlds</note> teaching that there are many Worlds, he could not restrain his tears, because he had not yet even subdued one. It became necessary for his teacher Aristotle to write a small book about the "single-world" <term>monocosmos: a philosophical treatise arguing there is only one universe</term>. Yet even with one world subjugated, Alexander's heart, more capacious than the Universe, gaped longingly for more:

->Go now, you madman, and rush through the wild Alps,<-
->To please schoolboys and become the subject of a speech.<-

# PROSIMETRICUM

-> One world is not enough for the youth of Pella <note>original: "Unus Pellæo juveni non sufficit Orbis." A reference to Alexander the Great, who was born in Pella and famously wept because there were no more worlds to conquer.</note>. <-

Truly, they dissuade us from dropping the anchor of our heart’s ship in the sea of earthly love within this dwelling of mortality; for it is a ridiculous error if we think these temporary and momentary things can provide quiet.

# PRELUDE

By my faith, it is most subtly argued that this racecourse of goads and this sea of dangers—the World—is aptly called a Labyrinth, since it is entirely *labor within* <note>original: "labor intus," a common medieval etymological pun on the word "Labyrinthus."</note>. Political and civil honors, even if they seem to promise us much rest, are lying, because the successes of this age are the lies of fortune. You may be illustrious with many titles and ancestral portraits, celebrated for great glory in arms, and well-imbued with various kinds of disciplines and the equipment of learning,

->Born of a wealthy lineage with ancient Janus.<-

Yet, as a finishing touch, you will find that motto most true: *labor lies hidden within*:

->Under much thunder and tumult are the Great Ones.<-

### §. 10.

Hence King Demetrius <note>Likely referring to Demetrius Poliorcetes, a Hellenistic king known for his turbulent life.</note>, being well-acquainted with the night of the world's clouds, its frauds, and its waves, used to say above all others that if anyone knew how heavy it was to bear a scepter, and what hardships, anxieties, and restlessness stable beneath the steps of Kings, scarcely anyone could be found among the common people—provided they had any regard for their own safety or rest—who would solicit a Kingdom, accept power, or even pick up a crown from the ground. *For who can be in honor without pain, in preference without tribulation, or in sublimity without difficulty?* What that distinguished King said regarding a kingdom must certainly be applied to all the allurements of this life, and proclaimed with full throats:

->How a slight little gain pays for heavy servitude!<-

*Observe the human heart from the rising of the sun even to its setting, walking through these marketplaces of the world; some are captured by the sweetness of a favorable breeze, others follow pleasures, others wander after riches—which are acquired with labor, possessed with fear, and lost with grief.* Magnificent words, by Hercules! O, therefore, you Courtiers of the World <note>original: "Cosmocortisani," a hybrid term implying those who serve the world as if it were a royal court.</note>, you err and slip utterly, while you [think] yourselves wisely...

# PROSIMETRIC
<note>original: "Prosimetricum" - a literary style mixing prose and verse.</note>

You think you act wisely; indeed, you persuade yourselves that great prudence and wisdom are found in conducting the affairs of this world, in acquiring honors and dignities, in pursuing pleasures, and in scraping together riches. You believe it is a mark of notable civility and elegance to frequent the fellowships and societies of men and to be publicly affable; to spend your days pleasantly and joyfully, to live in luxury, and even to hunt for pleasures. You think this is honesty—finally, you believe that to laugh, to dance, to jest, and to rejoice is the true life of man, and that he who does not do these things cannot live among men. But fie! Oh, you Phaeacians <note>A reference to the luxury-loving people from Homer's Odyssey; here used to mean "gluttons" or "lazy seekers of pleasure"</note> and mad clients of the world, you are blind; your concepts are empty and your prudence is false, because nothing but *labor lies hidden within*,

> Merely the vain phantoms of safety.

Those who ardently lust after the possession of riches and an abundance of gold and silver easily persuade themselves that these things will be sweet and honeyed to them; but they lie, and they are only *labor within*,

> Carrying nets full of hooked briars;

As Truth itself, that great Aesculapius <note>The Greek god of healing; here applied to Christ as the healer of the world's soul</note> of the world, Christ the Lord, bears witness: *Namely, that riches are piercing thorns.* Therefore, though our chambers, sewers, windows, and houses may all appear golden, they are nevertheless made of clay and are filthy. Such was that ancient Babylonian idol, Bel, which seemed to be entirely of gold, since it appeared as such on the outside, but inside it was actually clay. Daniel, that interpreter of divine secrets, uncovered this trickery, saying: *Do not be deceived, O King, for this thing is clay within and bronze without*,

> Bel was externally most shining, covered everywhere
> With bronze, but inside he was nothing but vile mud.

Reeds and canes growing in marshy and wet places seize the eyes of passers-by with their beauty and external greenness; but if they are opened, they are empty and displeasing to the sight. Oh, what a mystery, and how appropriate to the matter we are treating!

# PRELUDE

<note>original: "PRÆLUDIUM"</note>

—let us recognize! For is the world not, in the very same way, nothing but a muddy and foul-smelling swamp? Its honors and riches are like reeds and stalks, outwardly splendid and beautiful, but only in appearance; for within

They are nothing great, and their image deceives;
All that you see in the World is nothing but a grand void.
<note>This couplet emphasizes the Baroque theme of "Vanitas," where the world is seen as an empty illusion.</note>

Everywhere among nations and lands, many such illustrious provocations of the eyes and senses are seen; many great miracles of native beauty. For who does not know that in one place, the most pleasant green groves and the sprouting meadows of gardens are admired, where the purple of burning roses, the grace of the spring violet, or the vintage of the darkening grape are praised? Elsewhere, the small beds of budding flowers or the snow-white lilies are esteemed. Here, the Golden Dust of the <term>Philosopher's Stone</term> <note>original: "Sapientum Lapidis" — the legendary alchemical substance capable of turning base metals into gold.</note> is longed for; there, the pale glint of heavy gold entices; in another place, the rich veins of silver and lead ores are flattered. Furthermore, what else do the weights of glowing pearls and flashing jewels, or the prices of sparkling gems and berries seem to us, if not proofs of the most abundant charm and pleasure? And yet, alas! All these things, whatever they may eventually be, are mere pictures and empty fictions; *nothing but squalor and labor lurking within.*

For this entire life of ours is nothing but a lying dream, in which we do nothing but sleep; and while sleeping, we see nothing except empty and false images. Death itself, however, is the awakener, which, by opening our eyes, also discloses and reveals the truth of all things. That which we thought was good, pleasure, honesty, jubilation, and delight while sleeping, we shall recognize as nothing but evil, pain, labor, hardship, infamy, and reproach once Death itself has roused us. Accordingly, when we lie down in a bed of delights and fall asleep on the feathers of pleasures, our mind fashions wonderful phantasms for itself; indeed, we seem to ourselves to be wealthy, sublime, fortunate, and the happiest of mortals. It happens no differently to us lovers of this world, who—after wasting our oil and labor, after enduring immense toils—hoped that the desire for our goods, riches, and pleasures would abundantly satisfy us, only to be ridiculously deluded, left with a stench instead of a sweet fragrance,

-> Carrying nothing besides a great void. <-

# PRELUDE

For this nest of ours, which we call the world <note>Latin: *mundus*</note>, is a certain adulterous swindler, a hook-setter, and a most shrewd forger. Indeed, it incites every person to strive for the honors which it merely paints over; to crave the riches which it covers in soot; and to pursue the delights and pleasures which it offers. Yet it lies and mocks us, for whatever it polishes and touches up is empty, useless, futile, and mutilated. Away with such intolerable folly and greatest madness—namely, that of those blinded by the passions of the world and driven mad by fatuity.

> For all the anxious little labors of this Stygian <note>Referring to the River Styx; here meaning hellish or worldly</note> sphere,
> Which I know to be nothing, but held back as vanities,
> And phantasms emptier than a hollow vapor.

For the world passes away, and the lust thereof: its pleasures shine indeed like a lit candle, whose flame is beautiful and sustained as long as its fuel lasts; but when the fuel is spent, everything turns into smoke and stench.

> Riches are smoke, and honor a stench, and pleasure a briar,
> And whatever we love is but a likeness of smoke and thorns;
> And yet, is there any whom this smoke does not entice,
> Or whom this thorny, smoky bait does not press under its yoke with weeping!

Such is the end of all worldly things; for although the splendor of their vanity may cheer us now, in the end it will bring forth many loathings and remorses, and all things are

> Destined to depart into dust, and wind, and ashes,
> And into thin wisps of smoke.

-> §. II. <-

The ingenious fables of the ancients often contain great lessons, and I find something extraordinary in the story of Queen Juno, who was worshipped as the Goddess of riches. Pluto and Juno were therefore held to be the two Deities of wealth <note>Latin: *divitiarum Numina*</note>, to whom altars were dedicated and gifts sacrificed under this name: but in the character of Juno, the air is also signified...

# PROSIMETRICUM

<margin>Juno as the air</margin>
...was foreshadowed; and just as Jupiter represented fire, Neptune water, and Ceres earth, so Juno represented the air in the "comedy of the Gods." Consider now the twin duties of the Saturnian goddess <note>Juno, daughter of Saturn</note>, for she was both the Goddess of wealth and she represented the air, presiding over that region in which we breathe. But what did learned antiquity intend when it fashioned the same Juno as the Goddess of both the air and of riches? Without doubt (preserving the mystical sense of the philosophers), it intended to signify that in this world, wealth and air, majesty and summer heat, pleasure and the wind are the same thing:

> The world indeed anoints the outer lips with honeyed things,
> And is fashioned to move on wheels more charming than enough,

But inside it pierces with a thousand thorns, and fills the vitals with destruction and bitterness, because,

> As Juvenal <note>Roman satirist known for his biting social critiques</note> says, it overflows with more aloes than honey:
> The joys which the world creates with a friendly image are deceptive,
> O boy, through the art of Cypris <note>Venus/Aphrodite, goddess of love</note> for your own punishment.

That Almighty God and Creator of all things constantly mixes delights with sorrows and prosperity with adversity; where there is plenty, there is a swelling; where there is a nut, there is a cross; where there is wealth <note>original: "Dis," referring to the god of riches</note>, there is strife; where there is honey, there is gall. Ah, what a hypocrite the world is! Its conceptions breathe pain, its births smell of restlessness, the womb is a mere workshop of frauds, the private parts nothing but a dung-heap and a nursery of deceit; the cheeks and breasts of women are nothing but drops of funeral dirges; outwardly indeed they appear beautiful and pleasing, but turn the sack over once, and inside there is nothing but wickedness and falsehood.

> Go now, and catch the lethal arrows of the world,
> If such empty joys swim in so much gall.

Rightly, therefore, all these sublunary <note>things beneath the moon; i.e., earthly and changeable</note> matters and all the goods of the world are to be considered as nothing; and that motto should be carved upon a tombstone, which I leave as a perpetual monument for those born hereafter:

# PROSIMETRICUM

Indeed, it is entangled in a labyrinth: for the tiny, tender sprouts have need of incessant relief, refreshment, and vigilance; those reaching puberty require continuous guarding, and those more mature are often nothing but heartaches.

What pleasure, therefore, I ask, is there for the female sex <note>original: "fœmineo ſexui"</note> when we weigh the matter fundamentally through the entire span of life? Once their seed has been received in the mother's womb and endowed with the gift of every perfection and life, it suffers violence in that workshop <note>original: "ergaſterio," a term often used for a Roman workhouse or prison for slaves</note>; it draws breath through slippery enough cords, floats in putrid and foul waters, and is rolled about in the obscene wallowing-place of the womb. Once these enclosures are burst and the bars of that dark prison broken so that it may enjoy the sun’s radiance and the world’s bright lamp, for a space of at least two years it is bound round with ribbons and cradles as if with shackles and manacles. Thereafter, for the whole remaining time of life, it is always restrained by the strictest yoke, partly of parents and partly of a husband, and is fastened in by the tight pressures of garments. Their youth is spent not for their own sake, but to please men; and while they please them, they are meanwhile pierced by perennial torments. If there is by chance any little delight for them while men neigh after them and they are a source of pleasure, that joy is so vain and fleeting that in the course of only nine months it daily threatens the deadly punishment for this tiny pleasure. They cannot undergo this without a violent risk to life and the exquisite torture of all their limbs, as if that supreme Righteous Judge <note>original: "orthocrites," from the Greek for a judge of integrity</note> and just searcher of criminal actions, God, seems still to demand from them an account of the great fine by which they cast down all men and themselves.

Therefore, you might deservedly call woman the pinnacle of calamity, the origin of lamentation, and the beginning of groaning. If, then, as is the truth, so many and such great evils surround and envelop that weak sex, then by Hercules! <note>A common Latin exclamation of emphasis</note> those untainted virgins <note>original: "virgines incontaminatæ"</note> are born under a wished-for and fortunate star who, free and secluded in a blessed cloister, inhabit their sacred convents <note>original: "cœnobia"</note> before they know the value of this world's delights and the charms of fleeting pleasure.

# PROSIMETRIC WORK

By joining themselves with a solemn torch to Christ—who was a beggar on earth, naked and crucified—they may possess him in the heavens as the King of the pole and the soil <note>original: "Rege poli solíque," meaning King of heaven and earth</note>, the parent of light and life, and the measurer of death. Truly, what an incomparable reward! Oh, thrice-noble prize for these tender young virgins! It is that they may cling to him alone and meditate upon his service, praise, and glory. To him they will offer sacrifice with pure and chaste melody and a wondrous-sounding voice, while their lungs are filled by the swelling breeze of divine love. Anointed by the hidden nectar of its heat, they will be drenched to the very marrow with super-celestial delights, and by a far longer and brighter torch of honorable pleasure than can be enjoyed by those shut up in this earthly dwelling and foul prison of the world.

Nay, indeed, if you weigh all those things—and whatever delights the world possesses—against those joyful or delicious things which are in the heavens, they will seem like filth and stench. For whatever exists in this foul-smelling pit of Venus <note>The Roman goddess of love, here used to represent carnal or worldly lust</note> or earthly love ought to be called a seducer, arisen from the regions of the brothels.

Because this lower globe of ours is like a false and deceitful workshop, all of whose goods—I mean even the most noble and famous creatures—are nothing but signs, types, and certain marks of the riches and wares contained in that most ample storehouse of divine majesty. Who, therefore, if they are wise, will not most gladly exert themselves and fight for that wealthy <term>polyplusia<gloss>a Greek-derived term for "great wealth" or "abundance"</gloss></term> of the heavenly Jerusalem? How much effort is exhausted for tiny little towns, which cost so much labor, calamity, and blood? Or how much for a small scrap of earth or a minute little fortification? And yet, the entire world is but a tiny point compared to the measure of that heavenly City.

# PRELUDE

If, therefore, the earth—which seems so vast and so spacious to us—is so small compared to the axis around which the sun moves in its rotation, how tiny must all other smaller and thinner bodies be, if they are compared not just with that prince of planets <note>The Sun</note>, but indeed with the even grander things held within the interior of the heavens? I say more: even if all Greece stood in arms, if it wore down Troy in a ten-year war, if it burned the entire city, and if the battle was fought with the blood and death of so many most noble youths and heroes all for one Helen—alas, what a plague! For that reason, I boil over with a worthy madness:

->So foul an adulteress is sought by so great a war!<-
<note>Original Latin: "Expetitur tanto tam turpis adultera bello!" A common poetic sentiment regarding the vanity of the Trojan War.</note>

What, then, is it right for us to do for the sake of contemplating that uncreated beauty of God, for that most transcendent form of eternal truth or divinity? For the <term>hierodulia</term> <note>Sacred service or devotion</note> of Christians is incomparably more beautiful than the Helen of the Greeks; yet here, alas, an imaginary shadow <note>Original: "umbella," literally a sunshade or parasol, used here as a metaphor for worldly distractions</note> often bereaves us of heaven, of God, and of all good things, and involves us in eternal evils!

| | |
|---|---|
| O Man, a creature of God, | Why, since you are soon to die, |
| And to be reborn in the flesh, | Do you have so little care, |
| ->For everlasting glory?<- | |
| If you knew how great that glory is, | You would certainly not perish, |
| Nor would you so go about worldly things, | Or thirst so for human things, |
| ->Vain and transitory.<- | |

By Hercules, what a sweet excursion from a honeyed river! For what is more glorious, what is more victorious, than to have the whole world beneath one's feet after leaving the world behind? Oh, incomparable light! Oh, spark from an unquenchable brand! You, a strong and impregnable heart, you can do what no one else can: to effect, to entice—for who can tear away an adulterer, snared by the birdlime of his usual lust, from the long-established habit of filthy slipperiness? A mistress in the skin, for whom all the baths of the world are not enough for cleanliness.

# MIXED PROSE AND VERSE

> (Baths do not cleanse the crow, nor the harlot,
> For neither does the crow become snow, nor the harlot clean by water)
> <note>original: "Balnea cornicem non purgant..." This medieval proverb suggests that external washing cannot change one's internal nature or deep-seated habits.</note>

Can one be dragged from the deep filth of vices by prayer or by price? Divine grace and charity have indeed dragged and torn souls away, reaching even to the division of the soul; it has led away the Mary Magdalenes, the procuresses, the Pelagias, the Laises, and the Thaises <note>The author lists famous converted sinners and courtesans from antiquity and hagiography to show the power of redemption.</note>, and daily leads so many tender daughters, educated in the Sybaritic fashion <note>term: Sybaritic (luxurious or self-indulgent, after the ancient Greek city of Sybaris)</note>, away from parents, patrimonies, marriages, riches, and delights—leading them, as if from the breasts of the world, to the wounds of Christ. Therefore, in the face of such considerations, if the very *medicine of the philosophers* <note>original: "philosophorum pharmacum," likely referring to the Philosopher's Stone or universal panacea</note> were offered to me to spend, I would refuse it; and, to speak as I feel, I would value it at about what the poorest woman, Hecale <note>A reference to the poor old woman who hosted the hero Theseus; a symbol of humble poverty.</note>, would give. For, to finish in a word, I am now enriched by the knowledge of these things alone, resting sweetly in my own skin:

> Now I support and strengthen myself by my virtue alone,
> And I seek honest poverty without a lavish dowry;
> This is the one remedy most suited to my grief.

For I know that it is not expedient for salvation for everyone—and especially for me—to have the freedom of riches and honors along with health. Is this not a common theme, not only in divine but also in human literature? Are not the holy writings and sacred books full of this persuasion?

Does not a man, when he rises too high in a place, feel his brain turned upside down, so that he cannot judge well concerning the smallest things existing below? Similarly, the owl: the higher it flies by day, the less it sees, does it not? It is no different for us; established in high majesties and in the day and clarity of worldly dignity and prosperity, we lose the vision of true wisdom. *When man was in honor, he did not understand* <note>A paraphrase of Psalm 49:20, suggesting that worldly success blinds one to spiritual truth.</note>; because it is most true, and truer than truth itself, that pleasures, riches, and the flatteries of this world are the principal cause of the fall of so many wicked men, and of the horrible damnation of their souls.

<summary>The author argues that worldly wealth and high status blind the soul to spiritual truth, citing historical examples of converted sinners who chose the 'wounds of Christ' over luxury. He concludes that humble poverty is a safer path to salvation than the 'Sybaritic' life of the elite.</summary>

# PRELUDE

->Did not swollen fortune indeed deceive Croesus? <note>Croesus was the King of Lydia, legendary for his wealth, whose pride led to his downfall.</note><-

The foolish and insane World-Lover <note>original: "Cosmophilus"</note>, for whom everything flows according to his wishes, who enjoys the prosperous wind of fortune and rejoices in the smooth calm of his affairs—he who, I say, is beyond the reach of the storm and swims in rivers of delights and pleasures—cares nothing for God, does not think of death, does not fear judgment, does not shudder at hell <note>original: "tartarum"</note>, and has no concern for his soul or salvation. And this alone breaks his neck; this is the cause and occasion of his ruin and destruction.

->Here I am but a stammerer, because I am understood by no one,<-
->And an earthly boy will pluck such woven threads.<-

The moon, that mistress of the night, is not said to be darkened or suffer an eclipse except when she is full; for as long as she is half-full and curved into horns, she remains free from such a failing. In the same way, a man is not seen to fall away from the good unless he is honored with status and distended with riches. But these matters must be expanded upon more broadly here, and this sequence must be woven through: that same Phoebe <note>A poetic name for the Moon.</note>, when full, is further removed from the sun from which she borrows her light; so we, the wealthier we are and the fuller of resources, almost always live further removed from the Sun of Justice <note>A common theological metaphor for God or Christ.</note>. It is said of a certain sea fish that, noticing the sea is stirred up, it wanders through the waves secure and fearless, knowing as it were that it will not be caught by fishermen at that time. Not otherwise does the wise man, who has the matters of his soul at heart, rejoice in the tempestuous time of tribulation, knowing that through this he will be safe from carnal fattening and snares.

->For indeed riches, luxury, wealth, and honors<-
->Transform morals, but rarely for the better.<-

Then one lives like the Helots <note>The subjugated labor class of Sparta, often used in literature as examples of forced excess or debasement.</note>; one lives like a Greek, one carouses like a Greek <note>original: "græcatur, pergræcatur" - Latin idioms for living a life of luxury, excess, and dissipation.</note>. Truly, in prosperous circumstances, there is an excessive forgetfulness of human fragility; buried in the mire of pleasures and the hay of riches, we gluttonize and haunt taverns.

# PRELUDE

There is nothing that must be so greatly avoided, especially in the years of youth, as the habit of practicing secret vices <note>original: "furta," literally "thefts," but used here as a metaphor for clandestine sexual sins or "stolen" pleasures</note>; for this itch, and the wicked ruin of impressionable youth, once it has thoroughly taken root and miserably enticed the age of the first downy beard, can almost never be eradicated thereafter. The vice of lewdness is an utterly horrendous and nearly incurable evil.

> Medicine heals all human pains,
> But the habit of love alone is curable by no art.
> <note>A quote from the Roman poet Propertius, emphasizing that long-standing passion becomes a permanent state of being.</note>

The Ancients indicated this very thing quite aptly under the veils of mythical mysteries. Apollo was desperately in love with the beautiful Daphne; she, scorning her lover, rejected all his services as if she had been hardened into flint. She was so implacable, unbending, and tearless that she would not allow herself to be moved by prayers, nor would she listen to any manageable words, nor could she be induced by any price, nor moved by even the most terrifying threats to grant anything to his wishes. Apollo, somewhat ashamed that he saw the power of his own divinity frustrated, transformed the woman into a laurel tree—since he had been unable to pour his love into her. And as he turned over higher thoughts in his mind, while the fires of love burned through his heart desperately and stubbornly:

> Phoebus <note>Another name for Apollo, the sun god</note> loves this tree as well, and placing his right hand on the trunk,
> He feels the heart still trembling under the new bark,
> And embracing the branches like limbs in his arms,

He gives kisses to the wood. Desiring to kiss the laurel, because the hard Daphne had refused him, the wood also recoils from the kisses; as difficult as Daphne was, so rigid was the laurel; it would not permit sweetness and fled from his embraces. To what end, do you think, does this fable of the Ancients look? It is to signify the efficacy of habit in love, and how firmly it adheres to the soul, and how difficult it is for it to leave. Daphne was averse to Apollo, who, even though he had changed her into a laurel, truly loved her; and she, on the other hand, even though turned into a tree,

# PRELUDE

> If you drive her away, who will there be to sing such things?
> This light muse of mine is your great glory,
> Which sings of the head, the eyes, and the little red lips of a girl,
> And how her feet may move softly, etc.
<note>original: "Quam si dispuleris..." This quote likely refers to the inspiration found in romantic or "light" poetry.</note>

Just as Cupid was already winged, so his mother <note>Venus</note> was depicted by the Ancients treading upon a tortoise. But what was the reason that they painted wings on Cupid, yet a tortoise at the feet of Venus? The messenger of the Gods <note>Mercury</note>, full of wonder, addresses Venus thus:

> O Paphian Queen! <note>A title for Venus, referring to her sanctuary at Paphos.</note> What is this appearance? What does that
> Foul tortoise mean, which you, Goddess, press with your soft foot?

For the famous sculptor Phidias fashioned her in such a form; it is very well known that wings signify swiftness, while the tortoise is a sign of slowness, so that no one is ignorant of it. For that reason, the tortoise is called:

> Slow-stepping, grass-stepping, house-bearer, and thick of blood,
> Which Apelles of Cos painted beneath the feet of Venus.
<note>Apelles was a renowned painter of ancient Greece, famous for his "Venus Anadyomene."</note>

Since it has little blood, and perpetually carries its own dwelling around, and is hindered by the grass as it walks only in the meadows, is it any wonder that it moves like wool <note>softly</note> and slowly? Now the question returns: why, I ask, did learned antiquity add wings to the armpits of Cupid, and a tortoise to the feet of Venus? I shall say (by explaining this fable morally now; though at another time I shall explain it according to the laws of nature and most properly: by the wings, the Mercury of the Philosophers <term>Mercury of the Philosophers: a sophisticated alchemical substance representing volatility and spirit</term> is designated, and by the tortoise, the Salt of the World <term>Sal Mundi: the "central salt" or fixed earth in alchemical theory</term>, or the central salt, which arises as something fixed within or beneath it). 

Antiquity did this so that, by that emblem, it might ingeniously overshadow two effects of love. It indicates that he who loves has wings, with which he can carry himself in the swiftest flight into the house of her whom he prizes; but that he should depart from there happens as painfully and as slowly as if he had the feet of a tortoise, greatly weighed down or hindered.

Accordingly, the softness of the flesh miserably blinds and enchants men, and keeps them from the leisure of sublime things—especially those pertaining to the salvation of the soul—and most painfully of all, at some point, it obfo- <note>The text cuts off mid-word; the catchword "obfo-" likely leads to "obfocat" (suffocates) or "obfumat" (darkens) on the following page.</note>

# PRELUDE

Therefore, it is only too true what I have said: namely, that the vice of luxury <note>The Latin *luxuria* here refers specifically to lust or lewdness</note> is sometimes unlearned with the greatest difficulty and can hardly be hidden. What did Jupiter intend when he turned the girl into a cow? Was it not so that he might secretly carry out his thefts of love with his transformed mistress, and thus the maiden for whom he perished with longing might remain hidden? Indeed, he certainly intended this; but observe how his own cunning mocked him, and how the very caution with which he busied himself to cover her up actually revealed the matter. See how, by the same steps he took to hide her, he led others to the knowledge of his own lust and wickedness. For that girl, transformed into a cow, wherever she pressed her tracks, silently and cleverly

> Betrayed herself, and pressed down her name and her misfortunes;
> A letter instead of words, which her foot drew in the dust,
> Carried out the sad evidence of her changed body:
<note>original: "Prodebat, noménque suum...". These lines are quoted from Ovid's Metamorphoses, Book I, describing Io revealing her identity to her father.</note>

For since a cow has a round and cloven foot, as often as she trod upon the sand or gravel, she formed an "I" with the cleft and an "O" with the roundness. Therefore, with every step, and as often as she planted her feet in the earth, she expressed and, as it were, wrote out her name, **Io**. Thus, by the same path through which Jupiter wished his dear little friend to remain unknown, she became known. She never put her feet to the ground without simultaneously crying out "Io, Io," as if saying with a clear voice: "I, I am that Io who is the beloved of Jove; I am his darling, I am his delight, I am the rival of Juno," etc. The Sacred Pages <note>The Bible</note> likewise teach us that this same petulant spirit is stirred up in favorable circumstances; for was not that portent among men, that miracle of the world, known above the heavens for his many victories

> And for his Herculean strength, Samson,

resting in the lap of Delilah <note>original: "Dalidæ"</note> when he was seized and bound by the Philistines? And was not this carelessness the occasion of his ruin? Truly so; just as many of us, though still illustrious for our works of virtue, sometimes fail to provide for ourselves because we are too indifferent, and meanwhile

# PROSIMETRIC <note>A work combining prose and verse</note>

As long as we lie in the lap of pleasure and the flesh—which is a Philistine and a treacherous Delilah <note>original: "Philistæa & proditoria Dalida"; referring to the biblical figure who betrayed Samson</note>—we are often overwhelmed by enemies and fall into the ultimate captivity, which finally becomes the occasion of our destruction, ruin, and perdition. I shall skillfully place this matter before your eyes anew; hear these wonders.

On a certain day toward sunset, a wealthy man of great renown retired with his entire household to a most pleasant villa for a sumptuous feast, intending to indulge more freely in pleasure with his companions. Here the house was secluded and abundant; the chambers, especially the Master's <note>original: "Domini"</note>, were adorned with various tapestries, the couches draped with canopies, and nothing was not excellently prepared for pleasure. Among the servants, however, was a wicked man who, during such a cheerful drinking bout, mixed a lethargy <note>original: "lethargum"; a drug inducing deep sleep or coma</note> for the Master and his fellow servants. Thus, most were surrendered to a deep slumber as much by the wine as by the drug. 

At midnight, while the living slept almost as if dead, that vile betrayer of his Master received thieves and robbers—the scum and dregs of humanity—into the house through unbolted doors. When these men had plundered the building, they turned all their violence upon the Master of the house. It had been too little for them to have inflicted a great loss unless they also added a horrible spectacle: therefore, they carried the drowsy Master out of his bedroom and out of the house as if he were a corpse, and left him abandoned in an open field. 

Meanwhile, the sky was thrown into confusion by foul tempests; lightning flashed, thunder roared, and rain-clouds plummeted. Thus at last the drowsy Master began to stir, to look around, to tremble, and to think himself transported to another world. He was horrified and struck senseless to find himself on the bare ground, outside his bedroom, outside his house, without servants, beyond all help and solace, amidst rains, amidst the turbulent injuries of the air and storms, stiff with frost, abandoned under an angry sky, and in every way most wretched.

Do you wish for me to name this man at once? Grant me pardon: every one of us is that most ruined man when we make time for pleasure, to whom that most wicked traitorous servant—namely, the luxury of the world—offers a potion of cataleptic trance <note>original: "catalepsin"; a physical state of lack of response and muscle rigidity</note>. Thus we, the "good Masters," are led into destruction—

# PRELUDE

It is characteristic of one who is drowsy not merely to slumber, but to begin to suffer notably from a deep lethargy. We may be moved, plucked at, warned, or pushed, yet we are not roused from our stupor; those whom cataleptic <note>A medical condition of the time involving a trance-like state and muscle rigidity</note> inclinations overcome do not open the eyes of the intellect. Nor do we feel anything while we fall into a heavy sleep, intoxicated upon the bed of the flesh's delicacies. To be sure, the hawk sometimes flies into the heights, yet it continually turns its eyes back toward the earth so that it may snatch the prey it desires from there. We imitate the nature and habits of this kite <note>A bird of prey known for scavenging</note> when we imagine ourselves wise in our luxuries and refinements. For sometimes we do indeed seek the heights by "tasting" deep things and transcending the very clouds of heaven, but because we gape with desire for human things, we perpetually gaze at the ground.

->§. 13.<-

Let that greatest Doctor of the Church, Aurelius <note>Referring to Saint Augustine of Hippo, whose full name was Aurelius Augustinus</note>, present this delicate matter with the subtlety and breadth of his words, which my own ignorance and insignificance cannot achieve: *The trifles of trifles and vanities of vanities, pleasures, riches, and friendships hold us back and ensnare us here, tearing the garments of our flesh. Riches divide us; they grant pride, arrogance, and vanity.* I was once asked by a certain student of mine—one more modest and better than the rest—what sort of man I might perhaps become if I were suddenly to become wealthy. I immediately replied with a counter-question: "Tell me, my son, what sort of creature would you be if you were suddenly and secretly to become a lion?"

> You often ask, my son, what I might perhaps be like,
> When I become wealthy and suddenly powerful;
> Do you think I can predict my future character?
> Tell me, if you were to become a lion, what would you be?

I would have answered just as much: a lion and a rich man are the same thing, and not without reason. For as long as we are strong through the power of money—the root of all evils—and overflow with a torrent of riches, we then grow proud in the manner of a lion and go beyond our proper bounds. Then the little worm of pride in one's resources wounds and intoxicates our soul, and removes the light of reason; then, I say—

# PROSIMETRICUM

How pestilential is that swelling pride, that insane smoke, that infernal enchantress <note>original: "effascinatrix"</note> which inflates us, corrupts holy thoughts, strengthens our own passions, and provides both the material and the torch for vice. It entices us then, like the clear fountain of Narcissus <note>In Greek mythology, a youth who fell in love with his own reflection and died of longing</note> which miserably caused that enamored man to perish, and opens wide for us the path to the underworld. I may therefore rightly exclaim:

> O unhappy riches of all wickednesses,
> And wealth, the incitements to evils!
> In prosperous affairs, man is almost never not insolent;
> For strong are the feet that can tolerate such feasts:
> That dire lust, the companion of fortune, steals upon them;
> Neither the accustomed clothes nor the former hall please them anymore.

Those who keep silkworms <term>bombycum: silkworms</term> say that because those silken moths live upon the green leaves of the Mulberry tree, they are so tender and delicate that they are terrified by the slightest crash of the heavens or a peal of thunder. Often, they interrupt the work of spinning they have begun and die. In exactly the same way, we who are accustomed to "greenness"—that is, feeding upon pleasures—are so tender and soft that if ever we begin a good or pious work, as soon as the first opportunity to sin is offered or the first thunder of temptation rolls in, we desist from what we started, and thus we mostly die within our own cocoons <note>original: "fomentis," literally "warmth" or "bandages," here referring to the silkworm's environment</note>. Therefore, that flower and torch of Insubria <note>A region in Northern Italy; the author likely refers to St. Ambrose of Milan</note>, who is sweeter in deed than in name, and who seems to have had honey in his mouth before he had words, comes forth with his honeyed eloquence on this subject:

> Prosperous things have tripped up and enticed many,
> Whom cruel punishments were unable to break.

The vein of these verses is indeed thin, but their beauty lies in the virtue of their divine meter. Oh, our madness! But oh, the immense ocean of divine mercy and the unrewardable goodness of God! For that which we frequently imagine happens to us by bitter and unjust fortune is actually nothing other than the result of the paternal and merciful providence of God.

# PRELUDE

It happens to us just as it does with a wet nurse who, in order to wean an infant, smears her nipples with gall, mustard, or wormwood, so that the child, sensing the bitterness, withdraws from sucking the milk. In the same manner, like a most kindly nurse, God leads us—His pupils—away from the breasts of this world and the sweet milk of fleshly pleasures. He constantly brings our own weakness to our memory and leads us to a continual meditation on death, in which the entire happiness of our life consists. To this end, He deliberately and with forethought coats riches, pleasures, and honors with wormwood, aloes, and bitterness.

But to unravel this cord more widely in passing, extending it through a sort of triad <note>A group of three examples or figures</note>, the first of the three actors presents himself on this stage: Pausanias, the General of the Spartans. Once, inflated by a certain empty whirlwind of pride, he demanded of Simonides Magus <note>Likely referring to Simonides of Ceos, the lyric poet often associated with wisdom and memory</note> in a great crowd of people that he should bring forth some noble dogma from the cabinets of philosophy, or utter some memorable precept by which he might direct his life, morals, and entire way of acting. Simonides, in accordance with the prudence he possessed, and having perceived the King's insolence, wished to make him both holier and wiser. To cause those insane swellings of pride to subside so he would not become excessively arrogant, he urged him to keep death always in his mind and to constantly reflect that he lived as a mortal, and was therefore exposed to various miseries and would soon die. Indeed, what else did the Philosopher wish to say by this utterance, other than that no law is more proven, no precept more healthy, and no means or remedy more effective for blunting someone's arrogance and stubbornness, than to place before his eyes the vileness of his origin and the nothingness of his condition, and to recall to his mind his end, the Goddess of Funerals <note>original: "Libitinam" — the Roman goddess of funerals and burials</note>, and the funeral rites themselves? By Pollux <note>original: "ædepol" — a common Latin oath</note>, a truly excellent eulogy and a most distinguished dogma! 

But rarer things follow. Queen Semiramis <note>The legendary Queen of Babylon</note> once decreed in the tablets of her will that these characters should be engraved upon her sepulchral monument: **T. Q. Q. F. R. N. I. A: D. L. S. Q. Q. O.** <note>These initials likely form a Latin riddle or cryptic epitaph to be explained on the following page</note>

# PROSIMETRIC VERSE

-> Whoever you may be, now a King in need of gold, <-
-> Rolling back this stone, take as much as you require: <-

However, when Darius, the King of the Persians, had read these characters and understood their meaning, he was spurred on by a greed for gold. With the hope of finding a vast treasure set before him, he ordered the tomb to be opened. > Unless you were wicked, and possessed an insatiable hunger for gold,
> You would never have wished to pick the pockets of the dead. <note>original: "mungere peras" - literally "to wipe the pouches," a metaphor for stealing from the deceased.</note>

> Just as I lie here rotting; such shall you be.
> Though you be Caesar, or the Macedonian <note>Alexander the Great</note>, or the ruler of the whole world,

> Equal deaths await all men; learn to die.
> Let the rich man learn to die, let the King learn with the pauper, the flock,
> The learned and the unlearned, the youth and the old man.

And although this was a jest, and this Queen <note>Likely referring to Nitocris of Babylon, who according to Herodotus left a deceptive inscription on her tomb to shame greedy successors.</note> ordered it to be done only for the sake of striking him with shame, we are nevertheless mystically taught here that no better treasure is held in the world, none more excellent, than to have occasionally examined the bones of the dead. And truly, if anyone wished to listen to Death as a counselor, he would shortly become the wealthiest and wisest of men; for he would love all virtues, say farewell to all vices, send them away, and disregard all the vanity of the world. However, so that this triad may be completed, receive with impartial ears the following pithy saying <term>apophtegma: a concise, pointed saying or maxim</term> which must be subjoined. It is told of Zeno the philosopher that when he once inquired from the tripod of Apollo <note>original: "Apollinis cortina" - the cauldron or tripod from which the Pythia delivered oracles.</note> by what means he might establish his life honestly, direct his morals, avoid vices, pursue virtues, and in what way he might pass his life's span with honor, he received this response from the inner sanctum: *That he should consult those who have been released from the body.* <note>Meaning he should seek wisdom by reading the works of the dead.</note>

# PRELUDE

As I now more maturely weigh and examine this oracle of the Delphic God <note>The "Delphic God" refers to Apollo, whose temple at Delphi bore the famous inscription "Know Thyself."</note>, it seems that truth-telling God wished to teach him, and after him all mortals without exception, that there is but one way to pass through life holily and laudably, and to close one's final day in the highest happiness: to keep that grasping and scythe-bearing Fate, Death, constantly before one's eyes, and to know oneself. To know, I say, the moment; to know that one is a man who, as soon as he is born, already begins to die. He is an *example of weakness*, since nothing is weaker than man; he is the *prey of time*, because in a single year, month, or day, time snatches him away, stripping him now of beauty, now of sight, now of hair, teeth, and the strengths of the body:

->Man is a light fungus, who collapses at the slightest breeze,<-
->Who remains standing and firm in no single place.<-
->For now he is oppressed by cold, now dissolved by heat,<-
->And the funeral he carries today, tomorrow will be his own cross.<-

He is the *plaything of Fortune*, because when the dice are cast, she makes the rich man poor, and vice versa; the honored man contemptible, and the opposite; it all depends on the quality of the fall of the dice:

->If Fortune wills, you shall become rich from being poor,<-
->If this same lady wills, you shall become poor from being rich.<-
->If Fortune wills, you shall become a soldier from a leader,<-
->If this same lady wills, you shall become a leader from a soldier;<-

He is the *balance-scale of calamity*, because he experiences misery and prosperity placed and weighed in the equal balance of the scale;

->The Monarch of Gods and men is said to have long ago<-
->Furnished the life of mortals mixed with sorrows.<-

Therefore, as long as we enjoy this light, we seem indeed to live, but more truly we die continually; or at least we retain "life" in word, but in reality, we have lost it. Oh, how elegantly and politely a certain man—no less in holiness than in erudition <note>original: "erudition..." (text cuts off)</note>—described this fleeting life of ours...

It emphasizes that life is a constant process of dying and that human status is as unstable as a roll of the dice.</summary>

# PROSIMETRICUM

<margin>Our life, a dream, a ghost, a mockery, a dream-smoke, a shadow-smoke, a speck of dust, a little dew, a little flower, our body, a dung-heap</margin>

How famously he sketched our condition! When he said: *Our life is of such a kind, brothers—we who drag out a fleeting existence—as a game played upon the earth; so that, when we are not, we are born, and when we have been born, we are again dissolved. We are a dream that does not hold together at all, a ghost that cannot be grasped, the flight of a passing bird, a ship leaving no trace in the sea, dust, vapor, morning dew, a flower budding in its season and withering in its season.* <note>The author is likely quoting a Church Father, possibly Gregory of Nazianzus, on the transience of life.</note> Therefore, our life is the mockery of the ages and of time; we derive our shameful origin from a most foul matter, and we have scarcely emerged from that filth when we return into the same with a great rush, as it were. 

Man is a "dream-smoke" <note>original: "Somnium fumus"</note>—a poor little wretch whom his own imagination mocks at night, so that in his rest he sees himself as a sublime King on a magnificent throne; yet he wakes up having spent the night under the open sky at a crossroads, broken from the hard ground, stiff from the cold, naked from poverty, and famished from long hunger. 

He is a "shadow-smoke" <note>original: "Umbella fumus," referring to a parasol or sunshade providing a fleeting shadow</note> which, if you wish to grasp it with your hand, you cannot. Are not birds, or are not ships, also smoke? The former furrow the winds with the oarage of their feathers, the latter furrow the sea with the wings of their sails; but they leave only certain traces in their passage, and even these are such that no eyes, however radiant or sharp-sighted, can survey them. 

He is a "speck of dust-smoke," which prepares for itself a ruin all the more heavy the higher it allows itself to be carried by the breath of the winds. He is a "little dew-smoke," which has scarcely caught sight of the sun when it either yields its place out of reverence, or is consumed and melts away out of fear and admiration of such splendid majesty. He is a "little flower-smoke," which the sun alone sees open, fragrant, and dead. Since, therefore, we and our life are so many things, it must indeed be said that for that very reason we are nothing, and we must justly cry out:

> How mortal threads hang by a fragile string,
> ->As our wretched living rolls its heavy burden!<-

For if we look at our body, it is a narrow house, a workshop of miseries—by anagram, a "pig" <note>The author suggests a wordplay where the Latin 'corpus' (body) is rearranged or associated with 'porcus' (pig/filth).</note>—a dung-heap covered with snow, which a slight fever uncovers in a single day.

For whom it is better not to be born, or to be destroyed as quickly as possible, as the fable of Silenus <note>A mythological companion of Dionysus known for his wisdom.</note> from Tully <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman orator.</note> tells us; who, when he had been captured by Midas, is written to have given this gift in exchange for his release: he taught the King that by far the best thing for a man is not to be born, and the next best is to die as soon as possible.

It is handed down that he possessed such great power of eloquence, and was able to speak so effectively of the evils of this life, that men wished to place nooses around their own necks. I do not doubt that you have long known that there existed two celebrated philosophers among the Ancients, very different in genius and character, but little different in doctrine and dogma, one of whom

->Continually loosened his false lips with laughter,<-
<note>original: "Perpetuo risu laxabat falsa labella," referring to Democritus.</note>

->Renewed clear sighs with constant lamentations,<-
<note>original: "Planctibus assiduis suspiria clara novabat," referring to Heraclitus.</note>

The former hissed at the vanities and false insanities of this age; the latter wept for human miseries. And truly, with great reason, for I believe there is no one who does not feel certain abysses of sighs and lamentations burst forth from his heart, if he wanders in his mind through those most dejected exclamations of our nature, by which the princes of poets deplore our lot: a bubble of a bubble, a shadow of a shadow, a dream of all dreams, etc. <note>These are common metaphors for the fragility and unreality of human life.</note> If he runs through those complaints in his mind—that nature, like a stepmother, has favored the beasts more than men, since she armed them with instruments suited to their nature, but brought man forth unarmed; and that she made the beasts more long-lived and vigorous, but cast man down, possessing a softer temperament and skin, to constant passions of both mind and body. If, finally, he silently deliberates within himself upon so many passages of Holy Scripture, by which our nature is so far depressed that it seems in some ways to be placed below the worms. Would that we, the entrails of the earth, might sometimes weigh these things on the fairer scale of reason, and frequently and ardently consider with ourselves that we are earth, rot, dust, ashes, dung, and mere nothingness; I do not doubt that we would shortly clip our wings.

->Why do you, who are ash and dust and filthy earth, act proudly?<-
->Since you fall into ashes, just as you were ashes before.<-

# PRELUDE

Who, therefore, in the midst of the hardships, miseries, and calamities for which we are continually prepared, would dare to promise even the slightest thing for himself? Who, being wise, would perhaps swell with pride in his own lot, or grow insolent too freely in his own deeds, while he considers the various evils of human life? Who would trust in his own intellect, or in the goods of fortune, when he hears that Polycrates, the tyrant of the Samians <note>Polycrates (6th century BCE) was a powerful ruler of Samos famous for his immense good luck, which eventually ended in his execution by crucifixion.</note>, though most highly equipped with wealth and splendors, was fixed to a cross? Or that Croesus, King of the Lydians, the richest of all whom human memory celebrates, was subjected to the command of Cyrus, King of the Persians and Medes? Or indeed that Cyrus himself, who raised the horns of his power to an immense height, was placed in the prisons of others? Where truly are their courts now, and all their royal retinue? Where are all their former honors? Where are all the riches and wealth they previously possessed?

->All things seek again their origins, and look for their Mother,<-
->Thus that which was nothing before, returns into nothing.<-

->§. 14.<-

Man lives, therefore, in this court of misfortunes, and sails a most vast sea of all tribulations and storms. What do you think the human heart is? It is the *storehouse* of all miseries; but I shall yet paint it better to the life, and sketch it in its true colors: it is a *little valley*, where all the waters of tribulations naturally run down. Furthermore, alas, we do not examine these most certain truths within our souls while fortune breathes upon us with joyful breezes; rather, we push these things away from us with every effort while we feed on the fodder of pleasures and the delights of the flesh. In this, we imitate the nature of the Nautilus fish (so called because it has the likeness of a ship), of which it is written that in a silent and peaceful sea, it exposes itself to the sweet breeze to such an extent that, as if forgetful of its condition, forming the shape of a ship from its skin, it catches the winds and swims with its belly upward, nor does it fear to expose itself to the hazards of predatory birds or fishermen. Yet, when a stormy tempest appears, returning into itself, it seeks again the depths of the sea, and there it dwells and rests in security.

The very same thing is accustomed to happen to us, who in a time of prosperity—
