We, swelling and growing large, immersed in the marshes of our vices like frogs throughout our whole body, stuff ourselves with the wind of vanity. We long to excel over others and, at the peril of our own salvation, we forget that we are merely human. However, when adversity presses upon us, humbled and afflicted, we remember our humanity and seize a flight toward the secure asylum of repentance and the fear of the Lord. Experience in a house of mourning will demonstrate this to you openly and before your very eyes. For entering this place with wonder and weighing the grief for the deceased, you will see all things well and wisely ordered and composed. You will see everyone present there in the highest silence and quiet; and if by chance anyone happens to speak, his words are full of wisdom, just as if he were another Plato or Cato <note>Plato and Cato are cited here as the ultimate symbols of philosophical and moral wisdom</note>. What is even more to be wondered at: not only the men and women and others advanced in age, but even the maidservants—who at other times babble in the manner of geese—and the youths and the lowliest servants suddenly become wise, compliant, and conspicuous for their modest bearing, uttering marvelous sentiments.

*For you will hear some in that place saying that man is nothing other than a compendium of miseries, and that a certain philosopher truly hit the mark when asked, "What is man?" by responding among other things: "That he is a passing traveler and a guest of the place, and that he departs from this life as if from an inn, not from a home; for nature has made for us a lodging for staying a while, not a place for inhabiting." And they say that the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul in Hebrews 13:14</note> means the same thing: namely, that we do not have here a lasting city, but we seek one that is to come.*

# PROSIMETRICUM

Finally, the payment for life and honor depends upon the point of death. In short, all people seem to become philosophers when affliction has fixed its chair among them; establishing its school, it cools the passions of its disciples. And so, as distress—which is the mother of philosophy and wisdom—shapes them, they quickly escape into wisdom and continually seek out God.

That huntress of flies, the spider—that ingenious weaver and stretcher of the nets in which she entangles them—is said to be endowed with this marvelous property: when the sky is clear, she does not work, but when the air is cloudy and darkening, she works quite diligently and anxiously. Perhaps she does this so that she may later enjoy the serenity of the upper air and the brightness of the light. In this regard, a human is best compared to her; for truly, in the serene and tranquil time of prosperity, living idly, he refuses to work. However, on a dark day covered with clouds, when anxiety presses upon him, he cries out to the Lord and invokes His name. Then he rejoices to sweat diligently in labor and good works, permitting no time to be wasted. And thus, established in the chair of affliction and the cross, he courageously sustains the conclusions of his love toward God and excellently displays the demonstrations of the sciences.

->And so, skill comes to those in wretched circumstances.<- <note>original: "Atque venit sic tunc miseris solertia rebus."</note>

From this long series of examples, it is now rendered manifest that the "university" of all arts and sciences is actually penury and adversity. Indeed, it teaches everyone so perfectly and exactly that no one remains imperfect. Likewise, all arts are learned in the <term>place of meditation</term> <note>original: "phrontisterio," a Greek-derived term for a thinking-shop or place of study</note> of poverty; for want has made the most distinguished and numerous philosophers, orators, and poets:

> Bold poverty drove me from my hearth and farm,
> To make verses, and to study night and day. <note>A reference to Horace, Epistles 2.2.51-52, explaining his motivation for writing poetry.</note>

And indeed, it has been called by some, not unskillfully, the school of virtue; for it is an effective <term>gymnasium of virtue</term>, forcing even the unwilling to learn. Just so did it compel Zeno the Scythian, whom I brought onto the stage a little while ago when I was reciting the "senate of philosophers." For he, having been turned from a merchant into a philosopher, all at once...

Therefore, not unworthily, I shall sing concerning riches:

> Flee riches, a heavy weight for one who loves heaven,
> For they ruin the soul, and do not allow one to wish for the good.

# PRELUDE

Neither skill in conducting warfare, nor strength or military valor, will overshadow a Samson <note>The biblical figure Samson, here used as a metaphor for strength rendered vulnerable by sleep or spiritual ignorance.</note> dissolved in sleep: Therefore, true philosophers must learn that wisdom on earth which shall endure hereafter. ->By what means you may properly come to Him,<-

Whom if you see but once, you will immediately know all things. This is that eternal truth; this is the philosophy violated by no troublesome curiosity of the mind; this is that true and sincere wisdom, of which even a single drop is worth more than any vast sea of the wisdom of this life. *To know not many things, but one great thing—to protect oneself and one's salvation—is a great and many-layered thing*, because the wisdom of this world is foolishness before God. Nevertheless, lest we seem to carry our steps through many-hollowed paths and wrongly wander off-center, we shall proceed from our target and follow the rule exactly:

->Let us now follow the theme of our begun journey,<-

And let us enter our <term>Orthomagical</term> <note>From the Greek 'orthos' (straight/correct) and 'magia' (magic); referring to a "right" or divinely-aligned spiritual practice.</note> workshop, from which goods more precious than both Indias <note>Referring to the East and West Indies, symbols of ultimate worldly wealth.</note> are fashioned. For this most noble contest of the Sages has seemed to the <term>Immortal Adepts</term> <note>Those who have achieved the highest level of alchemical or spiritual transformation.</note> to be a calling together of all prudent minds into the pursuit of itself, as if it were the summit of human wisdom and a small granary of honest pleasure. In this place, incalculable gifts without number were crowded together, just as once all kinds of flowers and fruits were packed into the <term>cornucopia</term> <note>The horn of plenty.</note> torn from <term>Achelous</term> <note>A Greek river god who wrestled Hercules; his broken horn became the first cornucopia.</note> by Hercules.

# PRELUDE

You outrun others by many leagues; O sublime art, which are among the arts what the sun is among the planets! You embrace the cause within yourself, while others contain nothing but the effect; you are the ocean, the others but small streams; you possess your being in a state of completion <note>original: "in facto esse"</note>—as the philosophers say—while the rest are merely in a state of becoming <note>original: "in fieri"</note>;

->You are that House of Wisdom supported by seven columns;<-

You are she whom, from the very cradle of the world, the Arabs and Greeks have expressed through a thousand emblems, statues, and figures; you are that little branch and maiden of the Golden Age, adorned on all sides with jewels like a bride; you are the true Diana of Jove; you are that chaste wife of Ulysses <note>Penelope</note>, who remained inviolate for many years, even though she had no guardian and was besieged by a thousand suitors.

> Penelope lived safely through twenty years,
> A woman solicited by so many suitors.
> Penelope remained, though she lacked a guardian,
> Inviolate among so many lustful men.

You, therefore, are that uncontaminated and unfading Goddess, extensively shadowed forth by the ingenious ancients in their symbols and depicted in their images; you are that Golden Fleece of Thessaly, which the Greeks—burning with an incredible desire to learn your disciplines—carried away under the leadership of Jason <note>original: "Pelasgo," referring to the leader of the Pelasgians/Greeks</note> along with its protectress, Medea. But these things are as nothing if compared with those I am about to say. I fear I shall wither and fail, *O students of the Gold-bearing Art* <note>original: "Auriferæ Artis Spudastæ"</note>, unless you assist my undertakings, and unless your glittering flashes of praise and true voices of eulogy sound forth perpetually. And would that, under the weight of such great art, I might be like Pericles, who was said by Aristophanes to flash and thunder,

->(His voices were pure lightning-bolts of thunder)<-

Let us also send forth radiant flashes of public praise; but if we cannot hurl these forth according to a manly measure, then at least like the little birds...

# PROSIMETRIC <note>A work composed in a mixture of poetry and prose.</note>

let us break forth into small discourses, since no proclamation concerning the excellence of this Art can be so ample, no hymn so human, no song so sublime, that it is not surpassed by its immensity and exceeded by its height. ->§. 16.<-

The poets, those sons of fables, spun from their brains that the Gods heaped upon *Pandora* all kinds of gifts and rewards because she had brought forth a celestial and divine offspring—as can be sufficiently gathered from her name, which sounds the same in the Greek tongue <note>original: "Argolicè"</note> as "all gifts." This is indeed fabulous and invented, but it is certain that *Ortho-chemistry* <note>original: "Ortho-chymia"; meaning "True" or "Right" Chemistry.</note> exists as the mother of such an extraordinary birth of metaphysical progeny, the little son of the sun and moon. But what do you say to these things, *clients of a patronage so distinguished and so ancient?* Are you not seized with admiration when such unexpected news is brought before you, and you hear your Art polished with such great praises?

# PROSIMETRICUM

<margin>All pigs in Boeotia <note>A proverbial reference to the ancient Greek region of Boeotia, often stereotyped as a land of dull-witted or crude people.</note></margin> are found there; one can find among the ranks of Lawyers no fewer thieves than heralds. The art of minting money does not lack forgers, counterfeiters, and clippers of coins; nevertheless, despite their vice and fraud, the monetary system does not cease to exist. So, if there is any deceit or pretense in Alchemy <term>Alchymia: the art of transmuting metals and perfecting substances</term>, this is merely the tares among the wheat, the weeds in the garden to be utterly rooted out, and the fruitless briars to be cut down with the iron blade. The art must be guarded against these gluttons and blemished little creatures, but it should not be provoked by the heavy stings of curses or marked with a brand of censure. For indeed, those who gnaw at and reject an unknown art do little good; no wise man would do this—to revile and desecrate what he has not looked into—but rather he will venerate it and pursue it with all zeal and honor. Among all winged creatures, the one most highly commended for its taste and nourishment as a delicacy is

->That royal bird, who takes his name from Phasis:<-
<note>The pheasant (Phasianus colchicus), named after the river Phasis in Colchis.</note>

The most refined practices of the world must be pushed forward and pursued satirically; for that is the evidence of light and life, the scrutiny of profound learning, and the covering of what is precious.

But he who wishes to *eat* the kernel from the nut must use a nutcracker <term>nucifrangibulum: a tool for breaking nuts, here used metaphorically for intellectual or chemical labor</term> and strike the nut; thus nature presses her majesty into a mystic silence, and offers us the marrow of the chestnut or the almond only sealed away behind a rough and thorny covering.

Therefore, she represents herself only to the sight of the most acute craftsman. Clearly, that Great Lord of the whole universe has "en-kerneled" the greatest and most admirable things in secret, while leaving the smallest things in the open, so that He might rouse us to philosophize and to work. He wishes for the hidden to be made manifest; therefore, this must be dissected by a fire-named anatomy <term>pyronymica anatome: "fire-named" or "fire-working" anatomy, a common alchemical term for laboratory distillation or chemical analysis</term>, so that the Nymph <note>The "Nymph" here refers to the pure essence or "soul" of the matter being studied</note>, who is darkened by the force and energy of her composition and thickening, may come forth into the light through the ingenious resolution <term>resolutio: the chemical breaking down of a substance into its component parts</term> of the subject.

# PRELUDE

If they were to step forward—*good God*—how many and how great would be the mysteries rescued from the veils of nature, which are now neglected and fading away under the envious shadow of oblivion! ->They make white out of black, and black out of white,<-
->Crows out of swans, and swans out of crows.<-

Wherefore, just as a certain Spartan once did—whose name does not occur to me at the moment, though I have no doubt of the truth of the story—when he had curiously plucked a nightingale to discover what kind of structure belonged to such a melodious body and such a vocal, clear throat, and what the condition of such remarkable singing might be; having at last marveled at the tiny bit of flesh beneath the feathers, he defined the nightingale as "nothing but a voice." In exactly the same way, if you diligently shake out and observe all the methods of the Professors <note>original: "Cathedrarii," those who hold academic chairs</note>, you will find they cast out nothing but voices and names, nothing but long-windedness, word-battles, and a war of mere terms—or rather, Aristotelian spit. *And yet, philosophy consists not in words, but in things*; as if, forsooth, the entire rest of the world, and especially the Christian world, had not been able to see and experience more at any other time than that single Pagan <note>Aristotle</note>, whom it is well known stumbled enormously in many matters.

# PROSIMETRICUM

I desire; for there is nothing so incredible that it cannot be made probable by speaking, nothing so rough and unpolished that it does not shine through oratory and become, as it were, refined. Since I held this view, I acted even more boldly than those very men of whom I speak. Paracelsus <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a Swiss physician and alchemist who challenged traditional medicine.</note> is my friend, Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician (129–c. 216 AD) whose theories dominated Western medical science for over a millennium.</note> is my comrade, as are Aristotle and Hippocrates, but truth is more beloved to me. I shall stand by their side only so long as they stand by the side of truth; I shall agree with them only so long as they agree with truth and with themselves. *For by whomever truth is spoken, it is from the Holy Spirit.* <note>original: "à quocunque enim dicatur veritas, à spiritu sancto est"</note> Finally, you shall have business with me only so long as—and may faith be granted to this omen, for I do not live as a prophet empty of future events—some new star does not fly hither from elsewhere, by the novelty of which you are held fast, and run toward it as if to a new heavenly body. Nor is there any reason why I should pass over this, since such novelty once led and misled even Demosthenes, the prince of the Greeks.

For this man, while he was betaking himself to the school of Plato, once saw in the Athenian forum a huge crowd of men listening greedily to a new philosopher, Callisthenes, toward whom the people had run together in a mass out of an itch for novelty. Demosthenes also approached and heard him, and, captured by his chatter, he thereafter loathed Plato—who nevertheless easily excelled the other a thousand times over in the solidity of his teaching. Thus even now some people, even those who are often wise in their own judgment, are led and misled by novelty; they affect the allurements of speech like Young Ladies or the monkeys of Erasmus <note>A reference to a story by Desiderius Erasmus regarding imitation and superficiality.</note>, and they do not pay attention to what tastes of true wisdom.

In these my *Pragmatic Lots* <note>The title or subject of the author's current work.</note>, do not hunt for gilded eloquence or a decorated style, nor for discourses skillfully prepared and polished. *The speech which devotes itself to truth ought to be uncomposed and simple*, without folds or hidden layers. Let my words not delight, but be of use. For it is not my intention merely to stroke the ears and serve their allurements, nor to run about with theoretical and adopted pigments smelling of Cicero's <note>original: "Tulliana scrinia," referring to Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman standard for ornate oratory.</note> book-chests, nor to abound in mere grandiloquence. *Once the matter is understood, we ought to be easy in our use of words.*

# PRELUDE

> What I know is enough for me; I do not seek to be

I will labor, I say, not only with short verses (such as those of the dwellers of Elysium usually are) but even with signs, syllables, and indeed mere monosyllables, if it could be so done, to represent these great things briefly, as if in a mirror—namely, to intimate the truth *to you*, and the reality of the matter. So much will I be eager to gratify your minds: I will discuss the true, I will deal with the plain; for I have not been eloquent since yesterday or the day before.

->To use, if it is permitted, the common examples of the Poets,<-

Just like a pole which, when thrown into the water, immediately sinks to the bottom, but by the nature instilled within it, emerges again instantly. Thus truth is very often submerged, but at last triumphs with Adrastian Nemesis <note>The inescapable goddess of retribution</note>, surpassing all things, just as oil floats atop all other liquids. Clouds may cover the Sun for a time, and lies may likewise cover the truth; for by the judgment of Cato <note>Cato the Elder, known for his strict moral integrity</note>, right and equity can fall ill and be pressed for a time, but never crushed. Therefore, just as it is the innate condition of falsehood or error that, even with no one attacking it, it usually grows old and fades away, so on the contrary it is the property of truth, implanted by nature, that however much it is buried and despite many struggling against it, it is revived and grows.

For the power of truth is greatest, inasmuch as it easily defends itself by its own means against the cunning and cleverness of all wits, and against the forged snares of men. Since, therefore, the excellence of the Mago-chemical Art <term>Magochymica: A term blending Magic and Chemistry/Alchemy</term> is shown to be of such a condition that—despite many barking insanely against it and others most impudently raving against it—it could not be suppressed or put to sleep; indeed, even its most infested enemies, compelled by the reality of the matter, could not restrain themselves from praising such a Mysterious Art. I cannot, then, but wonder vehemently at the fate of certain writers of our own time, otherwise famous for their learning, who have dared to mutter, not against the whole...

# PROSIMETRICUM

...character, agility, and especially a vivacity of spirit and greatness of heart were present.

The very same must be said regarding our current proposition: it is surely no small proof of stupidity to celebrate a philosopher—even if he were more philosophical than Hermes <note>original: "Hermete licèt philoſophiorem"; referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with wisdom and alchemy</note>—or to sound the praises of a Commander—though he be more famous than Caesar—if his soul is not imbued with true wisdom and clothed on all sides with Christian virtues. Conversely, we see those "Narcissuses"—well-groomed, belted, the darlings of their parents—who are stupid, dull, mere "mushrooms" <note>A Latin idiom for someone who is brainless or grows from nothing</note>, and even perverse, intractable, and unteachable. *Hear these wonders:*

A young Lordling <note>original: "Dominellus"</note> and a poor Little Fellow <note>original: "Pauperculus"</note> go together to a merchant's shop. The former is in rich, studded, and bordered clothing; the latter in common, torn, and filthy dress. A calculation begins to be made about them: which one brings more value? Regarding the Lordling, there is no doubt he is estimated to arrive as burdened with gold and silver as he is charming in his dress and physical appearance. It is assumed the Poor Boy brings nothing besides his rags and his worn-out little cloak. But when they come down to business and each is examined separately, it is discovered that judgment has slipped up significantly. For he who was thought wealthy is found to be poor and without coins, shining only as far as the exterior appearance he was flaunting; whereas he who was counted among the beggars is found to have no patch upon his poor clothing that is not stuffed with shields <note>scutatum: a type of coin stamped with a shield</note> or ducats of the purest gold. Ha! Who would have thought it?

Rightly, therefore, and with great charm, did that most illustrious star of moral philosophy, Seneca, say: *A sword is certainly not good because it has a gilded belt or a scabbard set with gems, but because it has a subtle edge for cutting.* What then? Is not a steel blade often hidden in a rotten scabbard, and conversely, a rusty or leaden one in a jeweled one? Is there not often wisdom under a filthy little cloak? Do we not see...

> Have we not often seen many men, born from no great ancestors,

->§. 18.<-

For the World is nothing else but a theater,
In which each person presents his part in an image;

Here one plays the part of Croesus <note>A king of Lydia legendary for his immense wealth.</note>, another of Codrus <note>A semi-mythical King of Athens who sacrificed himself for his people; often used to represent the poor or the self-sacrificing.</note>, here a Cato, there a Fool <note>original: "Morionis" — a professional jester or simpleton.</note>; our life is certainly not unlike the theatrical stage. The Angelic Poet <note>Likely a reference to a Christian neo-Latin poet or a specific saintly writer.</note> played skillfully upon this theme:

> The common folk act out mimes on the stage: the father, the rich man,
> The son here, and another comes forth in the name of the poor:
> But soon, when the page has closed the parts performed,
> The true face returns, and the disguised one perishes.

In plainly the same way, you will find in that final catastrophe <term>catastrophe: the final resolution or "turning point" of a drama</term> of the Lord, that even he who here followed a mentor or advisor and sustained the role of a servant well, shall not infrequently be granted an eternal Royal crown among the Heavenly beings and the inhabitants of the Empyrean <note>The highest part of heaven, thought to be composed of pure light or fire.</note>; while meanwhile, not a few of the Aristocracy shall serve the most wretched slavery of all amid eternal flames, never to be released for all eternity.

Well done, then, fortunate Servants, whose rewards are measured by a happy and perennial liberty! On that day, there will no longer be any distinctions between the purple <note>The color of royalty.</note> and the beech-wood <note>The material of common vessels or rustic life.</note>, nor between the diadem and the peasant's cap <term>cudo: a simple cap made of raw skin</term>, nor between the scepter and the hoe <term>ligonis: a mattock or hoe used by laborers</term>, nor between the learned and the unlearned mind, nor between the rich and the poor, nor between master, servant, King, or Flock. A hard fate—alas, too hard a fate—for Kings, Princes, the Great ones of the age, the wealthy, the noble, and the learned: to be made equal to the unlettered, the dejected, the needy, the wretched, and—alas!—the common people so often trodden underfoot! This will clearly happen to the High-ranking when perhaps tomorrow, perhaps today, perhaps in this very little hour, the play (which we are acting) has its curtain drawn. The Duke of Alba, Ferdinand of Toledo, <note>Ferdinand Álvarez de Toledo (1507–1582), a famous Spanish general and diplomat.</note> is said to have been accustomed to say of the French, Portuguese, British, Spanish, and Italians, that some of them, when far off, seem wise, but when they stand near, they are fools; *others seem mad from a distance, but when inspected closely, are found to be wise; others seem foolish, and others wise, both from afar and up close.* It is therefore most certain that judgment slips regarding the gifts of the soul, even if the sense of sight is the sharpest of all. This is no wonder, since philosophy defines the limits of the uneducated and the peasants, but the power of vision occasionally deceives even the most skilled in their own art.

Just as it deceived Zeuxis, that most famous painter of Heraclea, when he had brought clusters of grapes he had painted onto the stage with such likeness and identity that birds flew down to eat them. However, Parrhasius, another most celebrated painter from Ephesus, had brought a painted linen cloth, over which he had drawn a thin veil with a very light and skillful brush, so similar to the real thing that it seemed true to everyone. Then Zeuxis, though wiser than the judgment of the birds, asked Parrhasius to remove the veil and show the painting. ->PRELUDE<-

Yesterday I deceived the birds, but today you have tricked me, the master craftsman. <note>This likely refers to a fable or a specific anecdote where a skilled person is outwitted by a cleverer ruse.</note>

Our sight errs, therefore, as we have seen—specifically in our judgment of the talents of some people's minds. But if we also consult our hearing and bid both parties to speak, we shall soon recognize those to be fools and dullards who seemed to us wise and learned, and vice versa. Hence, when once a wealthy man sent his young son to Socrates so that he might inspect the boy's natural disposition, and the tutor said, *“The father has sent his son to you, O Socrates, so that you might see him,”* the old Athenian <note>original: "Actæus," a poetic term for someone from Attica/Athens.</note> then said to the boy: *“Speak then, young man, so that I may see you.”* It was as if he were secretly suggesting that a man’s character <note>original: "ingenium," referring to innate talent or nature.</note> does not shine forth in the face so much as in his speech; that is, it is discerned not so much by sight as by hearing.

> Since, however, incorruptible faith is seen
> To be always wounded by the biting needle of envy;
> And since malice is the usual companion and enemy of virtue,
> By which celebrated honor is buried in foul poison;

Just as my Messenger eloquently and gracefully says: *“Just as there is no fire without smoke, so there is no virtue without envy; and, just as there is a shadow for those walking through the sun, so too is there the madness of malice for those stepping along the path of glory and virtue.”* And similarly, since envy is the follower of rising men and mortal successes—and since not even Jupiter himself pleases everyone, whether he sends rain or clear weather—and finally, since it is a most difficult thing to be able to provide a pleasing service to an ungrateful World, these people are worthy of brotherly pity rather than anger. This remains true until they eventually free themselves from the agonizing prison of their own malice, by which they are tortured in retaliation; let that be their rack <note>A "rack" (equuleus) was a Roman instrument of torture; the author suggests envy is its own punishment.</note>. Truly a rabid vice and an evil of the underworld! Oh, what a bloodstained beast! How pitiable is the heart you invade, and the soul you occupy and twist! What man, then, whose heart is otherwise wise, would complain about envy if he happens to suffer it? For is there anyone either more fortunate than the envied man, or more unhappy than the envious one? Is there anything more laudable, anything more worthy of everlasting praise, than to perform such wonders from which envy might arise in others?

> Is he against whom men are driven by hatred and envy!

Who *ever* envied the bad, and who *never* envied the good? Ah, envy, the companion of virtue, you who generally follow, and even hunt down, the Good! Although I can easily believe that many men—men otherwise distinguished for their learning—have refused to let their late-night labors <note>original: "vigilias"; refers to works written by candlelight</note> come to light for the sole reason that they greatly feared and dreaded the insults of chatterers and the mouths of barkers (such is the infinite "evil habit" <note>original: "cacoëthes," a Greek medical term for a malignant disease, used here for an uncontrollable urge to speak ill</note> of slandering today) which are accustomed to spare no writer, however wise. Nor is this without reason; for truly there is no one who entangles himself in more judgments than he who applies his mind to composing books, especially in this age, which has become so accustomed to archaic delights that unless one's aphorisms are subtle, polished, refined, and most carefully cultivated, they are hardly marketable. Thus, he who is permitted to remain hidden and withdraw under cover can deservedly triumph. Therefore, I had never decided to publish anything in print, especially since I am not unaware that in this kind of commentary, many before me have exhausted themselves in vain, and their books are now passed around as objects of ridicule; furthermore, I knew this century is by no means lacking a "nose" <note>meaning a sense of smell or critical discernment</note>, in which

> Even boys have the nose of a Rhinoceros: <note>A reference to Martial’s Epigrams, meaning even the young are mockingly critical.</note>

For this reason, I judged it much safer to *labor* quietly at home than to *come* into public with disgrace; because, as human morals are now, no thing, no business, no work is undertaken for such just reasons that there are not those present to pluck at it or pierce it with their curses;

> No one, by Pollux, will go safer than Antimachus or Homer;
> And envious Fate <note>original: "Parca," one of the three Fates of mythology</note> even twitches at the great Gods.

He who thinks of going into public takes as many censors against himself as he does readers; for *some* stir up complaints against him because he is wordy; *others* because he is brief; *this one* because he brings nothing new but treats an old act; *that one* because he departs from the common way of handling a subject; *that other one*...

<summary>The author discusses the "cacoëthes" or malignant habit of public criticism that discourages scholars from publishing their work. He argues that in an age of hyper-criticism, it is safer to remain private than to face the varied complaints of readers.</summary>
<keywords>envy, authorship, literary criticism, publishing, virtue, social commentary, Latin poetry</keywords>

# PRELUDE

One critic notes the style, *another* the thread of the discourse, *a third* censures the text itself; *many* are indignant because the work proceeds in a poetic manner, while *very many others* cry out against words they find barbaric, obsolete, or "a foot-and-a-half long" <note>original: "sesquipedalia"; a Horace-inspired term for overly long, pompous words</note> which they perhaps have not encountered before. In short, any commentator provides almost as many stones to be cast against himself as he glosses words.

For this reason, it has always been a matter of great fear for all wise men to publish anything for the common people; for that is to put one's hand into the most burning flame, to surrender oneself to the tongues of those who would stab him, and to twist the arrows of all curses toward oneself—especially if the matters under discussion are weighty and of great moment. Since, therefore, the hidden treasure which is celebrated here in oracular song almost transcends human grasp, I fear incurring a charge of treachery while I proceed to reveal its hidden mysteries so clearly and summarily, *especially because I know it is necessary:*

->To choose a subject equal to our strength, we who write,<-
->And to weigh for a long time what our shoulders refuse to bear:<-
<note>A paraphrase of Horace’s *Ars Poetica*, advising writers to know their limits.</note>

For it is the mark of an imprudent man to be ignorant of his own measure; *and furthermore*, because I remember that his own writings deceive every man and escape the notice of the Author <note>original: "Auspicem"; literally the one who takes the omens or initiates the work</note>; for just as even deformed children delight their parents and seem most beautiful to them, so too, iron-hard and ungraceful verses tickle their Creators <note>original: "Inventores"</note> and seem the best to them. From this it happens that, while they smile upon their own works, they easily allow them to come forth into the public light; but the "benefit" they obtain from this is that, where they falsely flattered themselves they would acquire praise and the glory of a name, they instead produce no small insult and disgrace for themselves; while their ignorance and stupidity, which previously lay hidden, is now made manifest to the whole world.

> Like mange and baldness more worthy of a laugh
> Which stood naked, though previously clothed in hair.
> The clever Monkey facetiously mimics human form
> And gesture, while he sits fitly upon the ground.

# PROSIMETRIC <note>original: "Prosimetricum"; a literary style mixing prose and verse</note>

> But the more he lifts himself up, the more
> ->the Monkey is seen to have a hairless backside.<-
> So too the boastful, whom a great name has driven,
> ->the more conspicuous they are, the more ridiculous they become:<-
> Since he who rashly takes on things greater than himself,
> ->if he becomes conspicuous, he also becomes ridiculous:<-

Who, I ask, would these things not terrify, even if he were the bravest Achilles? <note>The hero of the Iliad, used here to represent the pinnacle of human courage.</note> And truly, I judged that these matters should be weighed by me all the more firmly, as both the faculty of my talent and the convenience of my life are smaller, and there is now a greater abundance and richness of Treatises <note>original: "Tractatuum"</note>, not only by ancient Writers <note>original: "Scriptores"</note> but also by modern ones; consequently, there is a fiercer and more prone lewdness, and a desire for rejecting everything. Thus, in the present face of this ulcerated age, he who publishes his works seems to do nothing more than spread a table for detractors and critics, who tear apart and gnaw at everything served—I will not say with mere bites, but with violent snatching and crooked teeth—not only those things which displease them, but even those which occasionally please them greatly. They are like cats, which are accustomed to snarl at someone all the more vehemently the more elegant the morsel they feel has been offered to them.

And yet, for my part, I have always judged that a wise man should care nothing, or at least very little, for such backbiters, but should always hold them of no account;

> For what an envious crowd shall take from me while living,
> ->the trumpets of death shall return with a thousandfold interest.<-
> The heralds of a name never blare during life,
> ->but those things are accustomed to rise only after death.<-

Who, therefore, would not ascribe it to imprudence and faint-heartedness if someone, out of fear of those who rebuke and detract, were deterred from a work that is otherwise curious and wonderfully desirable to many? Because, as Ecclesiastes <note>A book of the Bible; the quote is from chapter 11, verse 4.</note> says: *he who observes the wind does not sow, and he who considers the clouds will never reap.*

Nor is there any reason why I should greatly fear the furrowed brows and censures of the Aristarchuses <note>A reference to Aristarchus of Samothrace, a rigorous grammarian of antiquity; used here to mean harsh critics.</note> and Critics. For just as I do not flatter myself, so I am not so led by their summaries that I would not willingly acknowledge having stumbled over some "stone of a stone" <note>original: "de Lapide lapidem," a play on words likely referring to a specific author named Lapide or a "stumbling block."</note>. In this, I would undoubtedly be acting more justly and reasonably than Virgil, that easily foremost prince of Latin Epic poets. After producing that most celebrated and scarcely ever sufficiently praised glory of the *Aeneid*, Virgil was so displeased with his own work that when, oppressed by disease, he saw death approaching, he earnestly and stubbornly begged his closest friends to abolish the work and commit it to be swallowed by the fire, judging it unworthy to be presented to the eyes of the Wise. It should therefore be permitted to me, with a thousand times better right, to sing in response:

> Day and night I polished these papers with pumice stone,
> Which a small spark will now carry through the void.
> I burned to write, but now Mulciber <note>Another name for Vulcan, the fire-god.</note> shall consume
> These written verses with his torch and crush them on the pyre.
> Thus we all wish to paint, thus we seek to fashion,
> Yet the finished labor itself displeases us by its very art;
> Hence, when I reread these trifles, I blush to have written them,
> For I sing many things worthy only of a filthy backside.
> That this work was snatched from the middle of the anvils <note>i.e., it is unfinished or unrefined.</note>
> Is witnessed by a foolish muse without a lyre.

->PROSIMETRICUM<-
<note>original: "Prosimetricum" — A literary work combining both prose and verse.</note>

I have accepted this from the beginning, lest I should go forth into the market without merchandise, or leave the tavern without paying my share <note>original: "asymbolus" — a Greek-derived term for a guest who doesn't contribute to the bill</note>, and so that I might demonstrate by my own example that in great matters, the will alone is usually sufficient. Therefore, whether I have achieved my intent or not, I leave to each person's own conscience, to time, and to experience; nevertheless, I have performed my part.

> But if strength should fail, our daring shall be
> Our praise; for in great things, to have willed is enough.
> <note>A quote from the Roman poet Propertius, emphasizing that the effort in a grand task is noble even if the execution fails.</note>

For if it is a great thing to master individual disciplines, how much greater is it to master them all? This is a necessity for those whose purpose is to speak both against and for all philosophers for the sake of finding the truth. I do not claim to have attained the capacity for such a great and difficult task, but I profess to have pursued it. Although I knew myself to be many leagues <note>original: "parasangis" — an ancient Persian unit of distance</note> unequal to this business, I nevertheless preferred to be subject to the display and mockery of all, and to commit myself to the theater of the world and the danger of reckless judgments, rather than deny my labor as an interpreter to my Mercury <note>original: "Paraphraestae Mercurio meo" — likely referring to his guiding intellect or the god of communication and alchemy</note> in so useful and religious a purpose. I was resolved to try every risk rather than follow him unwillingly, or to remain any longer wavering between hope and fear.

And although, again, the present condition of this degenerate age could easily deter anyone from such an undertaking—an age in which the minds of men are so idle and embittered that, if it were possible, they would remove all effort and utility from our midst—there will therefore be (unless I divine wrongly) six hundred <note>A common Latin idiom for "countless numbers"</note> who will understand and interpret *this fatal task of mine* <note>original: "hoc meum fatale pensum" — his destined labor</note> as the product of a foolish mind. Others, indeed, will see it as impudent pride, that I—who cannot present myself through great studies, practices, or the talents of my station—have dared to approach so arduous a matter. This is especially true in that branch of Art <note>Likely referring to Alchemy or the "Great Art"</note> in which other men, so illustrious and endowed with such experience and erudition, have always labored with the greatest diligence, and in which many, swept away by a shipwrecked despair of their own wit, have remained miserably stuck in the water.

<summary>The author defends his ambitious attempt to synthesize all philosophical knowledge, arguing that the noble intent justifies the risk of public mockery or failure. He acknowledges the difficulty of the "Art" he is practicing and the likelihood of being criticized by his "degenerate" contemporaries.</summary>

# PRELUDE

And yet, this is the one thing by which I hope to be able to defend that boldness of mine—or as my detractors might disparagingly call it—both before God (by whose ineffable grace and kindness toward me I have recorded these things, and they have been, and shall be, brought to a happy conclusion <note>original: "colophon," a scribal term for the finishing stroke or end of a book</note>) and before myself: namely, that I was led to enter this labyrinth, entangled with a thousand twists and turns and errors, not so much by the pursuit of favor, much less by the breeze of human honor—since I conceal both my head and my body <note>The author implies he is writing anonymously or in hiding</note>—but only by the impulse of a fated genius, a zeal for the public good, and the motive of unearthing the truth itself. This is an undared and quicksand-filled sea, almost unsearchable even with the longest plumb-line of reason; indeed, it is the most hidden and veiled mystery of all the sublunary secrets of God.

Hence, truly, to anyone who weighs the matter a little more justly, it should not be a cause for nitpicking, but rather for intense wonder: namely, how I—even as a stranger, without property or money while traveling, and possessing neither book nor companion—have nonetheless attacked this work (whatever its quality) with equal parts daring and fear. I have carried it through in the worst of times, when the burdens of extreme necessity and the most varied cares of procuring food and clothing extort one's entire focus. I have brought it to a harbor more truly "found" than "hoped for," under the guidance of the Most Knowing One. Just as He was the author of this present web <note>original: "telae," referring to the weaving of a text or fabric</note>, so I hope He will likewise happily guide, even unto the end, a mind easily conscious of its own weakness, and my very right hand.

> I was led around in many ways: by disease, by prison, and by want;
> Then dread drove all wisdom out of my soul;
> *Mice, lice, and dormice daily in my dreams*
> *Threaten me with the sorrowful punishments and evils of life;*
> There is no one of such firm character or great confidence,
> Who would not recoil with trembling blood and waste away with fear.

From these things it is now clearly evident that, by Hercules, the states of fortune did not breathe favorably enough upon these Symbols <note>technical term for emblems or allegorical signs</note> and their Symbol-writer; and therefore not—

# PROSIMETRIC <note>original: "Prosimetricum" - a work composed in a mixture of prose and verse</note>

I have not infrequently dwelled upon the opinion that perhaps God does not wish for these things to be brought forth into the public eye; for that reason, I had often resolved within myself to turn my mind away entirely from publishing them. Indeed, I do not know why the outcome has responded so little to my intended fate; but if by some chance, for the sake of my late-night labors <note>original: "lucubrarum" - works composed by candlelight</note>,

That famous Thales of Miletus (who, on account of the outstanding sharpness of his intellect, was once the first in Greece to be hailed with the title of "Sage") when he learned that Pherecydes of Scyros—a man of no common learning—had taken it into his mind to discourse upon the sacred mysteries before a gathered assembly, signaled to him in writing that it seemed better to him if he kept those difficult matters at home. He suggested that he should propose them for discussion only to invited companions of fairer judgment and more mature refinement; for those subtle and sublime concepts would bring no reward, or certainly a very meager one, to the grasp of the thick-headed and unskilled multitude. While I was meditating on this excellent lesson from Thales, *O men of readiness*, it frequently came to my mind—as I was writing something concerning that most profound part of the **Hermetic Art** <note>The tradition of alchemy and magic attributed to Hermes Trismegistus</note> which treats of the **Philosopher's Stone**—and it plucked my ear <note>A classical metaphor for a reminder or warning</note> that the burden I have taken upon my shoulders is of such a kind that it ought not to be rashly scattered among the common people, but rather it would be more prudent for it to be reviewed in a familiar gathering of learned men.

By my faith, it would be pleasing if the matter could be conducted thus: but where in the world, I beseech you, can you find those from whom those mystical things concerning the *heavy and pregnant Galena of the philosophers* <note>original: "Galena" - lead ore, here used as a metaphor for the raw material of the Great Work</note> are not hidden? # PRELUDE

Nevertheless, if you were to see what these men accomplish and how they act, and once you have examined the matter thoroughly, you will undoubtedly discover that they are ignorant not only of the <term>orthophysical</term> <note>original: "orthophysica"; meaning the true, natural substance</note> material of this Secret, but also of the knowledge necessary for directing and perfecting it, and finally of the proper method for its formation. Furthermore, you will see that they adopt things for themselves that are foreign and strange to the construction of the Stone, and indeed too contrary to it. Thus it happens that the longer and more expensively they have been intent upon the work, the more truly there befalls them that which one of our more deceptive writers had predicted: namely, that instead of the <term>Magiolith</term> <note>The "Stone of the Wise" or "Magian Stone"</note> they find a *moriolith* <note>A "Stone of Folly" or "Fool's Stone"; a play on the Greek word "moria" meaning folly</note>. With such minds, I ask you, who would freely and willingly reason about this matter?

*Therefore, Brothers inclined toward the art*, I have judged that my honest and concise poetry would be more laborious for me than their fantastical idleness, but more pleasing and far more useful for you. For unless they are utterly obstinate, they will at the very least be warned here about recalling their poorly instituted work; *it is commonly said that it is better to run back than to run badly*. And so, I reflect upon this repeatedly: it is not enough to know what you know, but it pertains to the public utility to reveal to the public, publicly, and in writing, what is of interest. 

Away from here, then! Stay far away, you crafty and proud men! We do not want eagles that fly sublimely among the pines near the sun, but birds, *we want birds* that fly low, that nest on the roof, and often *on the ground*. To such people, I whisper these things not in *meter* <note>poetic rhythm</note>, but as if with a voice and a more secret *chalk* <note>original: "creta"; likely referring to a secret mark or white stone of initiation</note>. And so that they may be speechless in retaining these things, I seal their mouths with the sanctity of a most holy oath. These *Inaugurated Brothers*, when they hold these things with us, will also join us in singing immortal thanks for such a great privilege to the eternal and unapproachable God. But now, to purge myself of all envy, I shall set forth the opinions of the Ancients concerning the Discovery of the Gods, at which point everyone should be summoned to judge which of them is true:

> Begin now to forge your verses on the deep lathe,
> And come to play your part, Little Poet.

Then at last the Lyceum <note>The school of Aristotle; here referring to the academic world</note> will seem bold to me; if either everyone reaches an agreement, or someone is found who has discovered what is true. Thus I might feel inclined to cry out, as Statius does in *The Young Friends*: "O, by all the gods of our fellow youths! I cry, I demand, I beseech, I pray, I wail and implore!" It is not over a trivial matter—as he complains—that capital crimes are being committed in the city:

> *The courtesan refuses to accept silver from her loving friend.*

But rather, let them be present, let them learn, let them take notice of what should be thought concerning the Invention of the Immortal Philosophers, and the sublime mastery of the *magolithos* <note>original: "magolithi"; likely referring to the 'magician's stone' or Philosopher's Stone</note> over which they preside. For all these things must be referred back to this inscription concerning the *Chemical Winnowing Fan* <note>original: "Chymica vanno"; a reference to the title of the work, suggesting a process of separating truth from falsehood</note>. Truly, the great disagreement among the most learned men concerning this most important matter forces even those who think they hold some certainty to begin to doubt. Come then, *men most fair toward the art*, see what aphorisms of the Adepts <note>Masters of alchemy who have achieved the Great Work</note> await our love of magic:

> I shall not relate these things to be sung in a lowly buskin <note>The boot worn by tragic actors; meaning the style will be elevated, not humble</note>,
> I am compelled to set out on a great journey to learned Athens,
> So that the longer path may release me from every torment;
> Let us gird ourselves to visit the ancestors of ancient Janus.

Let us survey the sacred tapestries themselves; let us taste the greatest of mysteries, which surpasses all secrets, and than which nothing is more hidden in nature itself. This is the goal toward which you strive and which you intend: I shall draw back the shadows by which the vision of mortals is clouded, and by which nature protects herself from the sight of the profane. I will demonstrate the Goddess herself—namely, the most adorned *Nymph*—and her bridal chamber, and *Diana* naked without her garment. Once she appears to you uncovered, I have no doubt that she will immediately provoke an incredible love for herself. Let this now be the final time to approach that which we have established.

-># PRELUDE<-

I shall impart the most holy gifts, so that we all—if we cannot do so with a worthy song, then at least with such praise as is permitted—might as suppliants venerate the incomprehensible power of God and the insuperable sublimity of the Divinity. For unless the languor of the human mind is illuminated by the radiance of divine light, it would most easily be led away into the most ruinous windings of ambiguity and the side-paths of error. I indeed adore and kneel before this power, prostrate and bowed low, not denying my fear; I tremble to sail across such an ocean of secrets in the humble and flimsy skiff of my small wit. In such a vast and swirling voyage, even the most clear-sighted pilot has reason to dread a shipwreck. Indeed, here the wisest men play the fool, nor can they gaze upon the unexplored centrality <note>The "centrality" likely refers to the "Center of Nature" or the divine core of alchemical matter</note> with unblinking eyes. For it is an abyss in which reason is swallowed up, a chasm in which all diligence is spun around, a sea in which every human genius is blinded and endangered by shipwreck.

Lest we, therefore, be led astray by some wandering star and be intercepted by the shallows and narrows of the quicksands, we must frequently look back to the North Star <note>original: "Cynosura"</note> of divine light, that teacher of Angels, and the eternal and infinite Word. Thus, where the little torch of human reason fails or is enveloped in darkness, that Light, acting as mistress and pilot, may direct the course of the voyage, uncover for us its hidden chests of treasures, and finally protect the work of its powerful right hand—lest such a sparkling brand of so great a mystery, suddenly rushing upon the weak eyes of our mind, should dazzle them with excessive splendor. Divine aid must be implored in the smallest matters; what then ought we to do in those that are arduous and greatest? That most sagacious Arabian magus, Alphonso <note>Likely referring to the legendary "Artephius" or a similar figure associated with the *Clavis Sapientiae* (Key of Wisdom)</note>, at the beginning of his book of more occult philosophy entitled *The Key of Wisdom*, speaks thus: *Let us first praise God, who is the inspector of all things, nor is there anything that may lie hidden from Him; for He is bound to His creatures through His word, and yet separated from them insofar as He transcends them.* Similarly, others beginning to treat of the physico-chemical Phoenix <note>The "Phoenix" is a common alchemical symbol for the Philosopher's Stone or the process of rejuvenation and perfection</note> say: *Turn your heart and mind toward God, my son, toward God, rather than toward the art; for the art itself is the highest gift of God, and He bestows it upon whomsoever He pleases.*

<summary>The author humbles himself before the overwhelming "ocean" of divine mysteries, warning that human reason alone leads to shipwreck without the guidance of divine light. He cites the Arabian philosopher Alphonso to emphasize that alchemical success is a gift from God rather than a mere technical skill.</summary>

# PRELUDE

...wonderful love, a love that transcends all others! I know indeed, and You know that I know, that the manner of loving You—O fire, which always burns and is never extinguished!—is to love without measure. For if that character Pamphilus from Terence <note>A reference to the Roman playwright Terence and his comedy 'The Eunuch'</note> was permitted to be so insane as to say to his Thäis:

> Love me day and night, long for me,
> Dream of me, look for me, think of me,
> Hope for me, delight in me, be wholly with me,
> Let my soul be yours forever,
> Since I am your most intimate lover.

If, I say, he believed he could demand this of a girlfriend through the wicked laws of a reckless Cupid, saying "love me night and day," why should I not flow in the love of God day and night, to the extent that I might think of Him incessantly—as far as the depth of my wound allows—and that I, a tiny little creature, might always run toward the embraces of the Creator with a wounded soul? In the year 1662 from the Virgin Birth, toward the middle of March, I once composed a bold poem which I handed to a certain Margaret in the street on a Sunday morning as she returned from church. It was in the form of a small bundle into which I had inserted a love note, with this motto written at the bottom: *You think of me, and I of you*; roughly in this tone:

### CONGRATULATORY POEM

->On her recovered health, with a tribute for the birthday of a most select and gifted young Maiden and little image, etc.<-

Receive this pledge of the modest love of my Phintis <note>A Greek name used here as a poetic pseudonym for a friend or lover</note>,
Which your lowliest servant sings to you with such divine omen:
You shall be the beautiful bride of a fair-haired husband,
Honey, headdress, vessel, parasol, little wheel, little lips,
Seat, speech, smooth-browed little hearth, pious little Rachel:
Beautiful, snow-white, youthful, tender, polished girl.

What service did I ever pay you, by what works did I bind you to me, to deserve such a heap of loves bestowed upon me? Ah, sweet sermon of my heart, O God who is charity, set me on fire! A burning or thirsty stag does not pant more greedily for clear springs than I frequently sigh for you.

I, who could deserve nothing at all, was sought out by you; moved by goodness and infinite mercy, beyond all my merit and before any right of mine, and out of your pure grace, you wished to show your omnipotence toward me. It was then that you drew me forth by your all-encompassing power <note>original: "pantodynamia"</note> from the darkness and shackles, from non-being into being, and willed that I should be something. Truly ineffable goodness! Oh, mercy *which I did not deserve, a love greater* than anyone can imagine! O Incomprehensible One! What, I ask, *tell me Lord*, did you see in me? What service did I ever pay you, with what works did I bind you to me, to earn such a heap of love? Ah, sweet sermon of my heart, O God who is charity, set me on fire! A burning or thirsty stag does not pant more greedily for clear springs than I frequently sigh for you:

> He who always loves, but is not loved, is wasted by a vulture,
> ->Alas, what grief! How long are the delays in love!<-

> ->Divine love knows no limit.<-

# PRELUDE

In that heavenly and most blessed dwelling of your Saints, for all eternity, it shall no longer be said of me—mournfully and shamefully—that "he clung to one of the citizens of that region" <note>A reference to the Prodigal Son in Luke 15:15, who "clung" to a citizen of a far country to feed swine.</note>, but rather "he clung to God, and is one spirit with Him" <note>original: "adhæsit Deo, unus spiritus est"; referencing 1 Corinthians 6:17.</note>. Oh, what a duck-like <note>original: "anaticam," likely a play on words or a specific mystical term for close-clinging attachment.</note> adhesion, a most sublime conjunction, and a transformation beyond the likeness of nature! It is the joining of rusty iron with the <term>orthochemical</term> <note>True or pure chemical/alchemical substance.</note>, with pure gold, with gold seven times refined—the joining of a man of ash and dust with God! Oh, an enthusiastic metamorphosis, unspeakably more wonderful and better than all Ovidian transformations, or even a thousand *Philosophers' Stones*! Alas, what a discord and a pause my hoarse strings produce! Ah Lord, my drum proclaims *you, you*:

->May you, O God, become rose-scented *grace and kisses* to me,<-
->Lie in my breast like a sun, in place of a lover.<- <note>original: "Philinnæ," a classical name for a mistress or beloved.</note>

Kiss me with the kiss of your mouth, wound my heart, lead me after you, that I may run in the fragrance of your ointments! Lead me, in a way, even if I am unwilling, so that you may make me willing; drag me while I am sluggish, so that you may make me run. There will come a time when I shall not need one to pull me, because I shall run voluntarily and with courage. Heap up, pile up, pour in, O Jesus, at this *crossroads*, at this *point-stop* of such a disparate eternity, of such an unequal wheel; I will bear whatever evils I can, for I am prepared for the whip. At your sacred rock, at your most holy stone-quarry I cry out; through a ten-fold voice, respond with an echo to the one who loves:

> O how much better, when the breast cries out "Jesus,"
> These jagged rocks echo back my Jesus!
> O love, O Jesus, as often as you are *called, you are loved*,
> You who, by your death, *take away and redeem* my sins!
> Where shall I flee? The Stygian robber *scales and hooks* me,
> Do you not *pity*, Love? "You shall *not be miserable*," He says.
> Therefore why shall I weep here? The rock sounds a *sharp cry: "faults"*;
> Do you *think* I will then be safe? "You *will be*."

> Which the bird, not learned, often repeats with a noisy sound.

<meta>This page continues the philological and etymological analysis of terms related to the afterlife and classical mythology, likely following a section on the Elysian Fields.</meta>

# The Strata and Meadows
## OF ELYSIUM.

1. That is, the Fields; for just as the word *campus* <note>field</note> derived its name from *capiendo* <note>taking/containing</note>, because it easily contains a notable harvest of animals or other things; so also *pratum* <note>meadow</note> comes from *parando* <note>preparing</note>, because it is surely *prepared* to receive fruit, in which, of course, only a scythe is needed to gather it.

2. That is, Full and stretched out with gold, etc. See more extensively below in the *Monuments of Deiphobe*, in the seventh Gloss.

3. That is, Mid-night, deep, or late night, etc. Otherwise and commonly called *concubia* <note>the time of first sleep</note>, because almost everyone then *lies down* <note>cubent</note>; or *conticinium* <note>the still of the night</note>, because *all things* <note>cuncta</note> are then *silent* <note>taceant</note>. However, the phrase *Nox intempesta* <note>dead of night</note> seems to me to be named and contracted from *intempestiva* <note>unseasonable</note>, perhaps because that part of the night is *unseasonable*, that is, inopportune for conducting small affairs.

4. That is, a Good voice, or more correctly a *virtuous voice* <note>proba vox</note>, as if *prohibiting* <note>prohibens</note> one from wrongdoing.

5. That is, Perpetual, everlasting, etc. For just as *sempiternus* <note>eternal</note> is composed of *semper* <note>always</note> and *aeternus* <note>eternal</note>, as if it were *aeviternus* <note>age-lasting</note>; so also *perennis* <note>perennial</note> is from *per* <note>through</note> and *annus* <note>year</note>, with the 'a' changed to 'e', as if lasting through all years.

6. This means, Bringing consolation and assistance, because *salus* <note>health/safety</note> is taken here to mean a remedy, a healing, etc.

7. In which, of course, the Golden Fleece of Phrixus's Ram is guarded by a sleepless dragon; derived from *luceo* <note>to shine</note>, certainly not by antiphrasis <note>a figure of speech where a word is used in a sense opposite to its meaning</note> because it shines the least (as is commonly believed), but more truly because of the frequent *lights* <note>lumina</note> of the sacrifices which are performed by night in this grove of *Mars*. He is so named because he presides over the *males* <note>maribus</note> making offerings there; poetically called *Mavors*, because he *turns great things* <note>magna vertat</note>, etc.

8. That is, Immortal, smelling of nard, always accompanying, etc. For a *shadow* <note>umbra</note> follows the body whether we wish it or not; named as if it were *imber* <note>rain/shower</note>, because all *shadows* are *rain-like* <note>imbricae</note> or *rain-bearing* <note>imbriferae</note>, that is, moist, smoky, etc.

9. It is most worthy of consideration what *Orcus* <note>the Underworld/Pluto</note> signifies here and elsewhere; named (according to me, the commentator) not indeed from *urgendo* <note>urging/pressing</note>, because it urges us toward death, but rather as if it were an *Opaque Garden* <note>Hortus opacus</note>, because it is surely the *beginning* <note>orsus</note> and *origin* <note>ortus</note> of all things.

10. That is, Triumphal, from the verb *ovo, -as* <note>to rejoice/triumph</note>, which is to be glad, and to demonstrate joy by shouting or singing; from which comes *ovatio* <note>ovation</note>, which is a minor triumph, in which sheep <note>ovibus</note> were sacrificed on the Capitol, just as bulls were in a major triumph. It is so named as if it were *ohatio*, from the interjection of one exulting, *ohe!* Or perhaps we can etymologize more correctly by suggesting the verb *ovo* is derived from the voice of those who crowd the side of the *ovant* <note>the one triumphing</note>; for they, full of joy, are accustomed to acclaim with a doubled "oo," from which (with the consonant 'v' interposed) I believe the verb *ovo* resulted, with the first syllable short.

11. Poetically used here for the sky, just as previously in the *Chorus of Philosophers*; named as if it were *holos lampros* <note>original Greek: ὅλος λαμπρὸς</note>, that is, "wholly and everywhere shining," because it always possesses a bright sun and is never darkened by any clouds.

The author explores the origins of words like 'meadow', 'ovation', and 'Orcus', often seeking deeper symbolic meanings behind their Latin and Greek roots.</summary>

# THE POST-PRINCIPLES,
### How and for what reason
#### THESE
### Sibylline Oracles of the Magical Nights were sealed and taken away.

-> §. I. <-

A certain one of my fellow soldiers in the study of the humanities and in youthful jests;

> More or less ten autumns ago, if I remember rightly,
> Disguising Sardonic joys <note>original: "Sardoa gaudia"; a reference to bitter or mocking laughter</note> with a festive face,

Congratulated me on my happy arrival (having recently returned, of course, to my native soil after completing my philosophical course at the Academy of the Ubii <note>The University of Cologne</note>, for the purpose of visiting my parent who was at that time suffering, as it appeared, from paralysis of the feet). And behold, this nosy and talkative compatriot, with scarcely one or two words fully uttered (for he was still on the threshold of our little hut), behaved just as if he had been expressly sent by a magistrate—which I certainly believed—being moved, as one could guess, by no small amount of barbarity. He began to sneer at me with hooked nostrils and, in the presence of another of my companions who was very closely joined to both of us, to rattle on mockingly and ironically like a fanatical witch, in almost this manner:

"Aha! We certainly thought you would have arrived in a carriage with four horses, and that you would have brought to our little town—which is currently not well-provided for—some masses of gold. (Indeed, the jester added, I am greatly surprised that the town did not even welcome your return with the firing of war cannons!) This was because a rumor was heard,"

> (Since envious fame flies suddenly)

"That I had hidden myself away in Chemical <note>Alchemy</note> studies; hence, to that same purpose..."

# NIGHT MAGIC. THE SIBYLLINE LOTS.

...having grabbed a certain iron counterweight from our shop, which my parents used to use to weigh their merchandise and goods for sale, that "word-shaper" <note>original: "logodaedalus," a Greek-derived term for someone who crafts clever or deceptive speech</note> tried to fish out of me how much that thing might be worth, and how much gold might be inside it. Smelling exactly where such a question was heading, I replied, "Nothing"; for I did not think you deserved to hear the truth, you who ask questions so deceitfully. Furthermore, after many jests were cut back and forth in this way, he said to me, "You possess a certain internal pride,"

# THE SIBYLLINE ORACLES.

In a former age, the more discerning minds devoted themselves with the utmost diligence to the investigation of hidden things and the most excellent branches of secret learning <note>original: "doctrinæ ſecretioris," referring to esoteric or occult knowledge</note> and natural mysteries. Through these, they served as a defense for all their subjects, both in times of war and peace <note>original: "tum ſagi, tum togæ," literally "both of the military cloak and the toga"</note>. In contrast, the modern age perversely cultivates and polishes the flimsy fantasies of litigation and useless insanities, by which that profitable and weighty "Philomagic" <note>term: Philomagia — a word coined from Greek meaning "love of magic" or "wisdom of magic"</note> of the Ancients has been wrongfully emptied of its value. The Senate of Wise Men <note>term: Sophi — from the Greek 'sophoi,' meaning sages or philosophers</note> from before our birth used to mark those nobler Muses with white chalk <note>note: a Roman custom of marking lucky or favorable things with white stone</note>; for their sake, they threw themselves into the most taxing clouds of trouble, so that by possessing them, they might make themselves and their fatherland more famous. In our time, however, not only does the mockery and distortion of this Art increase, but violence and abhorrence rage against such fruitful berries and the very summit of the mystic arts. Should I then finally approach the lovers of these arts themselves? Kings, Princes, and Nobles? Today this one, tomorrow that one, the day after another—until finally, I, one humble little man, have approached them all in order?

> Would you dare enough, with such a bashful brow,
> Little Eye <note>original: "Ocella," a diminutive term of endearment or a reference to a small, keen observer</note>, to speak beneath the gaze of the King?
> Alas! A task so immense is terrifying for a *small* man,
> Greater even than the labors of Hercules!

Shall the detractors and the oppressors of wonderful treasures mock and hiss at the hive of manifold mysteries flowing with honey, using their slanders and such sharp-toothed darts?

> Shall that man then hurl his jeers at me with impunity?
> Shall this one mock? Shall he provoke the Lyceum <note>note: The school of Aristotle, here representing the seat of higher learning</note> with his speech?
> Or the dancers and tricksters of the theater with their wit and satires?
> Or the infamous little book written with crooked venom?
> Not so, not so; the tongue that has spoken so madly
> Shall be wounded by the same madness of a blaspheming tongue.

I have therefore thought it right to appeal to and entreat our "Philomages" <note>term: Philomagi — those who love or practice the ancient wisdom-magic</note> who now dwell in Lethe <note>note: In mythology, the river of forgetfulness in the underworld, here implying the deceased masters of the past</note>, with wailing, tears, laments, sacrifices, and atonements, by whatever means I most conveniently could, so that they—now as deified spirits <note>term: Indigites — local patron deities or deified heroes</note>—might inform and imbue the students of wisdom who are still at work.

# THE SIBYLLINE ORACLES

I was torn apart, and my poor eyes were so blocked with rheum <note>original: "lema"; refers to the crusty discharge from the eyes</note> that I could see only with the greatest difficulty. I do not quite know by what winding path I was driven; I was surrounded by the rugged and uncultivated wildness of hills and sharp rocks. That sleep had indeed been long and—as it appeared—held me in a balance, as if half-alive and half-dead. Yet, by the benefit of that sweet, brief moment of death <note>A poetic reference to sleep as a "short death"</note>, I was returned a little more cheerful and far richer in the hope of better things; for to me then (as far as my mind remembers):

> I seemed to be reclining in the dark shadow of Hermes,
> Where a vein of the water of eternal liquid flows,

Into that place, I say, I was led and transported by a wondrous path—the place which poets and prophets depict and fashion as Elysium:

> Having been sent, happy, to the Elysian shores,

Where the souls of the pious, and especially the <term>Mystae</term> <note>Initiates into sacred mysteries or secret religious rites</note>, arrive after the loosening of the bodily chain. They travel by the way called the Jasper Path, which our Ancestors <note>original: "Aborigines"</note> once trod, for this is the journey for them:

> This glittering way, revealed in the glimmering night,
> Most ruddy with countless stars in the bright sky,
> Is called the Sapphire Path, well known even to the foliage;
> This is the way for the spirits to the fields of the happy palace,
> And the secret throne; and by night and day the <term>hypaethrae</term> <note>Roofless or open-air sacred spaces</note>
> Are celebrated by the kindled torches of the Guardian Spirits;
> For if you give the poets their rights, I would not fear
> To call this place the seat of the Senate of the Gods.

Whether in the body or out of the body, I am uncertain—*God knows*—whether it was a dream or a true restoration of things; I was wretchedly wrestling with ghosts <note>original: "larvis"</note>,

> Wondrous specters were wandering everywhere through the crossroads,
> Dreams ceased, if I could even call them dreams;

And I remember (unless it is still a dream) that as I turned my eyes toward that bright world, I prayed:

Struck slightly, I nevertheless hurried on,

Furthermore, a second sight there revealed such a filthy omen, that I can compare it to no portent described by any monster-slayer (not even as a shadow): for it had a seven-angled head, balding, with projecting teeth, eaten away and scorched by decay and scabies, bent, curved, pointed, and steeped in alum; the face fell all the way to the navel, fortified with a chin where we might have struck off calf-hooves. The nose was turned up, eagle-like, hooked, like the proboscis of an elephant. The mouth was full-cheeked, backward-facing, slanting, distorted, and viper-like. The teeth were like those of a boar, prominent, very long, just like those whitened stakes upon which we are accustomed to curve linens when they are bleached in the sun. The eyes were Cyclopean, pitch-black. The ears were like those of a wild ass, hanging, and deaf. The neck was compressed, like a cuckoo's, and swan-like in the manner of pitch. The beard was thick, goat-like, a foot long,
-> Filthy, linear, rough with bristly thorns. <-
The nostrils were curved back, slimy, hawk-like, breathing out a foul sulfurous stench <note>original: "mephitim," the poisonous vapors emerging from caves or the earth.</note>, exhaling asphalt, smelling of the Lake of Ampsanctus <note>A place in Italy famous in antiquity for its deadly volcanic gases, considered an entrance to the underworld.</note>. Having only shouted out (as I recall) a word of recommendation to Hermes Trismosynus <note>A variation of Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of the Hermetic tradition</note>, principally because I am seized by a certain mystical inclination and fate (so to speak) to observe that Chief of the Assembly <note>original: "Archisynagogum"</note>. I expect from him that those things I offer will be more earnestly brought to pass; I believe and hope it will be soon;

> You shall go, O letter, hastily to the Elysian fields <note>The mythical resting place of the blessed and heroic</note>,
> Carried along these paths, and delivered there; immediately
> All will unseal you with the amazement of a trembling Choir:
> For their minds will waver, often rubbing their foreheads in confusion,

# THE SIBYLLINE ORACLES.
<note>original: "SORTES SIBYLLINÆ." These were ancient collections of oracular utterances; here, the author uses the term to describe his own mystical writings.</note>

->From where, and why you come, they are ignorant, and what it may overshadow,<-
->That these tablets should come to them in the mortal *World*:<-
->But you, conscious of the biting cause, and revealing it,<-
->First clearing each detail in the noble manner,<-
->Then recounting your contents in order, you shall be fixed<-
->In the midst of the golden Hall by a thread, to be gazed upon.<-

I have delivered, I say, the entire transcript and the small bundle of satirical pages to Mercury <note>The messenger of the gods, here acting as a spiritual courier.</note> to be carried very opportunely to the past fellow-craftsmen—*empty* indeed in bulk, but *immense* in the weight of its matters. This was not because I thought (according to the judgment of some):
> That there are no Ghosts, nor subterranean kingdoms,
> Nor the River Lethe <note>The river of forgetfulness in the underworld.</note> for men to lick, nor wandering Spirits;
Not in the least! For those things exist, they truly exist, and I am certain of their existence through heavenly instruction. Rather, I did this so that by this great and anxious zeal of mine for resisting injury and assisting justice, they might more and more take pity and bring aid; *the Gods are favorable to those who try*,
> Fortune presses upon the timid, *but fears the brave*.

And indeed, I seemed to have predestined everything in a foreign tongue, both so that the First-Wise-Man <note>original: "Protoſophus"</note> might better understand those biting *reproaches* of sharp tongues, and so that they might be read to the entire Senate in that idiom in which Golden Magic <note>original: "Aurea Magia"</note> is most active. I also intended that they might all cry out with a single hand what work is especially needed here. Furthermore, I hoped that those Greater Lovers of Magic <note>original: "Philomagi Majores"</note>, the dead, would not find it burdensome to transcribe their individual conclusions or decrees to the Lesser Lovers of Magic <note>original: "Philomagi Minores"</note>, the mortals, in the Roman tongue <note>Latin.</note> as soon as my Aethalides <note>In mythology, a son of Hermes with an unfailing memory; here, a familiar spirit.</note>—that auxiliary and administrative spirit—should attempt his return. He travels on behalf of those who sought useful words and wrote down the most upright speeches, full of truth, from that sanctuary of the Fortunate Isles into our own World, by the Sapphire path, where messengers of such small manuscripts are accustomed to go and return. Therefore, the mockery, the yawning, and the wit of those indirect rebukers against the sons of Wisdom were *such as these*.
