# OF MAGICAL NIGHTS

## A prototype of the boastful noses <note>A metaphor for arrogance or "turning up one's nose" at others</note>, along with the pamphlets of the "Scourges of Magic" <note>original: "Magiomastigum"; those who profess to whip or punish magicians</note> who are professors of its sycophancy and mockery.

->§. 8.<-

Gold-seekers, Gold-losers, Alchemists, Coal-burners, and Chimney-dwellers boast that they have obtained their Art in the Valley of Venus <note>A reference to the "Venusberg," a place of carnal temptation and illusion in folklore</note>. From this, the very least they claim to know is the construction of the Gold-making Stone <note>The Philosopher's Stone</note>; by touch alone, they transform all things into gold like Midas. They carry around yellow mines, capable of being multiplied by an unfailing ferment—but these mines are in their bellies! For they waste away their entire substance to no purpose, always with a gaping mouth, like Tantalus <note>A mythological figure punished with eternal hunger and thirst</note>.

> They chase the gardens of Tantalus and the fleeing apples;
> It is a fraud and a joke painted with many shadows,
> They offer banquets far too narrow for a stinking Goat;
> *One* of them seems to hold the bull by the horns;
> *Another* to milk it, and a *third* to place a sieve beneath,
> Whatever wealth he had, whatever wages, when he had
> Turned it all into smoke and ashes, by Hercules, I do not wonder,
> He said, if any fare badly, since there is nothing more gaping,
> Nothing worse than the Styx, nothing more malignant than *that* Art;
> To have spent it all at once—was it not a beautiful thing to see?
> Oh, holy initiates! <note>original: "synetos"; those "in the know"</note> to whom these secrets lie open:
> Behold a ridiculous thing, Cato, and a most thick-witted joke,
> Worthy of your ears, your spleen, and your loud laughter!
> Whatever you do, Cato, paint *Catullus* <note>Likely a reference to the poet's wit or perhaps a specific contemporary fool</note> with coal,
> I have just caught the sun-following commoners in the night;
> From the *brine* of Midas, we know, any morsels used to come forth,
> But these noisy wasps are mostly like cicadas,
> For whom the cause of salvation lies in Mammon alone,
> They transmute anything into the dung of the belly's stench.

In color, as it appears, they are always the same, yet in scent they are vastly different,

But as many as there are, they are bag-snatchers, sycophants, and counterfeiters; for no one comes forward to testify except the fox, and no one fails to report the same thing: that this court is open only to the foster-children of true wisdom, while it is closed to every other person—truly an Attic Eleusis <note>Referring to the Eleusinian Mysteries, secret religious rites of ancient Greece.</note>, loved without a rival!

->As a flame differs from the sea, and the stars from the earth.<-

->§. 9.<-

Babblers, cowl-wearing rascals, vulgar craftsmen, bare-bottomed beggars, dealers in trifles, and cut-purses—they falsely and with pride assert everywhere that immense profit lies in their miscellaneous and deceitful tinctures and "hotch-potch" mixtures. They contend that metallic and mineral bodies possess prodigious powers, and that from these, by their own super-rare art (for "the eagle does not catch flies" <note>A proverb implying they only deal in "great" matters, used here sarcastically.</note>), they can fashion the Great Stone <note>original: "Magolithum," likely referring to the Philosopher's Stone.</note>.

# MAGICAL NIGHTS

...or that gold-making powder <note>original: "Pulvisculum Aurificum," referring to the Philosopher's Stone in powder form</note>, by the casting of which all lower metals might most swiftly be transformed into the most perfect and purest gold; these are surely soothing and well-rubbed sayings! But it is merely ancient paper <note>original: "palaepaphia papyrus," likely a reference to old, deceptive myths</note>, just as easily as a fox eats a pear!

> A tiny grain of that substance, dissolved into the deep,
> If the entire sea-god Nereus were made of *quicksilver* <note>mercury</note>,
> Could turn that whole wide-wandering sea into gold;

O Castalian horn <note>a reference to the fountain of poetic inspiration</note>, and old wives' nonsense, trifles and childish worries! That is unbelievable, even if Cato were to preach it to me; oh, you gluttons and braggarts! Behold the hyperbole, by Hercules, a hyperbole more hyperbolic than all the poets!

> O foolish works of men, O false brains!
> That they promise the wealth of Croesus <note>a king legendary for his vast wealth</note> to anyone;
> But how much wealth is stoned away <note>a pun on "lapis" (stone) and "dilapidatur" (squandered/stoned)</note> by the fools
> Blowing on the lying shadows of the deceptive *Stone*!

These field-wandering ash-scrapers, these Chemists, Sellers of Smoke, Makers of Dyes, and Soot-eaters, are stuck in the water and fishing in the air, or rather they are shooting at the heavens. They endure eternal agitations of the soul alongside the grammarians Priscian and Aelius; for day and night they are occupied and worn out, seeking *wool from a donkey* or *the sky from Atlas* <note>proverbs for attempting the impossible</note>, insofar as they might know who the *triads* are among the inhabitants of the underworld. Yet miserably, each one is deceived and deceives others; they tell fables, they play the fool, oh Hosanna!

> Though I had a thousand mouths and a thousand tongues,
> I could not distinguish all their nonsense,
> O Almighty Father! So may Argus <note>the hundred-eyed giant</note> guard me:

Are these the mystical "Theomagi" <note>God-magicians</note> and the brothers of the *Rosy Cross* <note>The Rosicrucians, a secret society of the era</note>? What does a dog have to do with a bath? Furthermore, what kind of divine magic do those cultivate who heap mountains upon mountains to thrust you down from Olympus? What kind of *mysteries*, I ask, do they inquire into, who more truly hunt for holidays! You are only adding oil to the furnace.

# THE SIBYLLINE ORACLES

->What kind of companions you are, the fool stands as witness;<-
->My unshaven father knows, ignorant at all hours,<-
->Nourished on a few scraps and a bit of porridge,<-
->Whose stable you initiates belong to, and what kind of *Theists* you are.<-

Babblers, Defrauders, Daedalists <note>Crafty or deceptive inventors, named after the mythical Daedalus</note>, buffoons, street-wanderers, and windbags—with only their inflated and talkative discourses, they claim to be richer than Croesus himself <note>A king of Lydia famous for his legendary wealth</note>. In reality, however, they are poorer than Irus <note>The beggar from Homer’s Odyssey</note>. They claim to have all the Indian gold mines at home, even though any one of them is almost forced to sell his soul due to poverty. Thus, possessing nothing, they are smoother than a hairless Liber <note>A reference to the smooth-skinned god of wine, Bacchus/Liber</note>. Truly, their extreme want and calamity are to be deplored—but oh, the frauds and intolerable deceptions!

> The horse desires the plow-handle, the lazy bull desires the saddle;
> Let each man, I pray, gladly practice the art that he knows.

Wanderers, Beggars, Epicureans, Saunterers, Bankrupts, and Charmers—they put on the mask of Chares <note>An Athenian general known for promising much and delivering little</note> and act like Antigonus, the King of the Macedonians, nicknamed *Doson* <note>original: "Dosonem"</note>, which is to say, *the one about to give*. This is because these babblers perpetually promise *Thessalian mares* <note>A proverb for something of great value</note> and *mountains of gold* with only words and bombastic dogmas. In truth, they speak *marvels about a lentil* <note>A Latin proverb for making a big deal out of nothing</note> and out of smoke. For they are impressive in title only—empty medicine jars and cowardly horses with fine trappings. Here is Rhodes, here is the leap! <note>A famous Aesopic phrase challenging someone to prove their boasts with action rather than words.</note>

> At last, with the time of life worn away along with prayers,
> And with their coins consumed in vain blasts of wind,
> I have found this much of the truth: *I know nothing, I have nothing.*

Smoke-sellers, Hearth-huggers, Oven-tenders, Nonsense-talkers, Law-breakers, and Purse-makers—fitting the Colossal spoils of Pygmies to themselves—they are exhausted by useless and futile labor. Of these men, we may not unsuitably joke:

> They seek to have difficult trifles,
> For the labor spent on foolish things is stupid.

# MAGICAL NIGHTS

The she-goat has not yet given birth even once, while their young kid plays about entirely upon the rooftops—oh, what Azanean evils! <note>original: "Azanæa mala"; a Greek proverb referring to dry or withered misfortunes, or perhaps a reference to the parched land of Azania.</note> Ha! See how the fire-dogs, the crook-footed ones, and the "lice of Plato" <note>A derogatory reference to pseudo-philosophers who cling to greatness like parasites.</note> hold to a rough and broken path! How fruitless is their entire life of wakeful watching! How they move not a single foot without the certain danger of a precipice!

Triflers, Boasters, Griffin-sophists <note>original: "Gryphosophistæ"; those who use complex, mythical-sounding language to hide a lack of wisdom.</note>, foolish-talkers, study-shunners, sulfur-drinkers—ignorant of every refined expression—they hawk themselves as shining with such excellent and distinguished learning that they are not bound to yield (by their own persuasion) even in the slightest to the Ancients. They claim to know the mystical God-magicians <note>original: "Theomagos"</note> so exactly, even if they have never seen them, that although they are shameful ignoramuses, asses, swine, magpies, and mere echoes, they are not ashamed to contend and dispute with the retired Minervas, Nightingales, and Swans. For they dogmatize so many methods, so many daily wonders, and finally so many new, unheard-of, and unusual things, that they seem to obscure Antiquity itself (of which they wish to be called the guardians). Authors of a more recondite and elegant character—though these boasters can scarcely sound out a word or two of Latin without hallucinating—they claim to understand perfectly without having read them; taught only by that chief-trifler Paracelsus <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), the famous Swiss physician and alchemist whom the author clearly despises.</note>, the juggler, impostor, charlatan, ointment-doctor <note>original: "iatralepte"</note>, prince of entanglements, and craftsman of enigmas, who is hated by *both heaven and earth*;

->If Bavius itches for a song, Mevius does not burn,<-
->The rascals of Penelope’s suitor, and of Alcinous.<-
<note>A parody of Virgil and Homer, mocking bad poets and lazy, gluttonous hangers-on.</note>

### §. 10.

These hellebore-maddened <note>Hellebore was used in antiquity to treat madness; to be "helleborose" implies one is fit for the asylum.</note> teachers of different doctrines, followers of Hermes, snarlers, attackers, and mimes—having broken the chain with which the Ruler of the World <note>original: "Cosmarcha"</note> used to bind them—have each withdrawn to a sumptuous side of the World so that they might fleece men of their silver with a thousand tricks and devices. The greater part of these men possess "this year's harvest" and "cock's milk" <note>Proverbial terms for imaginary or impossible riches.</note> or the "Horse of Sejanus" <note>original: "equum Seianum"; a reference to a legendary horse that brought ruin to every owner; a "cursed" possession.</note>, but by blinding the roosters they weave ropes out of sand, or pluck the hair from a bald man; and by sniffing after the Stone of the Wise <note>The Philosopher's Stone (Lapis Sapientum).</note>, they perpetually stumble upon the stone of the foolish. Following these are the vagabonds, who have their breeches and purses split open like a sieve. Others [seek] wives—

<meta>This page continues the author's critique of various fraudulent practitioners and pseudo-intellectuals, following a discussion of those who misuse ancient wisdom.</meta>

# THE SIBYLLINE ORACLES

They have deserted their possessions, their sons, their hearths, their daughters and altars, and the pleasant fields of their fatherland for the sake of a leisurely wisdom.

There are some who are even "voluntarily" poor, so to speak, because they can find nowhere to receive anything, or because no one wishes to give them a thing. *Very many* are likewise Counts, Barons, and Heroes by origin; the more illustrious they are by birth, the more knowledgeable they always claim to be. Nor are there lacking those who are called baptized Saracens or Jews—though they are in every way more crafty than the unbaptized—who have evidently learned through the <term>Kabbalah|A Jewish mystical tradition often misinterpreted by Renaissance occultists as a source of magical power</term> how to "mortify" Mercury in manifold ways, to bring it back to life, and to keep it from returning to life. Similarly, they claim to prepare all kinds of aconite <note>wolfsbane or poison</note> in a thousand fashions, so that they might serve against all diseases and an infinite number of medical accidents. They claim that the Hebrew language preserves the origins of all arts and the costly and most secret mysteries of public affairs, and they prove themselves to be inspired with a foreknowledge of things to come. They frequently recite their Rabbis, the Talmud, and the "harp of Nabolohu" <note>likely a mocking reference to a pseudo-biblical instrument</note> along with the "shrine of Solomon"; hence they are able to speak of the future no less than the past and the present. Oh, what loose broomsticks and <term>Abderitic minds|A reference to Abdera, a Greek city whose inhabitants were proverbially considered foolish or mad</term>!

Finally, there are those who make a solemn show of religion, wearing monks' hoods and walking barefoot through the towns, feigning the life of a hermit with hidden hypocrisy, to whom God has supposedly revealed his secrets as if to little children. O, they are sheep in dress, but foxes in deed! Oh, what "all-holy" Dianas! <note>original: "panagæas Dianas," a sarcastic blend of Greek and Roman religious terms</note> Woe to these "elm-beaten" <note>slaves or rogues</note> and "under-the-rostrum" loiterers! Will the evening of those skeptics and lamp-living thieves—who seek their food from the very flames—ever finally arrive? Their prince is the arch-alchemist <term>cacodemon|An evil spirit or demon</term>, the overseer of the night, who always smiles through the smoke; for the arch-novice only dances with other novices, and "the old man cackles with the old woman." <note>original: "cascus cacabat cascam," an archaic Latin proverb for like-minded fools associating together</note>

> Bring your cups with you, if you wish to recline with me,
> I shall provide the fat head of a crowned ass as a side dish,
> Which the elegant foster-children of Phlegethon <note>A river of fire in the underworld</note> and Dis <note>The god of the underworld</note> shall eat.

Deceivers, Boasters, followers of Icarus, pot-hunters, seekers of idleness, and world-destroyers—all smeared with the same whitewash—they infect whomever they meet.

### §. II.

Ah, what wagon-loads of stinging tongues! Oh, what famous titles—false, and false again! Oh, what slanders, sneers, and sarcasms, and with all the wantonness of madness, beasts of double-nature, triple-barbarians!

For who, being a sincere student of the <term>Philomagical truth</term> <note>Truth pertaining to the love of magic or divine wisdom.</note>, would not rebuke these detractors? Who would not consider these insults a most monstrous disgrace? Who would not challenge such lampoons and jeers to a contest? Whose soul, I ask, would these "jokes" not wound to the very core? I cannot—indeed, I shall not be able to—refrain from declaring war, or from sending the military cloak and the glove (as the saying goes), and descending into the field of battle with those shameless backbiters;

> Noble virtue, once branded, knows not how to rest,
> A just cause cannot fear even a speck of dirt:
> I will go, I will go, and I alone will stand in fierce arms,
> And I will offer my very skull to the midst of their swords.
<note>original: "bregma" (Greek), referring to the top of the head or skull.</note>

Lest anyone should think that I am only courageous when the arena is first opened,

> And merely a loud-mouth at home, in the manner of a rooster,

I, even unarmed, easily the most remote of all the little worlds, demand an explanation from these scolders in their own waters; and I do not fear in the least to clash with them on the <term>Tullian</term> <note>Referring to Marcus Tullius Cicero, the master of Latin eloquence.</note> or <term>Ovidian</term> plain—that is, in the ancient and recondite plain of the Philosophers.

When Alchemy—the most learned teacher and mistress of the arts—has driven them upward from the dust of the earth and the most abject condition of ignorance with the sparks of her solid wisdom, they rise up against her, block her light, attack her sons with curses, and repay the benefits they received from her with bitterness, to her contempt.

Regarding Minerva, who leapt forth from the head of Jupiter without a mother, they proclaim she arose near the river Triton, and for that reason was called Tritogenia (for the Boeotians call the head *trito*). This is because in the times of King Ogyges, in the year 2189, she first appeared in Vestal dress at Lake Tritonis, from which the Triton stream breaks forth. Wisdom is not undeservedly called a Goddess for this reason: because she was born from the brain, where the seat of wisdom lies. A golden rain also decorated her birthday at Rhodes (an island so named for its wide rosebeds), so that it might endure in the memory of men when she was brought into this light. ->§. 13.<-

There is something yet beautiful and delicate, but no less curious, regarding this matter; if you please, let us wander a little further. I have often observed, and I think it worthy of great admiration, that surely in the nighttime, the more brightly and clearly the moon shows herself, the more, on the other hand, the dogs bark at her with a louder voice and noise, twisting their sharp eyes toward her. Investigating the reason for this while in a state of deliberation, I finally found that I could devise no more suitable explanation than this: if I say that the dogs, looking at the moon, discern in her—as if in a shining mirror—their own image, likeness, and shape. From this, they imagine that another dog similar to themselves is present there, and for that reason they bay, as dogs are frequently accustomed to do when they see others.

> And the deaf Moon proceeds to complete her courses.

It proceeds, completing its course with swift motion; and in a similar fashion, it usually happens to the advocates of more majestic wisdom. Thus, I say, the malice of the <term>Thymelarii</term><note>Originally referring to stage-performers or jesters; here used as a derogatory term for low-level critics or "buffoons" of science.</note> shouts and barks against the Wise-Magicians, whom they would even wish to blind. This is truly a brutal madness and a hellish bile—oh, hatreds loathsome to heaven and born of the devil! It will perhaps seem marvelous to some why the owl was anciently dedicated to Minerva <note>The Roman goddess of wisdom.</note>; but besides others, this chief reason (in my judgment at least) can be assigned: that other birds haunt and pursue the owl if she ever appears during the day, because she has clear, bright, and shining eyes which the other birds seem to want to gouge out. In exactly this way, the World would wish to tear away the wisdom, honor, and reputation of the Lovers of Magic.

The <term>Polemopatres</term><note>Literally "fathers of war"; military theorists or veteran commanders.</note> in their instructions, by which they inform those studious of military discipline, command a general who is desirous of victory to always arrange his army so that he does not fight with the sun in his face;

->For they say, *the sun snatches away the sight and the face first*;<-

And for that reason, one must never fight against its glittering rays. How perfectly this applies to those whose minds have been totally invaded and occupied by hatred and envy of the Spagyric Sun! <note>The "Spagyric Sun" refers to the "Sun of Alchemy" or the ultimate light of chemical transformation.</note> These men, envious of the glory of its incredible mysteries, wished to bury Alchemy in perpetual oblivion and dismiss it from the memory of men. But these blind and mad fools did not heed the precept of the learned military writers: for they began to battle not only with the sun in their faces, but even to provoke Hyperion <note>A Titan associated with the sun.</note> himself—the very storehouse of all nature's wonders—to war, as if to cast Jupiter himself from his throne. From this, it is very easy to divine what those who dared to undertake such an ill-advised thing will suffer in the conflict,

->For the glowing *sun snatches away the sight and the face first*:<-

Thus our Titan, and that shining torch of the human mind, Physico-chemistry, strikes those mockers blind according to the merit of their blasphemy, and with the glowing rays of its profound wisdom, it dulls their sight.

The historiographers, those secretaries of the wonders of their age, when setting out to describe the triumph of Julian Caesar <note>Julian the Apostate (r. 361–363 AD), the last pagan Roman Emperor.</note>, that terror of the earth, know not with what grandeur of words, what weight of sentiment, or what grace and vein of eloquence they might most skillfully proclaim him. For who would not marvel greatly? This Emperor, celebrated for his victories and spoils, was carried upon a triumphal throne (drawn by forty elephants) and received into the Roman Capitol with such immense pomp, applause, and the joy of the common people. Likewise Domitian, who is said to have been brought in not by a two-horse, four-horse, or six-horse litter, but upon the shoulders of men?

# LAUREATE LETTERS,
->or<-
# RATIFIED PRAYERS.

**H**ermes, now and forever immortal, the presiding High Priest of the Muses’ and Magic’s seat, thrice-greatest <note>original: "Trismegistus"</note>, sends greetings to Philomagus <note>A pseudonym meaning "Lover of Magic"</note>, a mortal and most powerful defender and spreader of our practice and name, in Him who is the true and only salvation, and the only refuge.

There is no reason, my Plautine Philosopher <note>Likely a reference to the Roman playwright Plautus, suggesting the recipient is a "student of the human comedy" or drama</note>, why you should further tear or exhaust yourself with wounds and cares in this undertaking; we have fully regarded the pious zeal of your soul, and by its impulse, we release you from your vows. We here dwell eternally among the "magionic" <note>A coined term for magical-harmonic</note> valleys and fare well; for you, there remains the "inter-order" of Claudian and Merlin <note>Referring to the Roman poet Claudian and the legendary wizard, suggesting a bridge between classical and British prophecy</note>, which is the twelfth from my hidden tomb, and when you come to us, I shall applaud you in person for this great role of yours. For we have faithfully received, by the hand of Mercury our Herald, your suppliant books concerning the injuries inflicted upon you; therefore, whatever has been prepared by us in this matter, and the responses given by the voice of the most learned Messenger <note>original: "Diactoris," an epithet for Hermes/Mercury</note>, you must now disseminate and make known; open every lip:

> Proceed to feed your mind upon sacred studies,
> And remain always moderate and humble.
> You leap beyond the Muses <note>original: "Aonidas," referring to the inhabitants of the Aonian mountains</note>; may your life endure as you pray,
> Thus a hard youth will be a solace to the old man.

Meanwhile, see that you live continually as a widower and a virgin <note>A command for ascetic celibacy to maintain magical purity</note>. Given from the Hall of the Immortal Adepts <note>term: Adeptorum (Adepts) — those who have reached the highest level of alchemical or magical initiation</note>; on the Ides of May, in the year 1666 from the arrival of my Orb.

I perceived, therefore, from the very first unfolding of the little lot <note>The "sorticula" refers to the practice of drawing lots for divination</note>, the greatest faithfulness and skill of Mercury <note>The messenger god, associated here with communication and interpretation</note>. Just as a painter, who wishes to make a display of his readiness in painting upon some tablet, turns so much study and so much wakeful vigilance toward it! With what diligence, I say, does he take care that with a skilled and right hand he may delineate as perfectly as possible the idea conceived in his mind! In the same manner my "Circumpes" <note>Literally "Round-foot," likely a nickname for Mercury or a specific messenger figure</note>, like one perfected by the art of Parrhasius <note>A famous painter of ancient Greece known for his realism</note>, was vehemently and uniquely occupied in showing, quite graphically, the image of all nature, which had been so greatly defiled by the stains of wrongs.

*Secondly*, I was not to doubt that this aforementioned Herald <note>original: "Caduceatorem," the bearer of the staff of Mercury</note> of the decrees of this council of the Unyielding Magi <note>original: "Irreducum Magorum"</note> was established for now and forever, and that a certain esteem was won for him, whatever foreign things he might inspire; or, however he might command, and whatever he might approve or reject, the Archimandrite <note>A high-ranking official or abbot</note> with the Suffete <note>A magistrate or judge</note> of the rest of the Sleepless Ones <note>original: "Insopitorum"</note> would exist as the cause of his willing it so.

*Thirdly*, it was proclaimed by our Past Masters or Adepts, and they sanctioned it by their own decree, that they wished—by right or by wrong—to have the nobility of their majestic judgments proclaimed as openly as possible. This was to be done under the inscriptions of the truth-singing Prophetesses, but especially by the majesty of the responding Cumaean Sibyl <note>The most famous of the ancient Greek prophetesses</note>. They decreed these should be gifted with a Latinity by me (though I am a poor fool, supported by no aids of the arts or letters), which walks more loftily than any other tongue or idiom, and wanders through both houses of the Sun.

Regarding their right to act among men, they are commonly said or believed to have been unmarried,

> Whatever songs the Virgin inscribed upon the leaves,

But, however that may be, this is most certain: no oracles surpass the Sibylline ones in power. Indeed, the books of the foretelling Sibyls were once held in such faith and estimation among the Roman people that all the sons of Romulus <note>The Romans</note> believed the future events and fates of their city were contained within those codices.

> Hence toward the rocks of Avernus, and the dark
> Caves of the Sibyl, the nations stretched from every side to ask.

I say they were once held in such great veneration among the Romans that they appointed the most noble men as guardians, exempting them from all civil disturbances and duties. The Romans guard nothing, not even their sacred rites, as diligently as they do the Sibylline oracles. Furthermore, it is recorded that the <term>Duumvirate</term> <note>A commission of two men</note> was instituted by Tarquin <note>Tarquinius Superbus, the last King of Rome</note> and delegated to inspect the leaves of the prophetic papers, so much so that the greatest faith is owed to the aphorisms of the Sibylline rhapsodists. *Fourthly and finally*, all have agreed in unison that this "Little Work of Right Magic" <note>original: *Orthomagiopusculum*; a Greek-Latin hybrid term coined by the author</note>, smelling of the lamp under the torch of night-watches, should be made known and composed late at night from the mouth of the Wing-footed God <note>Mercury</note>. By this, when I reflect upon it, they have clearly indicated the highest pursuit of wisdom. Just as the Spartans <note>original: *Lacones*</note>, as we read in the monuments of history, used to handle their greater and more difficult matters at night, they were mindful of that famous proverb: *counsel comes in the night* <note>original: *in nocte consilium*</note>. For nocturnal quiet is most suitable for taking wise and useful counsel regarding affairs.

-> §. 18. <-

In the beginning of the world, God established the firmament in the midst of the waters, so that it might separate one from the other, saying, *let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters* <note>Genesis 1:6</note>. The "Golden Orator" <note>likely a reference to a specific commentator or Chrysostom</note> reads it: *let there be a partition, let a wall intervene to separate the waters, lest they mingle with one another*. Of these waters, I can indeed say that *some* are a symbol of the tumults of the day, and *others* are a type of the quiet of the night. Let there be, therefore, a space between the waters, and let it separate the floods from the floods, lest the business of both flow together. For it is impossible for one who has been excessively active during the day to enjoy the hidden things of the night; nor is it granted to find the leisure for arduous and sublime wisdom amidst the tumults of the day and the occupations of the light.

Hence also the Athenians, who flourished with singular praise for wisdom and all disciplines, rejected the insignia of Eagles which the Valentinians <note>referring to the Roman Emperors Valentinian I or II</note> carried on their military banners and adopted the Owl, a bird that flees the light. They even engraved it on their coins as a symbol of wisdom, for which reason it is also called the bird of Pallas and dedicated to Minerva, the Goddess of Sciences, to denote—

...that the period of first sleep, or the night, is more suited to studies than the day; just as the excellent Royal harper <note>King David</note>, Daniel, Isaiah, and Zechariah expressed: *I meditated in the night with my own heart; Night is my illumination in my delights; I looked in a vision of the night; My soul shall desire thee in the night; I saw by night, and behold a man ascending upon a red horse, and he stood among the myrtle trees that were in the deep.* <note>These are composite translations of Psalm 77:6, Psalm 139:11, Daniel 7:7, Isaiah 26:9, and Zechariah 1:8.</note> For when someone powerful in the gravity of their person and authority speaks, all who are present are soon accustomed to fall silent;

> *And then there will also be a greater harvest from the Muses.*

And so the time of night, which is the mother of counsel and the nourisher of every arduous work, is most conveniently appointed for the thorough treatment of these mysteries.

# MAGICAL NIGHTS

While these things were being done, and having been somewhat awakened by all of this, I was more like one keeping watch or dreaming than one sleeping. And yet, when Celeripes <note>Latin: "Swift-foot," a name for a messenger or the god Mercury</note>, standing there before me, had opened his mouth with the greatest power and sweetness of charm, I seemed to be entirely soothed with immense joy. Immediately, my eyes were unspeakably drawn by that clear light of the face of my Transelysian <note>Likely referring to a being from beyond the Elysian fields, or a celestial realm</note> companion, who then represented an Archangel in no small way. My ears, tuned to melody, were affected by that most orderly golden pen—written by the fingers of our High Priest Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with alchemy and magic</note>—and hung upon the Attic eloquence <note>Refined, classical Greek style of speech</note> and the winning elegance of the words of my smooth-talking Mercury. With the sweet fragrance of his loud-sounding voice, like a certain divine Orpheus, he spoke partly in the tongues of men and partly in the tongues of Angels—that is, weaving his rhetoric now in a moderate style, now in a grand, rounded one. O, well-tended mouth! <note>original: "Evœ os curatum!" An exclamation of ritual joy</note> My heart opened within, and swelled with joy at the account of such great vigilance and care from the Deities who are so kind to their own, because at last the day of release had arrived, with our own Patrons taking the matter so wisely upon themselves. Furthermore, the Legate himself—on whose tongue is the greatest labor, under whose tongue is the sweetest honey, and what is above the tongue? Ineffable things, which it is a sacred duty for me not to speak <note>original: "mihi loqui religio," implying a taboo or religious silence regarding certain mysteries</note>—bore a name on whose morning the people of Israel shook off the yoke of the harsh Pharaonic mill. This is surely a symbol of our entire salvation, redemption, and liberty from the tyranny of the Tartarean <note>Infernal or hellish</note> serpent, enticing us with such spirit toward total success.

->§. 19.<-

Therefore, just as those who have been tossed by a long and dangerous storm upon the Ocean, driven here and there by waves and winds, cry out "Land! Land! Italy!"

### §. 20.

Having thus related with great faithfulness and in a concise manner <note>original: "Laconicè"; in the brief style of the Spartans</note> their opinions (concerning that hidden storehouse of riches and delights, the *Philosophers' Stone* <note>original: "Lapide Sapientum"; the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold and granting eternal life</note>), Hermogenes said: "Behold these signs, though trembling, insofar as they are soon to be offered to mortals. By the honor of the sacrosanct Trinity and of those my excellent Initiates, for the relief of the widowed and the consolation of the pious—doubting nothing of divine help, and fortified by His assistance and my own—begin and prophesy a 'saleable web' <note>a metaphor for a finished, useful work</note>, not one left unfinished, nor one made controversial by the ambiguity of proverbs. These men, in whose power it stood (while they were among the living) by the nod of God to reveal this peerless Art to whom they wished, have ordered these things to be delegated to you as a prayerful duty."

"Therefore, so that for the sake of True Magic <note>original: "Orthomagiæ"</note> and the lineage of those who conferred so great a gift upon you, *under your guidance*, it may forever set sail among those whom the triple Architect of heaven and earth—that ultimate First-Mage <note>original: "Protophilomagus"</note>—shall have called, or rather pre-selected, for the hidden things of this literature. Carry through the whole business in a simple series of tradition, and just as I suggest to you, full of meaning but not deceptive, without any intentional concealment, in a plain and concise course of order. For it is well enough known that no one can take these things for himself except him to whom Jehovah <note>The Hebrew name for God</note> has decreed to grant them; He alone both illuminates the darkness of these mysteries and darkens the clarity, so that one cannot grasp even the clearest and most evident things unless illuminated by Him, nor uncover the cloudiest things if they have not been enlightened by Him. Furthermore, I adjure you to dispatch these things fluently and without delay."

# The Cave of the Sibyls

1. Commonly referring to prophetic virgins; however, in a broad sense, every woman or girl whose breast receives a Divine Spirit, and who foretells and prophesies, is called a *Sibyl*, that is, the counsel of God. For the Aeolians <note>An ancient Greek dialect group</note> call the Gods *Sios*, while among them *Bule* is the word for mind or counsel. Therefore, we can call the *Sibyls* as if they were *Siobulas*—that is, those sounding the thoughts of God—to whom the Ancients surely gave this name because they announced the counsels of the Gods. <note>original: "Σιὸς... Βυλὴ... Siobulas"</note>

2. Here this means the middle, the practice, the way, etc. It is derived from *climbing* <note>Latin: "scandendo"</note>, because by this path we *climb* to the highest points of wisdom.

3. Here this means to linger, to remain, etc. Otherwise, *to linger* <note>Latin: "morari"</note>, when the first syllable is long, signifies "to act foolishly" according to its Greek etymology. As it is said in that famous line: "Claudius ceased to *linger* among men." This should not be interpreted as if the meaning were "Claudius ceased to act and live among men," but rather that through death he ceased to be insane and out of his mind, he who had lacked wisdom while alive. <note>A pun on the Latin 'morari' (to stay) and the Greek 'moros' (foolish), famously used by Seneca regarding Emperor Claudius.</note>

4. Commonly "on high," as if *above the mud* <note>Latin: "supra limum"</note>, etc.

5. More commonly these, as if *you give yourself to the way* <note>Latin: "viae te dedas"</note>, etc.

6. These little animals are of well-known significance. *Ants* <note>Latin: "Formicae"</note> are tireless, dwellers of the countryside, the agile nurslings of the All-parent Earth, etc. They are so named from *carrying crumbs* <note>Latin: "ferendis micis"</note>, that is, grains, for which "crumbs" is used metaphorically, as it is for bits of bread and all other things. For, properly speaking, *crumbs* are those little dust-specks that sparkle in the sand like gold or silver; hence the verb *to shimmer* <note>Latin: "mico, as"</note>, which is to glow red now and then at intervals, like the aforementioned dust-specks.

7. Here used for celebrated, distinguished, excellent, etc. Otherwise, *noble* <note>Latin: "nobilis"</note>, according to etymology, is a verbal form contracted from *knowable* <note>Latin: "noscibilis"</note>, in the same manner as "easy," "agile," and many similar words.

8. Or the *horn of plenty* <note>Latin: "cornucopiae"</note>; it is the same (just as previously mentioned in the Magic Circus) as the *Horn of Amalthea* <note>In Greek mythology, the goat-horn that provided unlimited nourishment</note>, endowed with this bright and most indulgent faculty: that whatever we desire sprouts forth abundantly for us from it. Some relate that there were two such *Horns*, from one of which flowed ambrosia and from the other nectar—the food and drink of the Gods. But this has no affinity or conformity with our philosophy and Golden Truth; *there is one Sun, one God, and one Earth, which produces all things as one through the One.*

<keywords>Sibyls, etymology, Emperor Claudius, ants, Cornucopia, Amalthea, monism, prophecy, symbolic animals</keywords>

# THE UNEARTHED GRAIN

1. In this passage, it is the same as a seal, a sign, or a signed document <note>original: "sigillum, signum, sive obsignatum diploma"</note>.
2. That is, the powers or capabilities of the magnet, or more correctly *magnetism* <note>original: "magnetismum"</note>; otherwise, "Divine Will" <note>original: "Numen"</note> is properly the nod and command of God.
3. In English, "brevity of speech," or a short discourse containing much in few words; called, as it were, *the custom of the Lacons* <note>original: "Laconum mos"; referring to the Spartans of Laconia, known for "laconic" speech</note>, that is, the grasping of many things in few words. The name is derived from the customs of the Lacedaemonians, to whom nothing was more hateful than long-winded talkativeness.
4. Here it is an adjective for that which belongs to meter, that is, it pertains to measure, song, or verse; otherwise *metricus* is also sometimes used as a noun, being the same as a poet.
5. That is, by devotion and holiness of life, by the seal of the soul, etc., because *Religion* <note>original: "Religio"</note> is used figuratively for anxious care, a scruple of conscience, etc.; named from "leaving behind" <note>original: "reliquendo"</note>, or rather from "binding back" <note>original: "religando"</note>, because it surely *binds us back* to God.
6. That is, by openness of soul, purity, integrity, etc., because *sincerity* <note>original: "sinceritas"</note> is etymologically the same as simplicity, that is, the brilliance of the heart, *like wax* <note>original: "sicut cera"</note>. Therefore, just as *simple* <note>original: "simplex"</note> sounds like *without a fold* <note>original: "sine plica"</note>, so that is called *sincere* which is *without wax* <note>original: "sine cera"</note>, a metaphor drawn from honey; for before it is without disguise—namely simple, pure, and unmixed—it ought to be *without wax*. Or we can interpret *sincere* in yet another way, and perhaps not without wit, as being as if *together with the wax* <note>original: "simul cum cera"</note>; for when we wish to divide the common fruit of the beehives with our partners without deceit, we are accustomed to share the honey *together with the wax*. But if we bring only the honey into the middle and keep the wax for ourselves, we defraud our partners and do not act with them with integrity and sincerity—that is, *together with the wax*. And from this, the spelling will be good whether it is written *sincerus* with a Latin 'i' or *syncerus* with a Greek 'y'.
7. Or "graphically," in English: elegantly, charmingly, accurately, "to the fingernail" <note>original: "ad ungvem"; a Latin idiom meaning "to perfection"</note>, etc.
8. That is, it is first titled; a metaphor taken from the ministers of the Church, who, when baptizing people, are accustomed to bestow names at the same time.
9. That is, seriously, deliberately, thoughtfully, etc., as if *by profession*.
10. Here it stands for "they affirmed," "they approved," etc. However, it seems to me to be said from "I shout" <note>original: "clamo"</note> by way of antiphrasis <note>a figure of speech where a word is used in a sense opposite to its proper meaning</note>, as if it were "I love" <note>original: "amo"</note>, that is, "I act secretly" <note>original: "clàm ago"</note>, because lovers act very secretly and shout the least.

...friend, and yet by me here, and elsewhere by Virgil, she is called *Deiphobe* <note>original: "Deiphobe"</note>, as if *phobæ*, that is, the hair and ornament of *God* <note>original: "Dei". The author is using a creative etymology to link the Sibyl's name to divine beauty.</note>: you have heard her deeds in part in our Sibylline Oracles. 5. Likewise, let those three words, *therefore the dark mother*, not pass without notable scrutiny, especially the last one; however, putting aside the tripod <note>A reference to the Delphic tripod of prophecy.</note> and borrowing the hook of the former: for these have been specifically combined in this way by intention, through long and tedious labor, and mature judgment. 6. Here she is distended and stuffed with the best juice; read more widely a little below in the gloss on the word *pregnant*. 7. That is, full of veins, or with veins; because *-osus*, *-lentus*, and frequently *-bundus* are the endings used by Grammarians to denote fullness, such as *aurosus* or *aurulentus* <note>original: "aurulentus"</note>, that is, full and *distended* with gold; *Amorosus* or *amorabundus*, contracted to *amabundus*, that is, full and as if in love *to the very bottom* <note>original: "fundo tenus"</note>; likewise *porosus* (porous), *gaudiosus* (joyful), etc., *florulentus* (flowery), *rosulentus* (rosy), etc., *esuribundus* (starving), *deerrabundus* (wandering), etc., that is, abounding and full of pores, joys, flowers, roses, hunger, and error. 8. I consider the history of the Phoenix (which is properly to be understood as the Philosophers' Stone) renewing itself to be well enough known; however, to me indeed, *Phoenix* seems to be named as if it were the *snow of Phoebus* <note>original: "nix Phœbi". Phoebus is the sun god; the author suggests the Stone is the "bright white" of the sun.</note>, that is, the splendor of the sun. 9. From which, namely, nothing has yet been born or arisen; hence the "third matter" is excluded, such as all Animals, Vegetables, and Minerals: for the word *virgin* is derived from incorruption and is shared with all things that we wish to signify as unpolluted, as if it were *virago*, because *she acts with force* <note>original: "vi agat"</note> and is ignorant of female passion. 10. *Nowhere not*, a roundabout way of saying *everywhere*; but the word *nullibi* (nowhere) is said as if *in no place*; *Necubi* (lest anywhere) is the same in sense. 11. This means she brings forth seed, because *semento* (to sow) is derived from *sementum*, which is the same as *semen* (seed); etymologically it is *sementifico* (to make seed), for which we say the contracted form *semento*, as if *I try the seed* <note>original: "semen tento"</note>. 12. Properly it means she revels in intercourse, said as if *she frolics like a calf with the penis* <note>original: "pene vitulatur"</note>, from which it seems to me the contraction was made; it is placed here acutely and aptly, because the *olochrysa* <note>Greek: "all-gold"</note>, that is, the ever-living matter of the Sages, continually takes pleasure in its own hidden and invisible seed. 13. That is, she grows, for *olesco* is properly *I grow*, as if *I shall be nourishment* <note>original: "olus esco"</note>: for the ancients said *esco, escis, escit* for *I shall be, you will be, he will be*. 14. That is, she emits seed, or makes sperm, as if *spermatificat*, for which the contracted form *spermatico* is used, or perhaps more correctly outside of meter *spermatizo* <note>original: "spermatizo"</note>, because the origin is Greek. 15. That is, she is heavy with child, since *pregnant* <note>original: "prægnans"</note> etymologically sounds like being *great before birth* <note>original: "grandem præ gnatis"</note>, that is, before any fruits. 16. That is, she gives birth, she makes offspring; for the verb *fœto* (to breed) is contracted from *fœtifico*, which is *I make offspring*, I am in labor, etc. 17. That is, she increases with progeny, for I think *sobolesco* (to grow by offspring) is said as if *I grow by the sprout* <note>original: "sobole cresco"</note>. 18. That is, she thickens and increases amply, because *alesco* (to grow) is said as if *I grow by nourishment* <note>original: "alimento cresco"</note>. 19. That is, and yet she suffers no loss or shipwreck of her virginity, because *eugium* <note>A rare anatomical term for the hymen.</note>, with the second-to-last syllable lengthened, is almost the same as the *hymen*, namely that thin little membrane in the female parts which is broken at the first intercourse, believed to be the enclosure of virginity; therefore, it fits the present purpose figuratively and through a change of terms; consult the Greek lexicon. 20. That is, not at all, as if *in no way*, a compound like "only" or "merely." 21. Or used as a deponent verb, *she is shipwrecked* <note>original: "naufragatur"</note>, which absolutely means to suffer loss, said as if *I break the ship* <note>original: "navim frango"</note>, from which it was contracted and forged.

### The Second Metric Laconism,
#### *under*
### Conscience and Experience;
#### *or*
### The Method, by no means a Knot.
<note>Laconism: A brief or concise way of speaking. The author suggests this "Method" is straightforward rather than a "knotty" or difficult problem.</note>

Just as the unveiled $^5$ matter must be led to its final completion: for there are at last $^6$ two things upon which the entire <term>Mastery</term> <note>Mastery: The "Magisterium," or the successful completion of the Philosopher's Stone.</note> of the Philosophers rests; namely, the due matter, and the rite, or the way of acting upon it. The matter is the greatest secret, but truly the way of proceeding with it is a secret above secrets. Since, therefore, in the first Laconism, the physico-chemical matter was offered nakedly $^7$ and openly, in this second one (lest anything be lacking for its use) the method of operating is treated in due time $^8$; in which most formidable $^9$ secret, as in the preceding one, I have held myself strictly to the middle path $^{10}$, adding nothing and taking nothing away; but just as I have transcribed $^{13}$ that in Latin $^{11}$ from the mouth of Evander $^{12}$, and as the Philosophers of the Past have announced that this must be carried out $^{14}$, so also I communicate the same here, most simply $^{15}$, to those consecrated to golden literature; otherwise, I shall immediately $^{16}$ fall back into nothingness.

# THE THRESHED GRAIN
### Kk 2

1. It is worthy of singular weighing and balancing upon a golden scale to consider what the name *Vesta* signifies here: that is, *a thing of value and substance* <note>original: "res vilis & treffis" - likely a play on the idea of the hearth as the core of the home</note>, which stands by its own strength and is clothed in all things. 2. That is, bringing joy and pleasure; named from *helping* <note>Latin: "juvando"</note>, because those things which are pleasant help the mind and the senses. 3. That is, genial, pleasing, etc.; for it is *salutary*; or perhaps more correctly *salarius*, an adjective derived from *salt* <note>Latin: "sal"</note>, which in the masculine gender, both singular and plural, is elegantly used to mean wisdom, delight, wit, and so on. 4. That is, *belonging to Jove*; for *Diana* was the daughter of Jupiter by Latona, born in the same birth as Apollo on the Island of Delos, whence she is also called *Delia*, and Apollo *Delius*. She is also called *Dictynna, Libera, the Night-Shiner, the Goddess of the Three-Ways*, etc. Furthermore, she is called *Hecate* because she is appeased by a hundred sacrifices; likewise *Lucina*, that is, the Goddess of childbirth, named by those in labor as *Juno Lucina*—*Juno* indeed from *helping*, but *Lucina* because she brings the offspring into the *light* <note>Latin: "lucem"</note>. This same goddess is similarly called the *Moon* <note>Latin: "Luna"</note>, namely because she shines *alone* <note>Latin: "una"</note> at night, that is, solitary and without her brother, or because she receives her *light* <note>Latin: "lumen"</note> from the sun, as if illuminating with a borrowed light. Furthermore, she is called the *All-Wanderer*, not truly from hunting, but because she is numbered among the wandering orbits of the seven planets. Additionally, she is called *Proserpina*, evidently from *creeping forth* <note>Latin: "proserpendo"</note>, for she seems to creep like a serpent while she is "mooned" <note>curved into a crescent</note> now to the right, now to the left. Moreover, she is *Triple-Born*, because she is believed to be the *Moon* in the heavens, *Diana* on earth, and *Proserpina* in the Underworld. Finally, she is *Three-Headed*, because she has three heads: the right a horse's, the left a dog's, and the middle a wild sow's, etc. All these things, though they belong to the fabled theology of the poets, nevertheless contain their own mystical interpretation, with which they are accustomed to veil these arduous secrets of the mind. 5. That is, *Revealed*, with the prefix acting as a negative, as if *shown without a veil*. 6. Here it is placed for *only*; merely, etc. 7. That is, clearly, frankly, as if *without play* <note>Latin: "sine ludo" - an etymological play on "sincerely"</note>. 8. Here it is an adverb for "opportunely," as if *in its own time*. 9. That is, the greatest of all, because *horrible* is elegantly and appropriately used for "grand," especially in these phrases: *a horrible secret, a horrible gift*, etc., because grand things and deep mysteries usually induce *horror, stupor, delay*, and admiration. 10. Or *neutrally*, that is, neither to one side nor the other, but as if indifferently in the middle; said as *ne*, that is, *not to either side*. 11. Here it means the same as plainly, openly, etc.; properly *in the manner of the Latins*. 12. That is, *of Mercury*, because Evander, or Evandrus, is a proper name for Mercury, whom they wish to be called as if the *care of merchandise* <note>Latin: "mercium curam"</note>, because he is thought to preside over merchants; but for our purpose, he would be more skillfully called *Viocurius*, that is, *running the way* <note>Latin: "viam currens"</note>, namely from the Gods to men and back again; or *Medicurius*, because he *runs in the middle* between the Gods and men; for between two people speaking, speech *runs in the middle* and is reciprocated. 13. I have transcribed this in Latin because *to copy* <note>Greek/Latin: "catagrapho"</note> properly means to write from another's original; look into a Greek lexicon for the root. 14. This means to be divulged, published, etc., because *to carry through* <note>Latin: "perfero"</note> stands figuratively for spreading abroad or promulgating. 15. That is, most openly, purely, candidly, *without deceit or folds* <note>Latin: "sine dolo & plicis" - the etymology of "simple"</note>. 16. Here it is aptly placed for "presently," "suddenly," etc.

# THE CHEMICAL WINNOWING
<page-num>258</page-num>

<image-desc>An oval diagram containing text, with words arranged around the outer perimeter of the oval. The words around the perimeter are: "In the art, a suitable fire is of no small importance." The word "Suitable" is printed upside down at the bottom of the oval.</image-desc>

### Symbols
### OF THE PERSIAN SIBYL. <gloss>1</gloss>

> **T**he hidden <gloss>2</gloss> spirit <gloss>2</gloss> of the world <gloss>2</gloss>, slowly and patiently,
> Must be cherished by you with a continuous and mild warmth:

---

1. Commonly called the *Persian* <note>original: "Persicæ"</note>, for *Persa* properly refers to one who is from Persia, whether male or female.
2. *The hidden spirit of the world must be cherished with warmth*, that is, the *Spirit of the Universe* <note>The "Spiritus Mundi" was believed by alchemists to be a universal life force permeating all matter</note>, which lies hidden in the material—revealed in the previous concise instruction <note>original: "Laconismo," referring to a brief, pithy statement</note>—as if in its own proper vessel; it must be guarded, softened, and nourished with a moderate and unhurried heat.

---

# THE THRESHED GRAIN.
<note>original: "GRANUM ERUTUM"</note>
Kk 3

<image-desc>An oval diagram containing text, with words arranged around the exterior perimeter of the oval. The words on the perimeter are oriented to follow the curve of the line.</image-desc>

->It is bent<-
->by art,<-
->it is.<-
->This<-
->nor<-
->for<-
->of art<-
->by placing<-
->through<-
->by placing<-

### Seals
### OF THE LIBYAN PROPHETESS.¹

> Let nature, by her own effort², both cleanse³ and prepare⁴ this,
> For by its favorable⁵ inclinations⁶, within the space of a year,
> From the raw—

---

1. Commonly called *Libyan*; for *Libyssa*, or *Libystis*, is she who is from Libya, just as a *Persian* is from *Persia*.
2. Here used for her rite, or rather, her manner, guidance, course, or track, etc. Otherwise, *nixus* <note>effort or labor</note> is properly the labor of those giving birth, defined as it were as the *extreme force of nature*.
3. That is, "And let it purify," because *purgo* <note>to cleanse</note> is derived from *purum ago* <note>to make pure</note> etc.
4. Outside of the poetry, you might perhaps do better, and more suitably to the matter being treated, by reading "and let it separate" <note>Latin: separétque</note> rather than "and let it prepare" <note>Latin: parétque</note>.
5. Here taken figuratively for those things which are inclined, well-disposed, or prone, etc. Otherwise, *pronus* is properly said of one bent toward the front part, as if "born forward" <note>Latin: prognatus</note> etc.
6. That is: by a genial, or natural instinct and inclination; moreover, *genium* and *genius* are named from *gignendo* <note>begetting or producing</note>. For a *Genius* is called a God who possesses the power of generating all things; hence water, earth, air, and fire, which are the seeds and elements of things, may rightly be called the Genius Gods; thus "my genius" is he who begot me, the parent of the race, etc.

*The bottom part of this page was also intended for an image, but there was no opportunity for me to attach it at this time.*

# THE CHEMICAL WINNOWING

<column-break/>

-> Always from the unrefined and impure, the pure eventually recedes at the end. <- <note>original: "Semper ab impro puro ultro purum in fine recedit." This text appears in a circular diagram in the original manuscript, symbolizing the cyclical nature of the alchemical process.</note>

### Aphorisms
### OF THE DELPHIC PROPHETESS.

> From your coarser, dissolved Black-Earth¹, there springs forth²
> A certain white-appearing³, divided⁴, egg-like⁵, consubstantial⁶ Nymph⁷,
> ->Pure and clear,<-

1. That is, Black Earth; because *Pnigitis* is interpreted as the *black rot of the earth*. <note>original: "Pnigite." A reference to a specific type of medicinal or alchemical earth, here used to represent the 'nigredo' or black stage of the work.</note>
2. That is: it buds, sprouts, is born, or arises. The word is derived from the adjective *venus* <note>meaning lovely or blooming</note> by likeness to *Spring* <note>Latin: ver</note>, because in the springtime things tend to shine, to "ear" (that is, to produce ears of grain), and to bud; it is said to come from *greenness* <note>Latin: viror</note>, because then the twigs begin to *turn green*; or even from *turning* <note>Latin: vertendo</note>, because at that time the season of the year begins to *turn* itself.
3. That is: appearing naturally white; perhaps contracted from *leucopaeus* or *leucophaeus* <note>Greek-derived terms for ash-colored or white</note>; consult the Greek lexicon.
4. That is: divided; because *erctus* is a participle from *erciscor*, which in ancient times was interpreted as "to divide," specifically the land; from this remains the terms *erctus* and *erciscundus* for "divided" and "to be divided."
5. That is: single-yoked and transformed, after the likeness of an egg <note>Latin: ovum</note>; hence *ovatus* and *ovaticus* is an epithet of Mercury, and specifically of the Philosophers' Mercury, which is indeed homogeneous and *egg-like* throughout, in which consists the principle of indestructibility.
6. In English, *consubstantial*, or that which is of the same and similar substance; from <term>ousia</term> (substance) and <term>homos</term> (one, similar, or equal).
7. That is: a Goddess like water; because the water itself is called a Nymph, as if it were the *Divinity of the water* <note>Latin: Numen lymphae</note>; hence a bride at a wedding is commonly called a Nymph, so named from the duty of washing, which also alludes to the name of the one marrying; for *Nymph* comes from <term>neon</term> and <term>phainesthai</term>, because she "appears new."

*Likewise, a part of this small page contains an image, placing the matter before the eyes, though it is not here drawn.* <note>The author suggests that the text itself creates a mental image of the alchemical transformation even where an illustration is absent.</note>

<summary>This page presents a cryptic alchemical poem attributed to the Delphic Oracle, using complex etymological notes to explain the emergence of the "White Nymph" (the purified matter) from the "Black Earth" (the initial decay).</summary>
<keywords>Delphic Prophetess, Pnigitis, Nymph, Mercury, consubstantial, alchemical stages, etymology, purification</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the author's philological and symbolic exploration of terms, following the previous discussion on "Laconism." The focus here is on the etymology of "Saga" and "Pecunia," alongside a symbolic diagram related to the Cumaean Sibyl.</meta>

# THE UNCOVERED GRAIN

->**Diana¹. Not rashly.**<-

<note>The diagram described below represents a symbolic seal or "grain" of wisdom, likely related to alchemical or mystical purity.</note>

->**Inscribed² for the CUMAEAN³ WITCH.**<-

->Pure, bright⁴, refined⁵, without mud⁶, crystalline, simple⁷:<-
->Which, being untouched, must yet be held by you in the fire,<-

->The spirit always... this... by which... our... is... to be handled.<-

***

1. See above under the second Laconism, at the fourth gloss. <note>original: "Visita suprà Laconismum posteriorem, glossemate quarto."</note>
2. That is: Brief writings on paper, from the noun *inscriptum* [an inscription].
3. Here it is used as a noun; otherwise *sagus, a, um* is properly and in itself an adjective. Therefore, *saga* is a woman skilled in sacred rites, or an old woman who knows much, so called as if "sagacious" <note>original: "sagax"</note>. For it refers back to the noun *priestess* <note>original: "sacerdotissa"</note> or something similar, in exactly the same way as, for example, in the word *money* <note>original: "pecunia"</note> the word *thing* <note>res</note> is understood. Indeed, *pecunia* in itself is a mere adjective derived from the ancient and obsolete *pecu* [cattle], or our *pecus*, because among the Ancients, cattle were the foundation of all wealth. From this resulted the adjectives *pecuarius, pecualis, pecuinus,* and *pecunius*, meaning that which pertains to cattle or flocks. There are almost infinite examples of this kind in the Latin language which are adjectives by nature but are usually used as nouns. Of this type are primarily most names of arts and sciences, such as Grammar, Poetics, Rhetoric, Dialectics, Logic, Physics, etc. Then many names of Regions, Places, Months, dignities, offices, trades, etc., in which certain nouns are always understood.
4. That is: Pure; for the adjective *putus* seems to me to be a contraction of *putatus* [cleared/pruned]; hence "pure putus" means "pure and unmixed," from which a "cleared account" <note>original: "ratio putata"</note> is one that has been made "pure."
5. Properly, it means cooked out by fire, purged, etc. For the origin of the word, consult a Greek lexicon or another superior Glossary. <note>The term "obryza" refers to gold refined by fire.</note>
6. That is: Clean, as if "without mud" <note>original: "sine limo"</note>, with the "in" being negative and the "n" changing into "l" for the sake of pleasant sound.
7. Here it has the same value as unmixed, not composite, etc. Otherwise, *simple* <note>original: "simplex"</note> properly and etymologically sounds like "without a fold" <note>original: "sine plica"</note>. Hence when we say *explicit* [it ends] for *definit* [it finishes], as in that saying of mine: *It ends [explicit], but the manual practice will reveal the rest.* The sense is, it is released "from the folds" <note>original: "ex plicis"</note>, because at the end, when we cease handling it, things are generally transparent and clear, having no more folds. Thus we are accustomed to use *implicitly* and *explicitly* for "hiddenly" and "openly," as if placed "inside" or "outside" the folds.

*I had also conceived of painting an image here, but I could not steal the time for myself on this occasion to find and establish it.*

It includes a symbolic inscription dedicated to the Cumaean Sibyl regarding purity and fire.</summary>

# THE CHEMICAL WINNOWING FAN

<image-desc>A circular diagram containing text. Around the top of the circle are the words "it recedes. Always from the end". Inside the circle, the title "Aphorisms of the DELPHIC PROPHETESS" is followed by a poetic couplet. At the bottom of the circle, text is written upside down and along the curve: "Purely thought, spontaneously into the pure."</image-desc>

## Aphorisms
### OF THE DELPHIC PROPHETESS.

> From your rougher, dissolved Black-Earth¹, there flourishes²
> A certain white-appearing³, divided⁴, egg-like⁵, consubstantial⁶ Nymph⁷,

->Purely thought,<-
->spontaneously into the pure<-

---

**1.** That is, Black Earth, because *Pnigitis* <note>original: "Pnigite"</note> is interpreted as the *black putrefaction of the earth*. <note>Pnigitis was a type of medicinal earth or clay mentioned by Pliny, here used to represent the 'nigredo' or black stage of alchemy.</note>
**2.** That is, it buds, sprouts, is born, arises, etc. The word is derived from the adjective *vernus* (vernal), by likeness to *Spring*, because in the springtime things are accustomed to shine, to form spikes (that is, to make little points), and to bud; it is said to come from *viror* (greenness), because then the brushwood begins to *turn green*: or even from *vertendo* (turning), because at that time the season of the year begins to *turn* itself, etc.
**3.** That is, appearing naturally white; perhaps contracted from *leucopaeus* or *leucophaeus* <note>original: "leucopa"</note>; consult a Greek lexicon.
**4.** That is, divided, because *erctus* <note>original: "ercta"</note> is a participle from *erciscor*, or *ercisceor*, which was interpreted in ancient times as "to divide," specifically the land; from which there still remains the phrase *erctum non erciscendus* (an inheritance not to be divided), for "divided" and "to be divided."
**5.** That is, of a single yoke and transformed, from the likeness of an egg <note>Latin: "ovum"</note>, whence *ovatus* and *ovaticus* <note>original: "ovatica"</note>; an epithet of Mercury, and specifically of the Philosophers, who is indeed homogeneous and *egg-like* throughout, in which stands the principle of indestructibility.
**6.** In English, "consubstantial," or that which is of the same and similar substance; from the Greek *ousia* (substance) and *homos* (one, similar, or equal). <note>original: "homusia"</note>
**7.** That is, a Goddess like water, because the water itself is called a *Nymph*, as if the Spirit of the water <note>Latin: "Numen lymphae"</note>; whence a bride at a wedding is commonly called a Nymph, so named from the duty of washing, which also alludes to the name of the one *marrying* <note>Latin: "nubentis"</note>; for *Nympha* comes from the Greek for *new* and *to appear*, because she appears *new*.

*Similarly, a part of this small page awaits an image, placing the matter before the eyes, but it has not been depicted.*

# THE UPROOTED GRAIN.

<note>original: "GRANUM ERUTUM"</note>

<image-desc>A circular diagram containing text. The text is arranged in a ring, with some words oriented upside down or sideways to follow the curve of the circle. Inside the circle, there is a central inscription and a couplet of verse.</image-desc>

->Diana¹. Not to be handled rashly<-

### Inscriptions²
### OF THE CUMAEAN PROPHETESS³.
<note>The Cumaean Sibyl was a priestess of Apollo in Greek mythology, famous for her prophetic books.</note>

> Pure, bright⁴, refined⁵, without mud⁶, Crystalline, simple⁷:
> Which, however, being untouched, must be held by you thus in the fire,

->The spirit, how far is this ours?<-
<note>The words in the bottom half of the circle "how far is this ours" are printed upside down in the original.</note>

---

**1.** See above in the *Latter Laconism*, at the fourth gloss. **2.** That is, brief writings on paper, from the noun *inscriptum* [an inscription]. **3.** Here it is taken as a noun; otherwise *sagus, a, um* [prophetic/wise] is properly and in itself an adjective. Therefore, a *saga* <note>original: "saga, æ, f, g"</note> is a woman skilled in sacred rites, or an old woman who knows much, so called as if *sagacious* <note>original: "sagax"</note>. For it refers back to the noun "priestess" or something similar, in exactly the same way as, for example, in the word *pecunia* [money], the word *res* [thing/matter] or something similar is understood. Indeed, *pecunia* in itself is a mere adjective derived from the ancient and obsolete *pecu* [cattle], or our *pecus*, because among the Ancients, cattle were the foundation of all wealth. From this resulted these adjectives: *pecuarius, pecualis, pecuinus,* and *pecunius, a, um*, for that which pertains to cattle or a flock, etc. There are almost infinite examples of this kind in the Latin language which, according to their form, are mere adjectives but are nevertheless mostly used as nouns. Of this kind are, first of all, most names of arts and sciences, such as Grammar, Poetics, Rhetoric, Dialectics, Logic, Physics, etc. Then many names of Regions, Places, Months, dignities, offices, trades, etc., in which certain nouns of their own are always understood. **4.** That is, pure; for the adjective *putus, a, um* [bright/pure] seems to me to be contracted from *putatus* [cleansed/pruned]; hence *purus putus* means *pure and unmixed*, from which a "settled account" <note>original: "ratio putata"</note> is one that has been made "pure" or clear. **5.** Properly, it means cooked out by fire, purged, etc. For the etymology, look in a Greek lexicon or another more excellent Glossary. <note>original: "obryza" - refers to gold tested by fire.</note> **6.** That is, clean, as if *sine limo* [without mud], with the "in-" being a negative and the "n" changing into "l" for the sake of pleasant sound. **7.** Here it has the same value as unmixed, not composite, etc. Otherwise, *simplex* [simple] properly, in itself and etymologically, sounds like *sine plica* [without a fold]. Hence when we say *explicit* [it ends] for "it is finished," as in that verse of mine: *It is unfolded, but the manual practice will reveal the rest.* The sense is, it is released *from the folds* <note>original: "ex plicis"</note>, because at the end, when we cease handling it, things are generally transparent and clear, having no more folds. Thus we are accustomed to use *implicitly and explicitly* for "hiddenly and openly," as if placed *inside or outside the folds*.

# THE CHEMICAL WINNOWING

<image-desc>An oval diagram containing text. Around the outer perimeter of the oval, words are arranged in a circular fashion: "Every", "thing", "is", "perfect", "at", "a fixed¹", "time". Inside the oval, there is a title and a two-line verse.</image-desc>

->### The Autograph of the<-
->## SAMIAN SIBYL.<-

> Until the Spirit stands forth⁴ entirely separated³ from the water²:
> The sign of which will be, if something not previously discovered⁵,

->In a small space<-

---

1. Here used for "fixed," "determined," etc. Otherwise, *certain* properly means clear, open, and undoubted, derived from *cerno* [I discern] for "I see," because those things which we *discern* are clear, undoubted, and evident. <note>original: "certo"</note>
2. This is taken and understood here philosophically, namely for the vital humidity, the innermost part of nature, the best part, the kernel, etc., and not without skill; for the word *aqua* [water] seems to be fused and composed from *a* and *qua*, as if "from which" we live. <note>original: "aquâ"</note>
3. That is, separated, set apart, etc. because *sejugis* or *sejugus* is an adjective contracted from *sejugatus*, that is, "unjoined from the yoke," which comes from *jungo* [I join], that is, "I drive into one." <note>original: "sejugus"</note>
4. Here it has the same value as "be," because *asto* [I stand by] is correctly used from time to time for *sum* [I am]. <note>original: "astet"</note>
5. Outside of the verse, however, and in your own work, you will more correctly read "beheld" rather than "discovered." <note>original: "repertum"</note>

# THE UPROOTED GRAIN
<note>original: "Granum Erutum"</note>

->**The Omens**<-
->OF THE PROPONTIC PROPHETESS.<-
<note>The "Propontic Prophetess" likely refers to a sibyl or symbolic figure from the Sea of Marmara region, used here to cloak alchemical secrets in prophecy.</note>

> Within a small mass¹, let it curdle itself in the heat;
> Its own lukewarm² fluid, eleven times over in turn,

<note>The oval diagram contains the following inscription around its border:</note>
Is the internal worker of a thousand things? This is the Salt of our sea, which swims in our level surface: Is he not the craftsman of the Earth?

->Soon let it be added<-

***

1. *In a small mass*, here signifies in a tiny quantity; otherwise, etymologically, a *mass* <note>original: "moles"</note> is a thing of great size and immense weight, having derived its name from *moving* <note>original: "movendo"</note>, because it can only be moved with great effort.
2. Here it stands for "somewhat cool," though otherwise properly speaking, that is called *lukewarm* <note>original: "extepidum"</note> which has *lost its warmth*, that is, it is no longer warm, meaning it is cold or hot; therefore, *lukewarm* and fluid air is equivalent to these sayings of the Philosophers: The Virgin's Milk <term>Lac virginis: a symbolic term for a white chemical precipitate or a specific mercurial solvent</term>, the slightly cool and liquid spirit, etc.

## OF THE PHRYGIAN SIBYL.

Here it is used as an adjective and metaphorically, so that it means nearly the same as "emulating art" or "follower," etc. For *simius, -a, -um* is an adjective derived from the noun *simius* or *simia* [ape], for that which belongs to apes, or pertains to the apes themselves—so called because they continually make something "similar," as if they were *mimes*, that is, imitators; or perhaps because they are "snub-nosed" <note>original: "simae"</note>, that is, with flattened nostrils.

# THE UPROOTED GRAIN
<note>original: "GRANUM ERUTUM"</note>

->The power of water conquers,<-
->perishable things flow together: But things of oak <note>meaning strong or enduring</note> are eternal; if the fire shall have conquered.<-

### Archetypes
## OF THE TIBURTINE PSALTRIST <note>The Tiburtine Sibyl, a legendary prophetess of the ancient world</note>.

->But because you seek to escape as the immortal Teal <note>original: "Boscha," a type of waterbird; here used as a metaphor for the volatile spirit</note>,<-
->Make sure your Central Salt <term>Sal Centrale: the essential, hidden core of matter in alchemical theory</term> always remains as a gift;<-

->The Elixir of the Whole<-

---

<margin>1. *The power of water*, here is the same as the *volatile* sum; the *dissolving* substance or nature, etc.</margin>
<margin>2. *Or they flow out*: for both are composed from the word "become," signifying nearly the same as the simple "I become."</margin>
<margin>3. *That is, Robust*, strong, constant, etc. For *quernus* (of oak) is an adjective from *quercus* (oak tree), which is used figuratively for a thing that is hard, strong, and unbroken.</margin>
<margin>4. In the present text, this is the *fixed* sum; the *coagulating* substance or nature, etc.</margin>
<margin>5. Otherwise and commonly called *Tiburtina*, because *Tiburs* refers to one who originates from *Tibur* <note>modern Tivoli</note>, which is a town in Italy, not far from the City of Rome.</margin>
<margin>6. *That is, your Hermetic* bird; for *Boscha* or *Boschis* is a bird that is fed while enclosed: therefore, it is placed here by way of likeness, sharply and astutely, for this glorious offspring of the Philosophers and of nature.</margin>
<margin>7. *That is, Full* of duty or gift, because *munis* is, as it were, dutiful, or one who gladly performs *duties*; hence the compounds *common* and *immune* (one who performs no duty).</margin>
<margin>8. Here it means, *let it overcome, let it conquer*, etc.</margin>

*Furthermore, I had dedicated a part of this page to an image, but I was not able to attach or paint it at this time.*

It includes detailed philological notes explaining the Latin word choices and their symbolic meanings in the Great Work.</summary>
