# THE CHEMICAL WINNOWING-FAN

->Divinations<-
### OF THE ERYTHRAEAN SIBYL.
<note>The Erythraean Sibyl was a priestess presiding over the Apollonian oracle at Erythrae; in alchemy, Sibylline verses were often reinterpreted as veiled instructions for the Great Work.</note>

->Thus shall the true Elixir⁵ of the whole Art go forth,⁶<-
->Which your Virgin,⁹ having labored,⁸ has brought forth for you, Vopiscus,¹⁰ and you shall rejoice.⁷<-

<note>The following text is arranged in a circle around the central poem, starting from the top and moving clockwise:</note>
->Which nature¹ has<-
->separated;³ for those<-
->power [and] art<-
->have substituted⁶ good things<-
->by their own gift.⁴<-

---

1. That is, the power of God, and the renewer of things; or that divine reason and artistic faculty by which all things were procreated: *for it is called "nature" [natura] from the fact that it causes something to be born [nasci].*
2. Here used for *separated* <note>original: "separavit"</note>; otherwise *sequestro* properly means to deposit something with a *sequestrum* (a mediator or trustee); so called because both parties *follow* [sequatur] the faith of the one who was chosen. 3. *Has joined, connected, or composed* etc. For the word *join* [jungo] is used as if to *drive into one* [in unum ago].
4. Here used for duty, matter, roles, etc. Otherwise, it is commonly accepted as a gift or merit. It is so named because *those who are of a mutual mind give it for the sake of duty.* 5. i.e., The Tincture of the Philosophers, the Fifth Essence (Quintessence), the Magisterium, the Mystery, etc. Indeed, *Elixir* is called an Arabic word, by which they commonly denote a spirit rightly extracted and preserved from gold, or a herb, or wine; perhaps from the word *elixo* (to boil), which is interpreted as "I cook with water"; whence the participle *elixatus*, and more commonly the contracted form *elixus* (boiled). *Elixir* is therefore said as if it were *elixum*, that is, thoroughly cooked in water; for the Ancients called water *lixa*, from which those who follow the army for the sake of base profit (such as washing or cooking) are called *lixae*; from ash, which was called *lix* by the Ancients, from which finally comes *lixivia* (lye), that is, water in which the ash [*lix*] has been boiled for the sake of washing, etc. 6. An archaic form used here by the necessity of the meter for *exibit* (it shall go out). 7. i.e., And you shall be delighted; for *to rejoice* [gaudere] is properly to be glad inwardly, silently, and within oneself, and does not look to another: because we are said to "rejoice" when the mind is cheered by some thing, yet no outward sign of it appears; on the contrary, one is said to "be joyful" [laetari] when the mind is so moved that signs of joy are produced in the face and gestures, etc. 8. i.e., She gave birth, for women are properly said to be *enixae* (having labored) when they are relieved of the pain of childbirth, as if they were conquerors; simply, it means *to strive under a burden*; metaphorically, to perfect something with much effort and labor, etc. 9. i.e., Your matter, mother, etc. See above the monuments of the Mother of God, in the *ninth* gloss. 10. i.e., The Crocodile or Basilisk of the Wise, etc. For a *Vopiscus* is one whom the mother *obtains* [apiscitur] by force, that is, acquires with difficulty; or one who is preserved by the help of nature, to whom he also brings help; absolutely, therefore, that which comes to its perfect birth or origin—namely the *disk*—shall be called a *vopiscus*. <note>Vopiscus is a rare Latin term for a twin who survives while the other is miscarried; here it refers to the successful extraction of the alchemical "child" or Stone from the raw matter.</note>

*The remaining part of this page was intended for an image or figure, which haste did not allow to be added.*

# THE UPROOTED GRAIN.

## The Transparent Mirror of Minerva¹,
<note>1. Minerva is the Roman goddess of wisdom; her mirror represents a clear reflection of hidden truths.</note>
->in which<-
->the gem and the lineage of the Philosophers<-

### *Never before has this new Egg been more clearly known.*

->THE CAVERN<-
->OF THE MIRROR OF MINERVA.<-

Through the ancient chaos, the things of the World are always the same: they are, they were, and they will be: for there is nothing new under the sun.
<note>This text surrounds the circular diagram, emphasizing the eternal cycle of matter.</note>

The line⁵ of common nature is woolly⁶ and slow;
It is unique, simple⁷, and almost everywhere a Sorceress⁸.
It receives a cheap⁹ and crude thing, and thus perfects everything,
Namely from a scrap of brass¹⁰, whatever you see in the World.
The motion is of one mode, it is a globe, and a spherical mass¹¹,
From whose vein¹² everything comes under the axis¹³ and the fold¹⁴:
The Artist therefore, like a second Ape of Nature¹⁵,
*Thus also, that which lies continually before one's feet,*
Ought to take for himself that well-known ancient thing;
That sun, which has always set, still sets upon the earth.

# THE CHEMICAL WINNOWING FAN

1. *That is,* the Wisdom of the Ancients; for the Ancients used Minerva—the Goddess of disciplines—mystically to represent wisdom, as if she were the "nerve of the Muses" <note>The author is playing on the Latin *Minerva* and *Musarum nervus*</note>. But to others, she seems so named from "admonishing" (*monendo*), because she advises rightly and well; to others, however, from "diminishing" (*minuendo*), perhaps because she diminishes the nerves—namely of the intellect and the brain; to others still from "threatening" (*minando*), as if threatening force: for she is usually depicted protected by military arms, and formidable with her aegis, shield, and spear.
2. *That is,* exceedingly bright, as if bright through the whole at once.
3. Here it is taken copulatively for *and, also, and furthermore, etc.*
4. By ancient Chaos, that is, the beginning of all things, as if "before time" (*ante aevum*); for it was born before all Gods and Goddesses, so named from the Greek *cheo* <note>original: χέω</note>, that is, "I pour," because there was made a confusion and mixing of all elements.
5. Here it is a path, a drawing out, or a course, etc.
6. *That is,* creeping, not hurried, etc. For it is an adjective derived from "wool" (*lana*), most perfectly suited to Nature, which always proceeds with woolly and slow steps <note>The author refers to the phrase *laneis pedibus*, suggesting a silent, slow, or cushioned approach</note>.
7. The same as *simple*, of which you can read a more copious explanation in the *Beginnings of the Cumaean Sibyl*, in the seventh or last gloss.
8. Here it has the same value as if I had said: It mostly acts or works in a manner unknown to us. For a Magician (*Magus*), named as if a "sage" (*sagus*)—a Persian word by which a wise man is signified among them—is both a noun and an adjective, just like the word for a beech tree (*fagus*); it comes from Magic, which is the perfected summit of natural philosophy, or the most absolute science of all natural things, as if it were "greatest-wisdom" <note>original: *maximosophia*</note>.
9. See below, the Egg of the Phoenix or of Helen, in the tenth gloss.
10. *That is,* from a raw and imperfect thing; for *Raudus*, *Rudus*, or *Rodus* is a noun signifying a raw and unrefined thing <note>Often used in alchemy to refer to crude ore or base matter</note>.
11. Here it is taken properly, namely for a thing that is grand and of immense weight, unlike above in the *Auspices of the Propontic Prophetess*, in the first gloss.
12. Here for "they grow," "they come forth," etc.
13. Here for the whole sky, the entire sublunary globe, etc. Otherwise, "axis" properly signifies that smooth wood upon which the wheel of a chariot turns, so named from "acting" (*agendo*), because the wheel is acted upon—that is, moved—around it.
14. Here for the innermost retreat of nature, the veil, the womb, etc.
15. If you desire to know the analogy of the word *Ape* (*Simius*), look back above at the *Arguments of the Phrygian Sibyl*, in the first gloss.

# THE CHYMICÆ VANNI
## [The Chymical Winnowing Fan]

1. That is, of the whole of nature; for **Jupiter**, among the initiates of nature <note>The "mystae" or those initiated into the secrets of alchemy and natural philosophy.</note>, is placed for the elements, or the entire universe of things. To this refer those sayings: *All things are full of Jove* <note>original: "Jovis omnia plena"</note>, *Almighty Jupiter*, Progenitor of Kings, of things, and of Gods, and Mother of the Gods, one God and all, etc. This is because there is no thing which so aids and fosters all things as native heat. Therefore, just as the Ancients named **Jupiter** from "aiding" <note>original: "juvando"; a common but folk etymology linking Jupiter to the verb juvare</note>, so on the contrary they called that God **Vejovis**, that is, an *evil Jupiter*, to whom the faculty of *aiding* had been taken away. For Antiquity celebrated certain Gods so that they might be profitable, and appeased others so that they might not be harmful, etc. Furthermore, he is called **Jupiter**, as if "father of Jove" <note>original: "Jovis pater"</note>, from which the name is composed and fused; because of which, speaking rigorously, he ought not to have—by a less than sound custom—the genitive *Jovis* (since this genitive is from the nominative *Fovis*), but *Jupitris* or *Jupiteris*. He was first, as I related, called *Jovis* from "aiding," but afterwards, with the other word added, he was baptized *Jupiter*.

2. That is, the riches and festivities of the Goddess **Ops**, who was the wife and sister of Saturn, by whom the earth is denoted. Most acutely indeed is she so named from the ancient adjective *opis*, which our ancestors used for "rich," just as we still call a poor and needy person *inops* <note>literally "without ops/wealth"</note>. For the Ancients, whose chief wealth consisted in cattle and agriculture, raised the Earth—the giver of such *wealth*—to divine honors in a certain way, and named her **Ops** herself, that is, the *opulent* one. She is also called by those same Ancients, not at all unskillfully, the *Great Mother* and the *Nurturing Mother*, because she nourishes all things; likewise the *Mother of the Gods*, as if all the Heavenly Dwellers had first been brought forth on earth and afterwards, on account of some signal merit, were carried across into heaven. Nor perhaps will he wander too far who assigns even this to a singular mystery, etc. In the plural, it signifies power, strength, faculties, abundance of mammon, etc. Because almost all riches are sought from the earth; they lie hidden and are generated in and from the earth, hence those sayings: *Wealth is dug out, Wealth is covered over, Wealth is engendered*, etc. She is also thought to be named from this: that by her *aid* <note>original: "ope"</note> the life of men is sustained, or because she is every *work* <note>original: "opus"</note> needed for living. Or, just as *humus* [ground] obtained its name from *humidity*, so also **Ops**, in Greek *ὀπὸς* [opos], that is, juice, moisture, ointment, or milk, which the earth milks and indulges us with from her most fertile udder, etc.

3. That is, of **Nature**, than which nothing is more ingenious, nothing wiser, nothing more sagacious, etc. See above, the *Prophecies of the Erythraean Sibyl*, in the first gloss.

4. Look into the latter **Lanismus** <note>A technical term likely referring to a specific alchemical process or vessel mentioned earlier in the text.</note>, above in the fourth gloss.

5. That is, in a moment, an instant, etc.

6. That is, according to the reckoning of time.

7. Traverse the **Egg** of the crocodile, below in the tenth gloss.

8. That is, *joined to only one*; it is said, however, *unijugus, -a, -um* and *unijugis, -e*, as if having, holding, or carrying *one yoke* [jugum] by pulling.

9. This is linear, etc. You have the etymology of this above, in the *Inscriptions of the Cumaean Sibyl*, in the last gloss.

10. That is, decently, rightly, well, etc. Derived from *rite* [ritual], because those things which are done according to ritual are right and settled.

11. That is, of its operation.

12. Here it stands for "separates," as also in the *Prophecies of the Erythraean Sibyl*, second gloss.

13. That is, everything, whatsoever, etc. Because it is a universal sign.

14. Here it is "to be corrupted," "to be destroyed," etc. Otherwise, *perdo* is properly "I lose."

15. Here used metaphorically for "to be completed," "to be perfected," "to be finished," etc. Otherwise, *patro, -as* properly means to work for children, as if doing the "work of a father" <note>original: "patris opus ago"</note>.

16. Here it is similarly taken figuratively, namely for "born," "generated," etc.

17. Here for "to be guarded," "to be preserved," "to be put away," etc.

18. That is, he will bring forth into the midst, as if "bringing out" [promet].

19. That is, by searching out, discussing, etc. Because to "wander through" <note>original: "peragrare"</note> is elegantly and metaleptically the same as to track, to investigate, etc. As if for the sake of inquiring, to go around the field, etc.

# THE CHEMICAL SIEVE

1. This title, concerning the *Egg of Helen*, was given place and occasion from that mystical and very ancient invention of the Ancients, in which they recounted that Helen, the most beautiful of girls, was the daughter of Nemesis and Jupiter. For it is remembered that Nemesis, when she fled the embrace of Jupiter, was changed into a goose; but Jupiter, turned into a swan, came upon her—that is, entered into her. Nemesis, truly, from that union, brought forth an *egg*, and a certain shepherd found it in a grove and gave it to Leda. She then stored it away, hidden in a chest, and finally, in its own time, Helen was born from it, whom Leda raised just as if she had been born of herself, etc. <note>The "Egg of Helen" is a common alchemical metaphor for the "philosopher's egg" or the vessel containing the prime matter.</note>

2. Here used for true, sincere, not disguised, etc. Elsewhere the word *genuine* <note>original: "germanus"</note> is properly used for that which has *germinated*, that is, what is produced from the same stock.

3. I know the <term>Adept of the Art</term> <note>A master alchemist who has successfully created the Philosopher's Stone.</note> will marvel greatly when he considers and perceives how acutely the word *foul* <note>original: "tetra"</note> fits here; it is taken materially, and at the same time it so cleverly alludes to the name of our matter, which is truly called, as it were, *foul*. <note>Likely a wordplay on "Tetra" and "Tetragona" or "Terra" (Earth).</note>

4. i.e., The exterior form, appearance, figure, etc. Because the surface of any thing is absolutely called the "face" <note>original: "facies"</note>, as if from "making" <note>original: "faciendo"</note>: for just as "species" comes from looking, and "figure" from shaping, so also from making, or from the *making* of a body, it is called the face, etc.

5. A periphrasis for "everywhere." For as we say, *to mix the sea or seas with the sky*, or *to confound them*, meaning to disturb everything and leave nothing undone; so also, *to seek by sea and land* means everywhere, and in no place not searched.

6. i.e., Twisted, intricate, false, sophisticated, etc. Because the <term>crocodile</term> is said by analogy to be a sophisticated question <note>A "crocodilite" was a famous logical paradox in antiquity.</note>, but properly it is a four-footed animal of the amphibious genus, living as much in water as on land, as if of a *double life*, because it dwells in both said elements, and desires not only terrestrial things but aquatic ones as well. In figure it is held to be not very unlike a lizard, but of almost incredible size, armed with claws, known only to Egypt and those regions washed by the Nile. Its skin is so hardened that it can be disturbed in no part of itself except for the belly alone. It was not for nothing, therefore, nor beside the point, that we drew it into a likeness with the Philosophical Python; for there is no animal that grows from such tiny beginnings into such great magnitude, since its eggs are no larger than those of a goose. But this is believed to be peculiar to it: that as long as it lives, it makes no end of growing. For four winter months it does not eat, and it is the only one among the rest of the beasts that lacks a tongue. Furthermore, this beast is terrible against those who flee, but conversely flees from those who pursue; it has dull eyes in the water, but very sharp sight outside of it. When it sees a man, it sheds tears, but soon devours him as he approaches; hence it has passed into a proverb, *Crocodile tears*, which is usually said of those who, under a veil of piety, deceive others. It seems to me, moreover, to be named by antiphrasis <note>A figure of speech where a word is used in a sense opposite to its literal meaning.</note>, as if it were *diligent for saffron* <note>original: "croci diligens"</note>, that is, *avoiding saffron* <note>original: "crocum vitans"</note>; since it flees saffron, the crocodile loves saffron not at all and even loathes its scent. Hence, those making honey in Egypt are accustomed to spread *saffron* beforehand, lest the crocodiles steal the honey, for they are wonderfully delighted by it in that manner.

7. i.e., With various and sublime ideas, fantasies, and hidden things; concerning the theme, consult the Greek lexicon.

8. Here it means that which is near, or with, next to, close by, etc. As in that phrase, *it flies near the ground*, it is placed for "eggs in the hedges," etc.

9. i.e., In the last or lowest place, as if on the *ground* <note>original: "topo"</note>, because *torus* is more frequently a place, such as a site, soil, mansion, habitation, etc.

10. i.e., One's own; derived from "near" <note>original: "prope"</note>, perhaps because that which is *proper* <note>one's own property</note> is most *near* to us.

11. Here used for most despised, most contemptible, etc. Otherwise, the word *stooping* <note>original: "cernuus"</note> properly means inclined, as if *looking downward*.

12. i.e., Greatly; from the particle *re-* increasing the meaning, and not denoting repetition, contrary to what is usually done in verbs. In nouns, especially adjectives, it is almost always an intensive particle, such as *recanus* (very gray), *recavus* (very hollow), etc. In the same way, therefore, *revilis* means very vile, or rather, doubly vile; derived from *villa* (country house), because all things in the villas are usually cheaper <note>original: "viliora"</note> than in the cities.

13. i.e., He pants, he ardently desires, as if he *doubly desires*, etc.

-># THE CHEMICAL WINNOWING-FAN<-

1. Here this means to begin, to commence, to undertake, etc. Because *to take auspices* <note>original: "auspico" or "auspicor"</note>, or rather *to seek an omen*, properly means to take signs from heaven, to predict the future from the song and behavior of birds, or to consult birds regarding the outcome of an affair. However, since the Ancients did nothing except by *taking auspices*, it has passed into common usage that we use the word absolutely to mean to begin or to set about some business.

2. Here this means nearly finishing, completing, etc. For *to incline* <note>original: "inclinare"</note> properly means to bend, but figuratively we say "to incline a matter" for that which is nearly finished or forged into shape.

3. That is, from the clean, bright, and snow-white waters; a part being put for the whole. Perhaps, moreover, the *wave* <note>original: "unda"</note> is so named as if it were *one* <note>original: "una"</note>, because it is surely gathered into itself and is as if one.

4. That is, a beautiful beast, a wild animal, etc. For *beast* <note>original: "belua" or "bellua"</note> is so named by way of antiphrasis <note>A figure of speech where a word is used in a sense opposite to its literal meaning.</note> from the adjective *beautiful* <note>original: "bello"</note>, that is, good, fair, etc. Or rather (as others prefer) from the noun *war* <note>original: "bellum"</note>, because it is the nature of beasts to wage *war* upon one another, for which purpose nature seems to have fashioned their weapons.

5. Here used adverbially for especially, first of all, primarily, before all things, etc.

6. That is, choose or devise for yourself some secret place; because a *recess* <note>original: "recessus"</note> in the present context is the same as a *seclusion* <note>original: "secessus"</note>, that is, a more secret place, empty of crowds and tumult, as if alone and separated from others. For *to secrete* <note>original: "secerno"</note> properly means to divide, separate, or discern. By likeness to this, hidden thoughts which can only be tracked down with difficulty are fittingly called the *recesses* of the mind.

7. That is, in which, where, etc.

8. Here this is almost the same as the *womb* <note>original: "matrix"</note>; for absolutely everything that preserves something in some way—whether in metals, animals, or vegetables—is called a *matrix*, as if it were the "preserver of matter" <note>original: "materiæ conservatrix"</note>. Furthermore, *nest* <note>original: "nidus"</note> is of well-known meaning, perhaps named from *stench* <note>original: "nidor"</note>, because the dwellings or chambers of birds are accustomed to be of a bad stench, that is, odor.

9. Here placed for continually, always, etc.

10. That is, not at all hard, tender, yielding to the touch, etc. As if *mobile*, because it can be easily drawn and moved in any direction.

11. That is, she who brings aid to one giving birth; for *obstetric* <note>original: "obstetricius"</note> is an adjective from *midwife* <note>original: "obstetrix"</note>, that is, one having care of those in labor. So named from *standing before* <note>original: "obstando" / "obsistat"</note> because she stands against the pain, or certainly against the fetus, lest, when the genital barriers of the womb are loosened, it should fall to the ground.

12. In this place it means parts, duties, etc. Revisit the *Prophecies of the Erythraean Sibyl* <note>A priestess of classical antiquity presiding over an Apollonian oracle; often cited in alchemical texts as a source of hidden wisdom.</note> in the fourth gloss above.

# THE CHYMIC WINNOWING-FAN

1. That is: *Of completing, finishing, perfecting*, etc. <note>original: "Consummandi, conficiendi, perficiendi"</note>
2. This is: *natural*, not *counterfeit*, etc.
3. Here it is used conjunctively for *and, also*, etc.
4. That is: Not *foul*, but delightful and harmless, as if of a *savor*—that is, entirely devoid of sharpness or acidity. *Menstruum* <term>Menstruum: In alchemy, a solvent used to dissolve solids, often compared to a nourishing fluid</term>, *nourishment*, etc. Named from *fostering* <note>original: "fovendo"</note>, that is, by warming or nourishing.
5. *Drop by drop*.
7. That is: Its former fleeting nature is changed, or the former disposition of its *Ostrich-like* <note>original: "Struthia"</note> beak *is turned*; so called, as I have explained elsewhere, from *Spring* <note>original: "vere"</note>, because the turning of the year begins then, etc. Because the *Ostrich* <note>original: "Struthius, vel Struthio"</note> is a wild, fierce, and predatory bird, the adjective *Struthian* is used for that which belongs to the Ostrich—namely, something fierce or tiger-like. For there are many such words in Latin usage which are both adjectives and substantives: *master, companion, servant, craftsman*, etc.
8. That is: A tamed bird, which is fed while enclosed like a *tame ox* or an *enclosed* one: see above in the Archetypes of the Tiburtine Psaltery, gloss 9.
9. This little verse fits very aptly here: *a skin* <note>original: "pellis"</note> *is so called from "driving away"* <note>original: "pellendo"</note>, *because by covering our injuries it drives them away*.
10. That is: Having or reflecting the colors of the *rainbow* <note>original: "iridis"</note>.
11. That is: It restores *substance and luster*; hence the noun *nidor* <term>Nidor: Usually meaning a strong smell or steam, here used to imply a potent, shining vapor</term>, derived from an intense odor.
12. That is: It fits, it suits, etc. For a garment or other clothing is said to "sit" skillfully and elegantly when it is fit and very well-suited.
13. This is a verbal noun from the supine *tinctum* [dyed], or from the noun *tinctus* [a dyeing], signifying in a passive sense that which is *dyed* or colored, or which can be dyed and colored, such as *dyeable wool*. But in our context, it is used rather in an active sense, whence *dyeing venom* <note>original: "tinctile virus"</note> here means a seed, or a medicine, or a "poison" possessing the natural power or virtue of dyeing; for *virus* [venom/potency] is used in both a good and a bad sense.
14. That is: Endowed with much vigor, again *living*, etc.
15. That is: A pure and beautiful color.
16. That is: It glitters, it shines forth, etc. Because *mico* [to flash] properly means to shine and sparkle at intervals, as *crumbs* <note>original: "micæ"</note> do—that is, as I have noted elsewhere, those little dust-motes in the sand that shine like gold or silver, from which the verb *mico* is derived.
17. Here it means it shines *greatly* and all around; otherwise the word *polluceo* [to shine brightly] properly pertains to sacred rites, meaning to dedicate or to vow; or rather to place offerings to Hercules upon the altar.
18. That is: With a most ruddy, healing color; for the word *venom* <note>original: "venenum"</note> is a neutral term that can be taken in both a good and a bad sense, just like *medicine* <note>original: "pharmacum"</note> and *potency* <note>original: "virus"</note>. These three are general terms for all things that have the power to change the nature of that to which they are applied; therefore, we can rightly call healing medicines *venoms, potencies*, etc.
19. That is: Ductile, easy, flexible, soft, manageable, etc.
20. That is: Reddish-yellow, glowing, etc. For *Gold* <note>original: "Aurum"</note> is said to be named from *aura* [a breeze/radiance], that is, from its glow or yellowness, etc.
21. That is: A bird born in secret, a *winged one*, etc. For a *bird* <note>original: "avis"</note> is so called from *pathless places* <note>original: "aviis"</note>, that is, the more secret places in which birds especially delight, etc.

# THE EXTRACTED GRAIN

->§. I.<-

O what a work, oh what a work! I have performed one single work, and you all marvel at it. O Nemesis, o Helen, o Jupiter! <note>The author invokes Greek deities and figures to express the magnitude and beauty of the alchemical achievement.</note> How stupendous, how hidden a mystery! O Phoenix, o Crocodile, o Nile! <note>These Egyptian symbols often represent rebirth (Phoenix), the raw matter (Crocodile), and the source of life or the "mercurial water" (Nile) in alchemical literature.</note> Do you now understand this profound secret? O bird, o egg, o work! O ornament of works, and the offspring of the Wise; <note>original: "Sophorum" — referring to the true philosophers or alchemists.</note> O marvelous work of works! These are the wonders of God, and the prodigies of the Almighty, the Work of the Highest Artist. Because of this, not only the Adepts of this Art <term>Adepts: those who have successfully achieved the Philosopher's Stone</term>, but even the Naturalists <note>original: "Physiographi"</note>—even those ignorant and inexperienced in these secrets—have taken up the inevitable argument to affirm that there is something of a certain Divinity upon the Earth, which its various effects, seen and experienced daily, testify to with shining evidence.

The Earth, they say, we know to be the only element that is never angry with man, but gratifies him again and again. The Waters turn into rains, swell into waves, and are cast down into torrents. The Air thickens with clouds and rages with storms. But the Earth is kind, indulgent, and always the handmaid for the use of Mortals. What things she generates when compelled! What things she pours forth freely and of her own accord! What scents, flavors, and aromas! What juices, textures, and colors! With what good faith she returns the interest on what has been entrusted to her! What things she nourishes for our sake! The consideration of the piety of the Earth’s most merciful vitals and most noble breast—which is never incensed against man, nor ever becomes irritated, but supports him in a God-like manner—could lead anyone into a state of stupor, so much has it been preached by many.

Waters are turned into impetuous rains, and are transformed into noxious hailstones; they swell and puff up into waves, and rush with force into torrents, and often, when they overflow, they sweep away beasts, men, and entire buildings with them. The Air, dreadfully dark, gathers into thick and black clouds, and threatens everyone with tempests, storms, and destruction.

# THE CHYMICAL SIEVE
<note>original title: "CHYMICÆ VANNI"</note>

Fire devours, ravages, and dissolves everything it consumes into ashes; yet of all the elements, the Earth—great as it is—serves the needs of Mortals! It serves most abundantly, bringing forth whatever pertains to their utility.

What a great force of all things she produces of her own accord, not only for necessity, but even for the highest pleasure of those whom she sustains! How many fragrances for the sense of smell, how many flavors for the palate, how many soft and smooth things for the touch, how many colors for the sight, how many minerals, how many plants, shrubs, and herbs for health does the fertile and lavish Earth <note>original: "Tellus," a poetic name for the personified Earth</note> bring forth!

And although she is trampled by the wicked footsteps of criminal men, or by the heavy and filthy tracks of brute animals—although, I say, her venerable and ancient face is defiled and dishonored in various ways, and even though her entrails are pressed and shaken—she does not become angry for that reason, nor is she filled with indignation. On the contrary, she seems to seize this as an opportunity for returning with interest what was sparingly lent to her; indeed, acting in this manner, she flourishes most politely and liberally. By repaying her debts in such a way, she perfectly deserves the Image <note>original: "Typum"</note> and title of the Deity, and merits being numbered among the Divine Powers. For the Deity also seems to have done the greatest thing possible, and to have reached the highest peak, when He compensated injuries with graces and offenses with favors.

# THE UNEARTHED GRAIN

Does she not bring forth offspring daily, and yet by no means wither within the cloister of her virginity? Is this not, I ask, that most indulgent Great Mother <note>original: "Mater Magna," a reference to Cybele or the primordial Earth goddess</note>, who milks all things for us from her bosom as affluently as possible, yet never rests from her fertility?

This is clearly that true Golden Tree, from which, if the fruits are plucked, new ones immediately grow back in their place. This is the precious pearl of the World; this is that most fertile vine of fruits, never exhausted by the vintage, producing grapes of the purest white and the deepest red. This is that fountain of Bernard <note>likely referring to St. Bernard of Clairvaux or an alchemical authority like Bernard Trevisan</note>; the Platonic Fountain, I say, well-watered, overflowing, and always flowing, in which an inextinguishable lamp burns; the Fountain from whence innumerable and most pleasant rivers of all faculties flow forth.

This is that inexhaustible well which brings forth fortunes and health to mortals. This is the *Pangaeus* <note>a gold-rich mountain in Thrace</note>, that enclosed garden, and a meadow of every kind of fragrance; the storehouse of nature’s gifts, the cabinet of riches, an ocean of delights, and a treasury of wealth. It is the self-moving work of the fingers of God, the very talent of Mother Nature, the perfectly finished vault of the entire universe, and the completion of all wonders; a most translucent Mirror, and a true example of uncorrupted virginity.

This is, to the life, that Phoenix renewing itself and bringing itself back to life,

->*Which was always the only undivided Bird;*<-

This is that amphibious animal, a crocodile of incredible magnitude, which feeds only beside the rivers of the Nile. It is surely the Eagle, which is said to keep its nest in hidden places—an eagle, I say, which transcends far beyond the grasp of fools, and is honored by the wise.

# THE CHEMICAL SIEVE

I might relate what can be said mysteriously; for the deeper I enter into its inner sanctums, the more I continually encounter other even more wonderful analogies. For this reason, for the sake of form, I shall enter the harbor, having first drawn a certain mystical symmetry from that [subject], and having related this brief but otherwise most certain path toward attaining knowledge of it.

->§. 3.<-

Whoever wishes to be a partaker of our profound Wisdom <note>original: "Sapientiæ"</note> ought to seek it in the simplicity and humility of his heart, because our matter <note>The "materia nostra" or First Matter is the raw substance alchemists believed could be transformed into the Philosopher's Stone.</note> is by no means sublime in reputation or appearance, but is cheap, humble, and simple; it is utterly hidden from the "wise" and is manifested only to those like itself.

Almost every error in this Art <note>Alchemy was frequently referred to simply as "The Art."</note> arises from an excessively subtle imagination, while each person devises for himself something new and unusual, when nevertheless nothing is more common, nothing more ancient, than chaos. "Let the Earth be opened and bring forth a Savior" <note>A common alchemical appropriation of Isaiah 45:8, suggesting the "Savior" or Stone comes from the earth itself.</note>; what need is there to want to fish in the air, when we ought to fish in the water?

Not long ago, but only a very few days past, I was on a ship with a certain Doctor—more wealthy than wise—and when a conversation arose (as is prone to happen among the Sons of Art) concerning this matter, he answered me in these very words: *“I certainly know the true subject of the Philosophers well enough, but I have conceived of it so subtly in my own intellect that I cannot explain myself, much less interpret it for others.”* Oh, what witty wordlessness! Therefore, I may say with the best of rights: truly this Art is a pure gift of God.

The living and proven matter itself is handed down eloquently and openly everywhere among almost all true Philosophers, and yet not one in a hundred thousand knows it for certain. This could not be the case unless God were singularly resisting it, since in this present day there are countless learned men endowed with the most piercing sharpness of wit.

For you might call this our "Golden Age" because of the arts thus reborn and the abundance of ingenious men; if the table of Jove <note>Jupiter/Jove; a reference to the "Golden Apple" or the "Judgment of Paris" regarding the most beautiful goddess.</note> were now to be given (just as once it was given to the most beautiful of the three), of all...

I touch upon, name, and designate this matter here—and in many other places besides—most simply (even intentionally), though I am easily the least of all men. Indeed, I believe there will be no lack of those who will say that I either do not understand what I write myself, or that I have dealt with it most obscurely. This arises entirely from their pride, or their supposed and personal shrewdness; they are unwilling to submit or captivate their intellect to the wonders of the Most High, but are always "wise in high things," <note>A reference to Romans 12:16, warning against intellectual arrogance.</note> whom God resists.

->§. 4.<-

For our most august art of Alchemy <term>Alchemy: here used not just as metal-working, but as a spiritual and physical pursuit of divine truths</term> is entirely likened to the Holy Scripture, that sublime school of Christ, which is a most deep river in which the lamb walks—that is, the simple man makes progress—and the Elephant swims—that is, every most learned man fluctuates with his opinions, errors, and doubts. <note>This "Lamb and Elephant" metaphor was a popular medieval and Renaissance trope used to describe the Bible: shallow enough for a lamb to wade, deep enough for an elephant to swim.</note>

I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth; what, I ask, is so beautiful before the sons of men? Because you have hidden this from the wise and revealed it to little ones—that is, to the humble, the simple, the poor, and those who are fools by the world's judgment.

For upon whom else shall the Spirit of God rest—that Spirit of wisdom and understanding, that Spirit of subtlety and counsel—if not upon the humble, the simple, and the lowly of heart? A humbled heart is the dwelling place of the Holy Spirit, so that He may rest in that which He fills. But the heart in which "foxes have holes"—that is, which deceitful cunning possesses—and the heart where "the birds of the air have nests"—which windy elation occupies—is not the seat of the Holy Spirit, but of the malignant spirit, the spirit of this world, which rules over the sons of self-confidence.

God inhabits inaccessible light; He is sublime, immortal, and eternal, whose house is filled with the fragrance of ointment. He resists the proud in heart, but His conversation is with the simple. He is easy for the little ones, the humble, and the dejected, but "high" <note>meaning "out of reach" or "difficult"</note> to the wise, the great, and the inflated.

### Section 5.

Accordingly, whatever true wisdom can be found—whether in this earthly dwelling or in that celestial home of the Blessed Minds—comes from the Lord God. It is clothed in a humble, simple, and dejected habit, so that its heights remain utterly unknown to those who think themselves wise, and it is recognized only by the humble and the lowly. Where there is *humility*, there is *wisdom*, because humility is the indicator and the guardian of wisdom, just as pride is the indicator of folly. For this reason, Socrates—that divine shrine, as it were, of human wisdom—was the only one declared wise by the Oracle of Apollo, because he was so modest within himself that he candidly said, *that he knew nothing*.

Similarly, that most illustrious Morning Star of the Sun of Justice (this was John the Baptist), because he most humbly confessed himself to be a voice, air, and wind, was therefore exalted to such an extent that, by the decree of the Divine mouth itself, none was greater than he among those born of women.

That most Blessed Virgin of all, Mary, because she responded supplicantly from the bottom of her heart that she was a servant and a handmaid, was for that reason alone found worthy to be the one from whom God should be born, and from whose crystalline womb the Messiah should be brought forth.

# To the industrious commentator and the noble
# READER.

<margin>1.</margin> Having weighed with a more equitable balance of reason the deceits and artifices with which the children of this world trade, and by which they are infected and somehow sustain themselves; and with this sentence deeply engraved upon the tablets of my heart: *He who seeks to be enriched shall not be innocent* <note>A reference to Proverbs 28:20, warning against the moral dangers of greed.</note>, my spirit was continually stirred within me to devise a means and a way by which I might live honestly and without guilt, and be of use to my neighbor. Therefore, to explore the knowledge of more recondite <note>hidden or secret</note> mysteries, I hid myself away in the <term>Chemical Art</term> <note>original: "Chymicam Artem"; referring here to Alchemy and the preparation of chemical medicines.</note>, especially when I discovered that through this very science, without offending God, I could most securely serve and assist my own soul and my neighbor.

2. Furthermore, since Almighty God—after I had incurred great expense and endured great labor—heard my prayers and illuminated me through His Spirit of Truth, I have been moved by true Christian charity toward my neighbor. I chose not to hide this light, so mercifully shared with me, under a bench or a table, but to set it upon the table so that it might shine around and serve mankind. For I do not intend to bury the talent granted to me out of envy, but to do the greatest good through it. And since this can be done very fittingly through my <term>Universal Medicine</term> <note>original: "Pharmacum Catholicum"; 'Catholic' here is used in its original Greek sense of 'Universal' or 'all-encompassing'.</note>, I have allowed this little work, committed to the press, to go forth; for the verse says:

> *Your knowledge is nothing, unless another knows that you know it.* <note>A quote from the Roman satirist Persius.</note>

3. In this little work, the well-disposed reader is instructed in the truth, and shall see that I have written not from mere opinion, but from my own experience, all for the sake of wandering Lovers [of the Art], as a comfort to those longing for the Art, and for the benefit of Doctors. In favor of all these, I have determined to keep by me such a Universal <term>True Medicine</term> <note>original: "Orthomedicinam"; from the Greek 'ortho' (right/correct) and Latin 'medicina'.</note> (namely, the true <term>Potable Gold</term> <note>original: "Potabile Aurum"; a legendary alchemical life-elixir made from gold dissolved or rendered into liquid form.</note> which can never be lead back— <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "redu-", likely meaning "reduced to a metal again".</note>

## Preface to the Commentary
### *Concerning the*
# UNIVERSAL MEDICINE
<note>original: "Pharmaco Catholico"; here "Catholic" is used in its original Greek sense of "universal" or "all-encompassing," referring to a panacea.</note>

->*How a true Lover of this arduous Mystery ought to be qualified and intentioned.*<-

1. As many as desire to walk in this light of nature must first be, as much as possible, of a pure and undefiled conscience, and hold a firm and holy intention. They must likewise be patient, and moreover, exceedingly chaste and devoted to sobriety. For in a gluttonous, impure, and wavering heart, the spirit of truth—namely, of God—finds for itself neither rest nor a dwelling place. Therefore, divine grace and the inspiration of the Holy Spirit in the *Chemical science* <note>original: "Chymica scientia"; referring to the sacred art of alchemy</note>, which might benefit the soul and one's neighbor, is by no means to be hoped for. Hence it has passed into a proverb: *Alchemy either finds a man honest or makes him honest.* For the closer one approaches the knowledge of temporal and perishing things, the more immediately he approaches the Creator and the knowledge of Him; and again, the better one knows his own Maker and the Founder of all things, the more intimately he loves that same Creator and strives to conform himself to His will.

<summary>The author asserts his altruistic motives for sharing his medical secrets and outlines the strict moral and spiritual requirements necessary for a student to succeed in the alchemical arts.</summary>
<keywords>Universal Medicine, Alchemy, spiritual purity, medical cures, consumption, ethics in science, Creator</keywords>

--- Page 353 ---
<meta>This page continues the preface to the commentary on Universal Pharmacy, establishing the spiritual and ethical foundations required of the practitioner.</meta>

->PREFACE TO THE COMMENTARY ON UNIVERSAL PHARMACY<-

2. The All-knowing and Almighty God is the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the desired end, the goal of our intention; He who, through the rays of His divine light, must lead and direct us toward that goal. Blessed indeed are those who, with the diligent sharpness of their intellect, seize this light, and through it are illuminated and called away from errors. And even assuming that out of human frailty—*O upright and sincere Son of the Art* <note>A traditional alchemical address to the student or initiate</note>—you should fall from the light into the darkness of sins through the continuous impulses of the infernal dragon, you shall not despair on that account. Instead, as soon as possible, you shall return to the Father like the Prodigal Son of the Gospel, mourning your fault and seeking grace and pardon. For you should know for certain that to sin is human, but to persevere in those sins is diabolical, while it is divine to always spare and forgive. Therefore, doubt nothing; persevere in your purpose, since God is known and accustomed to give even greater things freely to the ungrateful. By this, you will remember that to be of good will is a burnt offering <note>original: "holocaustum," referring to a sacred sacrificial offering</note> far most pleasing and holy to God; for the act finally follows the will, hence that proverb:

->*If strength is lacking, yet the will is to be praised.*<-

3. Not without reason did the Angels of the Lord also sing during the Mystery of the Incarnation of our Savior Jesus Christ: *Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will.* O Lord, just as we forgive and are prepared to dismiss the past and future sins of those who have offended us and are yet to offend us further, so do You also pardon and grant to us; just as we give and pardon, so our ready and good will is compensated a thousandfold.

4. Silence <note>original: "Taciturnitas," the hermetic vow of secrecy regarding alchemical secrets</note> is likewise no small point in our science. For although, by reason of your own person, you might show yourself ungrateful toward your good God on account of this grace you have obtained, and you might violate the Holy, then that happens only from your person alone. You alone are obligated, before the severe judgment of God in that horrible deluge of fire, to excuse and mourn your own committed errors.

<summary>The author exhorts the student of alchemy to maintain a pure will and seek divine forgiveness, emphasizing that spiritual integrity and the vow of silence are essential to the "Art."</summary>

# A Necessary Word,
### WHICH
### The Translator must speak, before he proceeds.

1. A page glanced over in passing usually seems worthless, yet when read ten times, it often shines bright. It is therefore necessary, my excellent reader, if you desire to obtain any fruit here, that you repeat your reading several times and weigh it attentively. For although the matter is treated quite crudely and nakedly, it is nevertheless wrapped in a great pomp of ceremonies; yet not everything therein is ancient nonsense or darkness, but there is also a light among them, which if you are able to see, will undoubtedly be a certain guide for you toward the <term>Art</term> <note>original: "Artem"; likely referring to Alchemy or the Hermetic sciences</note> in the future.

2. You will say, however: "I hate that rattling kind of men, greedy for their own advantage, who wish to seem to have blessed posterity with vast treasures when they either do not know them themselves, or having gathered them from elsewhere, go about proposing them with the mouth of a Sphinx" <note>original: "Sphingico ore"; meaning to speak in riddles or enigmas</note>. Let it be as you say; what does it matter? Are gems any cheaper because they are second-hand? If you can rescue them from their own filth, do not be anxious about the one who entangled them.

3. Therefore, let no desire for nausea or impatience come upon you if you are immediately less able to grasp the things touched upon in this Commentary. Do not perhaps cast the blame on me, believing the translation was not well performed; it has certainly been most carefully weighed, corrected, and is far plainer and more illustrious in its method than the German Original <note>original: "Germanicum Autographum"</note> itself, which was written in a style that was not coherent, but utterly rude, tumultuous, or hurried.

4. And if the care and diligence which I took in transferring this <term>Account</term> <note>original: "Relatione"; a formal report or narrative</note> were fully perceived by you, I do not doubt—though you might pronounce it rashly—that you would consider it more mine now than his under whose name it is sold. For I would have much preferred to compose such a booklet anew than to have unraveled it from such knotty and slippery papers. However, I do not wish that title to be given to me at all, but only to signify this: an Author must see to it that he writes books, not merely copies them; it is permitted to imitate and to borrow something, but not to steal.

# COMMENTARY ON THE UNIVERSAL PHARMACEUTICAL.

### Chapter One.

### *Concerning the universal solvent of all metals and minerals.*

<margin>1.</margin> Here, in this chapter, I shall instruct and inform you, fair and eager Lovers of Art, in the highest truth and with a sincere heart. I shall do so in simple words which are to be understood literally; therefore, pay heed to my words, and repeat your reading until you have attained a fundamental understanding and the true meaning of this little book.

<margin>2.</margin> Furthermore, you should know that two types of solutions are found among the philosophers. *The first is* when matter is reduced by the "first matter" <note>original: "materia prima," the primitive, unformed substance from which all things originate</note> back into its first matter—namely, into its first original principles—as if into a certain "dry water," which is called not only Mercury, but also Sulfur. This dry solution is achieved through *Magical* elements by means of an open fire. *The other* solution is the astral type, achieved through the "seed," which is a dry liquor that flows and melts like wax. In this solution, we generally observe a separation, because the solvent <term>menstruum: a solvent, often used in alchemy to describe a substance that dissolves solids into their essence</term> takes to itself only the most noble soul from the metallic Sulfur already previously obtained, and it does so while leaving behind some dregs.

<margin>3.</margin> And just as this solvent relates to Sulfur, it behaves in the same way toward the magnet of Sulfur, namely Salt; for these have proceeded from its blood and its state. Therefore, this metallic fire works only upon its like, and remains as a solvent inseparably joined with its solute. Truly, how and with what things these two sublime reductions and solutions are accomplished, you shall gather from my following teaching—namely, through the *Magical* elements.

### *Concerning the elements in general.*

# COMMENTARY

just as if from a mother, all things are brought forth and formed into this world. When elemental things <note>Latin: *elementata*, referring to physical objects composed of the four elements</note> are corrupted, those same elements resolve themselves back into their origins. None of these visible elements exists purely on its own, but is mixed to a greater or lesser degree, and they are mutually transmutable into one another. For water is made from earth, and earth again from water; air comes from evaporated water, and through the condensation of air, water returns; fire comes from kindled air, and this fire, through extinction, becomes water. This water, through intense cold, becomes earth, and through heat, it becomes stone or sulfur. All of this is carried out by the conflicting and concordant qualities of the elements. From repugnant qualities, an "antipathy" or struggle arises; however, from concordant qualities, a "sympathy" follows, providing support. This victory—that is, destruction—is the cause of new generation. From this, the truth remains irrefutable from its very root: that everything here below has arisen from the elements, and similarly, one thing is transmutable into another. Every elemental thing is destroyed by its own contrary and concordant qualities, and thus, under another form, is resolved again into its elements. In this context, destruction is nothing other than the abolition of the old form and the elevation of that specific substance into a new form and a better essence.

2. Just as everything beneath the moon <note>The "sublunary" sphere, or the earthly realm subject to change and decay</note> has its origin from the coarse and visible elements, so too do the elements draw their beginnings from their superiors. For just as in the Archetypal World <note>The divine realm of pure ideas or patterns</note> *all things are in all things*, so in this corporeal world *all things are found in all things*, though in different ways according to the nature of the receiver. In this manner, elements exist not only in celestial bodies, but even in the Angels, etc. In the lower world, there are crude forms and material elements; but above, they are of the property and nature of a certain more excellent and heavenly essence, and from there our crude material elements draw their origin. For fire has its principle from the Sun, Mars, and their dwellings; air from Jupiter and Venus; water from Saturn and Mercury; and the Earth now takes its origin from the Moon and from all of these together.

So also, when the Sulfur of the Sun <note>Sulfur here refers to the active, combustible principle within the gold.</note> is abundantly fed and kindled through Sulfur, then the bond is weakened, and the joining spirit—namely the Mercurial water <note>The "mercurial water" is the passive, fluid principle that binds the substance together.</note>—must dry up due to the multitude of fire and migrate into another element which agrees with it in a similar quality. Because of this, it is immediately taken up by its neighboring element and is transmuted into the nature of the receiver.

### Chapter Five.

->*On the nature and property of the first principle, Mercury.*<-

1. The common Mercury of metals is of a hot complexion; its own qualities are moisture and heat. Hence, it maintains a harmony with the Air, and the philosophers understand Mercury itself to be under the element of Air because of the great affinity it holds with it. It is by nature fugitive <note>volatile or easily evaporated</note>, both spiritual and corporeal, like saltpeter <note>Latin: nitrum</note>, to which it is especially devoted above others, like fire or spirit. Mercury has much Sulfur but nothing of Salt; it is specifically assigned to the lungs because of the element of Air, which the lungs cannot do without. Mercury, like a spirit, pervades and penetrates both other principles—namely *Salt* and *Sulfur*, or rather the *body* and the *soul*—which it joins together through natural heat and constantly binds.

2. The philosophers call Mercury the medium for joining the soul with the body; for it carries the soul in its belly and dissolves the body so that the soul can dwell and take delight in it. Besides this penetrability and other properties, it is of a dissolving nature because of its radical moisture <note>the essential fluid or "life-grease" believed to sustain living beings</note>, and it is uniquely to be used in infirmities that draw their origin from viscous tartar <note>a term for stony or hardened metabolic deposits in the body</note>. By no means can the vital spirit or mercury, which for the most part sustains itself near the heart, be without this sulfur, because the heat of nature is fostered and nourished by this sulfur. And just as a material fire is strengthened, sustained, and grows powerful by the application of wood, it happens in no different a way with our intrinsic fire.

### Chapter Seven.

### *On the property of the third principle, namely Salt.*

1. Salt is the preservation, constancy, and hardening of all things; it alone preserves against corruption. For this reason, nature has joined it as a companion and protector to all fixed <term>elementated things</term> <note>Objects composed of the four elements</note> or constant created beings. It is the most constant fiery principle of all, which must preserve the other *two* <note>Sulfur and Mercury</note> in their being and state, and it is of an earthy nature.

2. The "Earth of the Wise" is salt, which alone is indestructible, incombustible, and unconquerable. Because of its most powerful and excellent virtues, the ancient philosophers likened Salt to the divine majesty, ascribed to it a certain divine power, and even called it <term>Electrum</term> <note>A precious natural alloy of gold and silver, here used metaphorically for a high spiritual substance</note>. Unless God, the <term>Physiarcha</term> <note>The Ruler of Nature</note>, had ordained this principle as a safeguard for the two weaker principles—sulfur and mercury—His creation would have had to perish and be reduced, as it were, to nothing. It is the radical truth itself; unless Almighty God had created salt, the <term>Philosophers' Stone</term> <note>The legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold and acting as an elixir of life</note> could never be made: for salt alone performs the preservation and <term>fixation</term> <note>The process of making a volatile substance stable in fire</note> of every thing. It is most notably detected in the blood of men and in the bladder.

3. The salt of all metals is their <term>malleability</term> <note>The ability to be hammered or pressed into shape without breaking</note>, and it is due to a lack of salt that they are non-malleable; <term>Saturn</term> <note>The alchemical name for Lead</note> proves this, as it is for the most part salt, as its <term>calcination</term> <note>Reduction to powder by heat</note> testifies. The salt of metals is a truly sublime medicine: whatever mercury and sulfur provide in medicine, Salt attempts to improve and strives to surpass. This happens because it melts more easily and spreads itself out, and thus preserves the human sulfur and vital spirit, defending them against all diseases.

->Chapter Eight.<-

### Whether the Universal Medicine is to be found in the seven stars—that is, in the seven metals—or truly in gold and the "prime matter"?

<margin>1.</margin> All philosophers who, before now and up to this very day, have written concerning the Universal Medicine <note>The *Medicina Universalis*, a legendary alchemical substance capable of curing all diseases and perfecting base metals.</note> and the prime matter <note>original: *materia prima*; the formless primal substance from which all things are created.</note>, are not only of clashing and repugnant opinions, but are also so obscure that no foundation can be established in their discourse. For at times they intend common Mercury and Saturn <note>In alchemical code, Saturn refers to the metal lead.</note>, while immediately after they seem to signify saltpeter or vitriol alone. They also use these or those names for themselves, even when they understand something far different. There have been very few philosophers who did not always introduce and describe the matter metaphorically or otherwise by some involved path. Indeed, they treat more fully the medicinal virtue, power, and efficacy than anything regarding the thing itself. Thus, it is no wonder that we can hardly distinguish it well, or know where we might find it, or how—once we have knowledge of the matter, without which nothing can be accomplished—we ought to proceed most briefly and certainly. Hence it is said, *for concealing the matter, they have revealed only the effect.* I, however, am going to give here as open and certain a demonstration as has ever been made before me. For I shall deal here most lucidly, not with the virtues, but more truly with the matter itself and how it is to be drawn into medicine, using common words and a simple style; this is because almost all philosophical books overflow with the proclamations of titles, yet concerning the matter, there has been great doubt until now.

<margin>2.</margin> Therefore, I commend to you again, under the seal of your conscience, that our matter is to be compared to the whole world and the entire globe of the earth, namely as far as its virtues are concerned. For it is the attractive force <note>original: *vis attractiva*</note> of all mineral and metallic things, because the *Soul*, or *Spirit*

### Chapter Eleven.

## On the nature and properties of Mars, or iron.

The philosophers say, *He who is ignorant of Mars, knows nothing of the Art* <note>original: "Qui ignorat Martem, non novit Artem"</note>, that is, he who does not know or recognize the qualities of iron is no craftsman. Furthermore, he who does not know how Mars—through that which lies hidden within itself—is to be destroyed and likewise reduced back into its own "first matter," will be able to bring little aid through his chemical stratagems to that invincible martial leader of war in his time of greatest necessity.

2. Mars <term>Mars: the alchemical name for Iron</term> possesses a solar, hot sulfur; on the outside it appears *white*, but truly on the inside it is *red*. Its Salt has been so ripened and animated by its own sulfur that it gives much trouble even to that fleeting thief, namely Mercury. For the Salt of Mars is able to constantly coagulate and fix Mercury, especially when ancient Saturn <term>Saturn: the alchemical name for Lead</term> comes to its aid, armed with his double sword and weapons. Without Saturn's help and assistance, Mars will be able to accomplish nothing difficult or heroic against his enemies, nor in favor of his friends. This is for the reason that coagulation (as all philosophers testify along with me) is found to occur only in Saturn. However, I have indicated somewhat above by what path the stubborn Mars may reach a balance and a treaty with this Saturn, and how he may make himself a sharer in Saturn's help. For it is necessary that Mars first be reduced to its three principles, and this is done through *Magical fires*, which are the philosophical elements and the keys to salvation. Therefore, see that you grasp my meaning skillfully; reread my writings often, until you have firmly fixed a fundamental understanding in your mind. This cannot and will not happen if you imagine that I am using a "buskined" or overly-theatrical philosophical style <note>original: "cothurnico-philosophicum"; referring to the high boots worn by ancient tragic actors, implying a pompous or deceptive tone</note>. Just as I have described and depicted these things for you, so they shall always stand before your eyes in no other form, appearance, or figure, like a beautiful painting.

### Chapter Thirteen.

## *On the nature and property of Venus, or copper.*

1. Lascivious Venus <note>In alchemy, Venus is the traditional name for the metal copper.</note> possesses a body that is entirely earthly, which is filled with a certain sublime solar sulfur; however, because of the weakness of the bones and the infirmity of its impure dwelling-place, this sulfur could not establish a stable residence therein. When the body must be destroyed, the soul departs and deserts its habitation. Whoever now knows how to nourish and preserve this soul through *Magical* elements in the fire, and afterwards extract it from the calcined body, has obtained the true meaning of this little book, for he will be able to rejoice in the light that shines for him. This sulfur, with which Venus is clothed, far surpasses the solar sulfur in its color, because the sulfur of the sun is notably improved by the sulfur of Venus. For just as the true sun <note>The "sun" here refers to gold.</note> nourishes itself with the blood of the *green lion* <note>term: green lion (vitriol or raw ore used as a solvent)</note>, and thus becomes entirely blood-red and ignited; in the same way, gold also delights in, feeds upon, and strengthens itself with the tincture of Venus and Mars. ### Chapter Fourteen.
### *On the nature and property of the fugitive Mercury.*

1. The ancient Philosophers placed Mercury only at the second table of honor, which is greatly to be wondered at, since Mercury is by nature noble and proud, and raises himself above all the stars to denote that his seat ought by right to be higher, and that the supreme honor is due to him; seeing as the highest secret of human health is to be found within him. Furthermore, he is companionable to all the stars on account of his astral seed <note>The "astral seed" refers to the celestial influence or life-force that permeates minerals</note>, and whichever planet he joins himself with is strengthened in its own position: thus, if that planet be malicious, this one is rendered even more malicious; but if it be benign, then that one is improved through the union with Mercury and strengthened in its purpose. In short, Mercury is like a neutral and political man who willingly offends no one but pleases everyone. Otherwise, he is by nature hot and fiery in his entire being. The metallic fire is so effective within Mercury that his body must remain in a state of continuous flux <note>original: "continuo fluxu"; referring to the liquid state of quicksilver at room temperature</note>.

2. And although this Mercury has many virtuous medicinal faculties and powers within himself, he is indeed still far from being the Mercury of the Philosophers <term>Mercury of the Philosophers: a sophisticated alchemical substance, distinct from common quicksilver, believed to be the "soul" of metals</term>: for the Mercury of the Philosophers is the Mercury of metals, which is never [merely] hot and cold, or dry and hot, etc. This is because it embraces within itself the qualities of the four elements; common Mercury, however, is hot in its entire being, therefore it cannot be the Mercury of the philosophers. And although this is so, one must not for that reason despise or reject it, since the ancient Sages always held it in high and sublime regard, seeing as they adorned it with the moon and marked it with the sun in place of a well-earned crown.

### Chapter Fifteen.

## On the Phlegmatic Nature and Property of the Moon.

1. The Moon exercises her astral influence, by the aid of cold Saturn, upon the mineral of silver, which serves as a receptacle for lunar faculties and further communicates its goodness to mortals. And just as the Moon holds her influence over silver and specifically demonstrates her operation within it, so too does she govern the brain within the microcosm <note>The "microcosm" refers to the human body, viewed as a miniature reflection of the entire universe or "macrocosm."</note>; hence it follows that the "lower Moon"—namely, silver prepared for this purpose—may fundamentally heal all defects of the brain. This is because this faculty was communicated to the silver by the "upper Moon"; for that which is below is like that which is above, and so forth. <note>A reference to the famous Hermetic maxim from the Emerald Tablet: "As above, so below."</note> And while the upper Moon is hindered in her benign operations by other contrary aspects <note>In astrology, an "aspect" is the angle planets make to each other, which can be harmonious or discordant.</note> which stand in opposition to the Moon—wishing to effect something other than what the Moon intends, or otherwise seeking to infect her—then by this means not only is the lower Moon (as the receptacle of the superior virtue) weakened in its spirit and its operation impeded, but the human brain also suffers accordingly, following the nature of the superior infection. Thus arises a kind of astral disease by which the microcosm is afflicted; these infirmities can scarcely be cured in the common way through vegetables <note>Plant-based medicines.</note>, since they are situated in a lower and unequal grade. For these reasons, we must take up such a medicine for this purpose that persists in a more sublime grade, or at the very least, in the same grade as the affliction; for example:

2. If the Moon is infected and suppressed by very wicked, poisonous, and opposing planets, the human brain, as its receptacle, is then weakened or infected. ### Chapter Sixteen.

### *On the nature and properties of gemstones.*
### *Namely, how they are to be reduced to the sublime medicine through the Philosophers' Universal Solvent?*

1. Gemstones have their beginning and origin from the astral "first mover" <note>The *Primum Mobile*, or the outermost sphere of the heavens in classical astronomy</note>, just as both the highest and lowest metals do. For this reason, gemstones correspond in their colors, sulfurs, and other properties with the seven stars above <note>the planets</note> and below <note>the metals associated with them</note>. They perform their work only after they have first been unloaded of their earthly chains and the bundles of the earthly curse, and have passed away into the three principles <note>Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury</note>, which is achieved through the Universal Solvent <term>Menstruum Universale: a powerful liquid capable of dissolving solid matter into its spiritual essence</term>. The same solvent that dissolves metals into sulfur and salt must also be employed for the extraction of the gemstones' colors and salt, since all things were brought into a certain body by the one *spirit of the world* <note>original: "spiritus mundi"</note>. This *spirit* is the Universal Solvent, in which there is a certain attractive power for all things, both mineral and metallic; it is called by Basil <note>likely referring to the alchemist Basil Valentine</note> "*All in All*." Believe me, that the *spirit of the Earth* must lead its sulfur out of the earth and back into the earth again; hence, in this *spirit* lies the supreme secret of the entire chemical science. Without this *spirit*, we would not have been able to notice the goodness of our Creator within gemstones.

2. And so that you do not overlook the medicine which is found in gemstones, know that every one of the gems has its own star from which it receives its power and operation, just as metals do. Whatever metallic medicines accomplish in the seven principal members of humans, gemstones likewise effect. For the Garnet <note>original: "Granatus"</note>, if it is of the sidereal influence of Saturn under its angel Orphiel <note>In esoteric tradition, Orphiel is the angel governing the planet Saturn</note>, heals ailments of the spleen, just as lead does, because both hold a single star which flows its nature from above to below. From this it follows that minerals, vegetables, and even some animals of a single kind possess the same virtue.

### *Concerning the medicine of Vegetables and Animals, which manifests itself in those two kingdoms, and sympathetically relates to the primary medicine.*

I. We say, and it is true: *Man, wine, and gold are benevolent toward one another.* Wine possesses an effective, strengthening Spirit with which it can refresh the heart of man. Wine revives the spirit in the elderly, which otherwise lies buried so deeply within them—as if dead—that we cannot even perceive it; but truly, when wine is drunk by men and has made a certain conjunction with the animal and vegetable spirit, the vital spirit—namely, Mercury <note>In this context, Mercury refers to the "vital principle" or quicksilver of life, not just the liquid metal</note>—is excited by this and expanded through the entire body, so that all the limbs perceive it and are moved by it. It possesses such a friendship, like a certain burning sulfur with metallic sulfur, from which it follows that no Potable Gold can be made without it. The spirit of mercury extracts the tincture from the sulfur of the sun <note>The "sulfur of the sun" refers to the essential soul or essence of Gold</note> as the innermost part of the soul, while the spirit of wine extracts the innermost from these innermost parts, because there the dregs—which are not to be introduced or drawn into the tincture—separate themselves again. The tincture is a dry sulfur, which is dissolved by the Mercury of the Philosophers and unites itself with it so that the solute cannot be [separated] from the solvent...

In memory of what has been discussed, I shall add to the conclusion of this small book a very brief repetition concerning the *Magical* elements, the Universal Medicine—or truly irreducible Potable Gold <note>Latin: "Auro Potabili"; a legendary liquid medicine refined from gold believed to grant longevity</note>—and the Universal Solvent <note>Latin: "Menstruo Universali"; the "Alkahest" or substance capable of dissolving all others</note> through which this must be so sublimely prepared. For that reason, deign to pay sole attention, because in this summary I shall place the entire kernel, plainly and fully stripped of its husk, most clearly before your eyes.

### Chapter Seventeen.

->*Concerning the medicine of Vegetables and Animals, which manifests itself in those two kingdoms, and relates sympathetically to the primary medicine.*<-

1. We say, and it is true, that *Man, wine, and gold are mutually benevolent to one another.* Wine possesses an effective, strengthening Spirit with which it can refresh the heart of man. Wine revives the spirit in the elderly, which otherwise lies buried so deeply within them—as if dead—that we cannot even perceive it. But when wine, drunk by men, has formed a certain conjunction with the animal and vegetable spirit, the vital spirit—namely, Mercury <note>In this context, Mercury refers to the "vital principle" or quickening force within the body, not just the liquid metal</note>—is excited by this and dilated through the entire body, so that all the limbs perceive it and are enabled to move themselves. Mercury governs the microcosm <note>The human body, viewed as a miniature reflection of the entire universe</note>, and wine is the vehicle of both universal and particular medicine. What is more, the spirit of wine <note>Alcohol or distilled essence</note> is not only a vegetable solvent, but also a mineral one. It possesses such a friendship as a certain burning sulfur has with metallic sulfur; from this it follows that no Potable Gold can be made without it. The spirit of mercury extracts the tincture from the sulfur of the sun <note>The "sulfur of the sun" refers to the essential soul or color of gold</note> as the innermost part of the soul; the spirit of wine, however, extracts the innermost from these innermost parts, because there the dregs—which are not to be introduced nor drawn into the tincture—separate themselves once again. The tincture is a dry sulfur, which is dissolved by the Mercury of the Philosophers <note>A specialized alchemical substance, distinct from common quicksilver</note>, and unites itself with it so that the solute cannot be separated from the solvent.

Thus, in the Mummy <note>original: "Mumia"; in alchemy, this refers to the vital life force or "balsam" preserved in a body, rather than a literal Egyptian mummy</note>—that is to say, in the human heart—the supreme medicine for our health is certainly to be found. However, because it is not always possible to have a fresh human heart available for use in medicine, it is appropriate to use that which is closest to the heart in its place, or otherwise to prepare specific remedies and cure "like with like" <note>original: "simile sibi simili curare"; a foundational principle of early medicine and homeopathy</note>. Yet, through this specific method, we are not as secure as we are through the Universal Medicine. This is because physicians do not always agree in their judgment, and they touch upon the cause and foundation of an illness only very rarely. Furthermore, several members of the body often labor and fall ill at once, and what is suitable for one is sometimes harmful to another. In the Universal Medicine, however, this is not to be feared at all; for in the heart, in gold, and in wine, all the virtues of animals, minerals, and vegetables are gathered into one. All these exist for the solace and utility of the human race, which can congratulate itself highly for this and give thanks from the bottom of its heart to God, the Creator of all things, for this most excellent medicine.

5. To the Eternal Monarch of the Heavens be praise, honor, and glory for His grace, which He grants me in describing this little treatise of mine. It is published not out of vain reputation, but only because I see that through various and diverse lengthy philosophical writings, the world has fallen into such error and sedition that it is lamentable to behold. Many people torment and torture themselves in vain, seeking where there is nothing, squandering not only their wealth but also irreparable time, and yet discovering nothing. Therefore, it is right that someone should hasten here with the material and the key <note>the "key" refers to the secret knowledge required to unlock alchemical mysteries</note> before the whole world collapses into error and the honest men themselves despair. To these men, I pray for temporal fortune and everlasting salvation. For the rest, I commend my Commentary to God, the most superabundant fountain of all sciences, who will give its honest meaning and understanding to whomsoever He wishes in His own time, *Amen*. It remains true, therefore, that *Man, wine, and gold love one another.*
